docs.title: LunCoSim Documentation
docs.text:
An open-source workbench for authoring, simulating, and operating space missions with USD, Modelica, and Rhai.

Document version0.1 Release dateNovember 2026 LunCoSim version0.6.0-dev LunCoSim source commitc84fba03ae41c1c48548485e0effd8c152b3621d Applies toLunCoSim desktop and browser builds StatusLiving document; updated with each release LicenseOpen source; see the repository for details

Abstract. LunCoSim combines a composed OpenUSD scene, continuous Modelica models, and discrete Rhai mission policy into one running simulation. This document describes the project model, the authoring workflow, the runtime contracts that connect the three formats, and the evidence required before a result is trusted. It is written for engineers, mission designers, educators, and tool integrators who need to understand both what to author and why the runtime behaves as it does.

Contents

  1. General — purpose, installation, first run, perspectives, Twins, and the format boundaries.
  2. Tutorials — guided lessons from a first drive to a validated, shareable Twin.
  3. USD — scene composition, physics, typed ports, programs, materials, and asset addressing.
  4. Modelica — continuous behavior, cosimulation, the Lunica workbench, libraries, and experiments.
  5. Rhai — scenario lifecycle, task trees, commands, events, tests, and reusable policy patterns.
  6. Shaders — WESL material parameters, texture layers, USD material binding, terrain rendering, and quality budgets.
  7. UI & Settings — global and project settings, HUD surfaces, theming, and runtime-authored UI.
  8. Reference — command line, controls, manifests, file formats, HTTP API, mission control, validation, and troubleshooting.
The authored formats and the runtime that projects them into a live world. Each fact has one owner.

docs.title: About this document
docs.text:
This guide documents the behavior of the shipped application and the contracts an author can rely on. Where a capability is partial, experimental, or limited to one platform, the limitation is stated in the relevant section rather than implied by silence.

The documentation follows the same ownership rule as the software:

  • USD owns scene structure, geometry, materials, physics schemas, and typed connections.
  • Modelica owns continuous equations and state.
  • Rhai owns events, commands, mission sequencing, and authored verdicts.
  • TOML owns project and asset configuration.
  • The runtime owns projection, scheduling, physics integration, and rendering.

A reader who remembers only one rule should remember this one: do not reimplement a fact in a second layer. A wheel position belongs in USD, a motor curve in Modelica, a waypoint mission in Rhai, and a download declaration in Assets.toml.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Convention Meaning Bold A user-interface label, a perspective name, or a term defined in the glossary. Monospace A file name, command, attribute, property, or literal value. > A menu path, for example File → Open Twin…. Note boxes A constraint, a platform limitation, or a warning about a common mistake. Code blocks Authored source or a command to run. Shell blocks use a POSIX shell unless marked otherwise. Version numbers LunCoSim is under active development; command and schema details can change between releases.

Paths in this document use forward slashes. On Windows, substitute the platform separator where the application accepts a native path. Logical asset addresses such as lunco:// and twin:// always use forward slashes.

docs.title: How to use this document
docs.text: A new user should read Installation, run First mission, and then read How it fits together. An author who already knows the workbench can go directly to the format chapter for the layer being edited. An integrator should start with Integrate your stack and the HTTP API. An instructor should read the Tutorials overview and the lesson descriptions before using the classroom track.

docs.title: Current status
docs.text:
LunCoSim is under active development. Model coverage, platform support, and tool maturity vary. A successful build, a clean parse, or a green scene test is evidence about a specific claim; none of them is a general accuracy certificate. The Validation chapter explains how to separate preflight, runtime behavior, requirement coverage, and physical accuracy.

Release builds and notes are published on the GitHub releases page. Community links are in the site footer.

docs.title: General
docs.text: This part introduces LunCoSim as a system: what it is for, how it is installed, how the workbench is organized, and which format owns which fact. It is the part to read before authoring a project. The remaining chapters assume the vocabulary and ownership rules established here.

docs.title: Purpose of this part
docs.text:
A LunCoSim project is a folder of ordinary domain files — USD, Modelica, Rhai, SysML, and TOML — that the runtime composes into a live world. The first task of the documentation is therefore to explain the boundaries between those files before explaining the tools that edit them.

The chapters in this part answer four questions:

  1. What problem does LunCoSim solve, and what does it deliberately not solve?
  2. How is the application installed, launched, and navigated?
  3. What is a Twin, and how does it differ from a folder or a single file?
  4. How do the authored formats and the runtime interact?

docs.title: The system in one page
docs.text:
The runtime opens a Twin, resolves its manifest, composes the default USD stage, admits Modelica participants and Rhai programs, and then advances a fixed simulation clock. The UI, the HTTP API, and scripts all use the same typed command and query surface. Rendering observes the resulting state; it does not own it.

Layer Owns Typical file Manifest Project identity, entry scene, search roots, project settings twin.toml Scene Hierarchy, transforms, geometry, materials, physics, ports, connections .usda, .usdc Behavior Continuous equations, state, and physical conservation laws .mo Policy Events, commands, mission phases, tutorial flow, test verdicts .rhai Assets External bytes such as libraries, rasters, textures, and fonts Assets.toml Runtime Projection, scheduling, physics, rendering, and the command bridge Rust / Avian

The rule that makes this decomposition useful is one fact, one owner. When the same value is authored twice, the copies eventually disagree, and the disagreement is usually discovered only after a mission has been tuned around the wrong one.

docs.title: Reading paths
docs.text:
The part is written so that it can be read linearly, but not every reader needs every chapter.

Reader Recommended path New user Installation → First run → First mission Project author Twins → How it fits together → the format chapter for the layer being edited Tool integrator Integrate your stack → HTTP API → Mission control Instructor Tutorials → First mission → Validate and share Contributor How it fits together → USD → Modelica → Rhai

docs.title: What the reader is expected to know
docs.text:
The documentation assumes familiarity with a 3D content tool, a text editor, and the idea of a simulation model. It does not assume prior knowledge of OpenUSD, Modelica, or Rhai; each format chapter introduces the subset LunCoSim uses and points to the upstream standard for the full language.

Some chapters use vector arithmetic and basic control concepts. A reader who has tuned a PID controller or assembled a jointed mechanism will recognize the examples. A reader who has not can still follow the workflow; the examples state the intended behavior before showing the source.

docs.title: Scope and status
docs.text:
LunCoSim is a workbench, not a certified analysis tool. The documentation distinguishes three kinds of statement:

  • Contract. A behavior the runtime enforces, such as rejecting a force connection from a program that is not declared realtime-safe.
  • Convention. A recommended authoring pattern that the runtime does not enforce, such as keeping mission decisions out of Modelica.
  • Limitation. A capability that is partial, platform-specific, or not shipped, such as native FMI import being unavailable in the browser build.

Read the limitation notes before planning a workflow around a feature. The Validation chapter explains how to turn a successful run into evidence and how to state what that evidence does not prove.

docs.title: First run
docs.text: When LunCoSim opens, you are looking at a workbench, not a single fixed editor. The same Twin can be viewed as a running mission, a scene assembly, a graph dashboard, a USD document, or a Modelica model. The first run is about learning where those views are and how to open a working scene.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
Area What it does Title bar File, Edit, View, Window, and Help menus; command palette; transport; perspective tabs Viewport The live 3D scene, selection, camera, and ground interaction Side panels Twin files, Entity tree, Inspector, Environment, Spawn, Telemetry, Ports Bottom dock Graphs, timelines, logs, and document tabs Status bar Update notices, simulation state, and transient messages

The exact panels depend on the active perspective. View → Reset Layout restores the authored default for the current task.

The View perspective with the First Drive sandbox open. Panels and tabs change when you switch perspectives.

docs.title: Perspectives
docs.text:
Choose a perspective from the title bar or View → Perspectives:

Perspective Use it for ◉ View Operating the live mission in a full-window scene ⚒ Build Composing the scene from assemblies, entities, and the Twin's files ↗ Analyze Comparing signals in Graphs, with Telemetry and Ports ✎ Editor Editing one explicit USD document in an isolated preview ∿ Lunica Modelica text, diagrams, compilation, and experiments

Switching perspectives preserves the Twin and the simulation. You are changing the layout and the visible tools, not restarting the world.

For a detailed tour of each task and its controls, see Perspectives.

docs.title: Open the tutorial catalog
docs.text:
The authored lesson catalog is under Scenarios → Tutorials. Tracks include Start Here, LunCoSim, How It Works, Navigation, Sandbox, Rover Driving, and Modelica.

Each entry is a tour, an exercise, or a challenge:

  • A tour explains where things are. It advances with Next and Back and does not certify that you performed an action.
  • An exercise advances only when the simulation observes the requested result.
  • A challenge is a longer open-ended task.

Selecting a lesson loads its authored scene when the lesson needs one, then starts the lesson's Rhai scenario. This is the easiest way to see a working Twin without building one first.

docs.title: First five minutes
docs.text:
1. Open Scenarios → Tutorials → Start Here → Lunar Rover Lab for the full 30-minute classroom exercise, or Scenarios → Tutorials → Sandbox → First Drive for a five-minute rover drive.
  2. Wait for the scene and the lesson card to settle. The viewport shows the practice yard; the card explains the current step.
  3. Click Take control. Selection is not control: you must claim the rover before your input reaches it.
  4. Drive with the displayed bindings. The defaults are W/S for forward and reverse, A/D to steer, and Space to brake. The lesson uses input_hint(...), so it always shows the bindings currently configured on your machine.
  5. Follow the on-screen objective. When you reach the marker, stop inside it. The lesson checks the simulation state, not a timer.

If the rover rolls over, use Right rover. If you lose the view, use Return camera. Both actions preserve lesson progress.

docs.title: The empty viewport
docs.text:
A new session may start with an empty persistent world shell. That is expected: the sandbox is an explicit scene or lesson, not an implicit startup default. Use the viewport actions to open the featured lesson, choose a recent Twin, or open a scene from the Twin browser.

A Twin without default_scene opens as a file browser rather than mounting a world. That is also expected; the manifest has not selected a stage. See Twins and twin.toml.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text: Symptom Check The vehicle ignores your input Click Take control first; selection is not control. The viewport is empty Open a scene or lesson; a Twin with no default_scene does not mount a world. An asset is missing LunCoSim asks before downloading declared external assets. See Assets.toml. The app will not start on a port Choose another free --api port. A lesson card does not advance Read the current objective; an exercise waits for the simulation, not for a click.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Continue with First mission for the suggested learning path, or read How it fits together to understand what the lesson is doing behind the scenes. For the complete keyboard and camera reference, see Controls.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text: LunCoSim uses four core authored formats, one optional requirements format, and one external asset format. Each format has a different job, a different editing tool, and a different runtime consumer. Understanding the division is more important than memorizing the syntax of any one of them.

docs.title: The authored formats
docs.text:
Format File types Owns Edited in USD .usda, .usdc Hierarchy, transforms, geometry, materials, physics, typed ports, connections, program attachments Build, Editor, or an external USD tool Modelica .mo Continuous equations, state, parameters, acausal connectors Lunica or an external Modelica editor Rhai .rhai Events, commands, tasks, objectives, tutorial flow, test verdicts A text editor, the Rhai editor, or the REPL TOML twin.toml, Assets.toml Project identity, entry scene, source roots, settings, external asset declarations A text editor or the Twin settings panel SysML .sysml, .kerml Requirements, structure, and verification mappings A text editor; support is bounded

The first four are the core. SysML is optional and is described in Validation and Integrate your stack.

docs.title: The external asset format
docs.text:
glTF carries mesh geometry, materials, and a node hierarchy produced by a content tool. It is not a USD layer: USD composition does not parse .gltf or .glb. A USD prim points at the file with a payload or reference arc, and the renderer imports that file through the glTF loader.

Format File types Owns Produced in glTF .gltf, .glb Mesh geometry, materials, node hierarchy Blender or another content tool

The default lunco:assetMode = "scene" attaches the whole glTF scene and keeps its hierarchy, materials, and lights. lunco:assetMode = "mesh" attaches one mesh primitive as Mesh3d, which a mesh collider can consume. lunco:assetLabel selects a named sub-asset. See Addresses and assets.

docs.title: USD owns the world
docs.text:
A USD stage describes what exists and where it is. It contains the prim hierarchy, the transforms that place parts, the geometry that is rendered and collided, the materials that shade it, the physics schemas that make it move, and the typed inputs: and outputs: properties that connect it to other components.

USD does not contain the equations that decide how a motor responds to a throttle command. It may contain a reference to a Modelica source, but the source itself is a separate file. USD also does not decide when a mission is complete; that is Rhai policy.

docs.title: Modelica owns continuous behavior
docs.text:
A .mo file contains classes, equations, parameters, and connectors. The solver advances the equations over time. Modelica is the right place for a motor curve, a battery model, a thermal network, a control law, or a fluid system.

Modelica does not traverse the scene, find prims by name, or react to a keypress. It exposes inputs and outputs; the USD wiring decides what those values connect to, and Rhai decides when a mission phase changes.

docs.title: Rhai owns discrete policy
docs.text:
A .rhai file is a program attached to an entity. It observes the simulation, reacts to events, issues typed commands, advances a task tree, and publishes objectives or verdicts. It is the right place for a waypoint sequence, a tutorial step, an authority handoff, or a test assertion.

Rhai does not integrate physics or replace a controller. A per-tick script loop that reimplements a solver duplicates the runtime and makes the scenario less deterministic.

docs.title: TOML owns configuration
docs.text:
twin.toml identifies the project, selects the default scene, declares the Modelica and SysML source roots, and stores project settings. Assets.toml declares external bytes such as libraries, rasters, textures, and fonts.

TOML does not contain geometry or equations. It is a manifest, not a scene file and not a cache. The actual downloaded bytes live in a cache addressed through logical URIs.

docs.title: How a change travels
docs.text:
A typical edit crosses several layers. Consider changing the rover's drive behavior:

  1. The author edits Drive.mo in Lunica and compiles it.
  2. The Twin's [modelica].paths makes the source discoverable.
  3. A USD program prim names the source with info:sourceAsset.
  4. The component's outputs: properties expose the values other components may consume.
  5. A connection on the consuming prim names the source port.
  6. The runtime admits the participant, samples outputs at communication points, and applies the resulting forces.
  7. Rhai observes the motion and decides whether the mission objective is met.

At no point does the author copy the motor equation into USD or the waypoint list into Modelica. Each file keeps its own fact.

docs.title: Choosing the right format
docs.text:
Use the following questions as a guide:

Question Format Where is the part, how is it shaped, and how is it attached? USD Which mesh or scene did a content tool export? glTF, referenced from USD What equations govern its continuous behavior? Modelica What should happen when a condition becomes true? Rhai Which scene opens, and where are the sources? twin.toml Where does the terrain raster or library come from? Assets.toml Which requirement does this test verify? SysML plus a Twin verification mapping

If a fact seems to belong in two places, the usual answer is that one place owns the data and the other owns a reference to it. A USD connection owns the wire; the Modelica class owns the equation that produces the value. A Rhai scenario owns the mission decision; USD owns the marker prim the decision refers to.

docs.title: Portability
docs.text:
The domain files remain in their standard syntax. A .mo file can be opened in another Modelica tool, a .usda file can be opened in another USD application, and a .gltf or .glb file can be opened in any glTF viewer. LunCoSim-specific behavior is carried in:

  • LunCoProgramAPI and related program attributes;
  • typed inputs: / outputs: properties and USD connections;
  • lunco:// and twin:// asset addresses;
  • the twin.toml manifest and its settings table;
  • LunCoSim schema extensions such as lunco:suspension:restLength.

A file that uses these extensions is still a valid file in its base format, but another tool will not interpret the extensions. That is expected: the extensions are the workbench's contract, not a replacement for the standard.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not encode equations in USD attributes.
  • Do not put mission decisions or timers in Modelica.
  • Do not integrate physics in Rhai.
  • Do not treat a .gltf or .glb file as a USD layer; reference it from USD and let the renderer import it.
  • Do not hardcode a cache path in a USD layer; use lunco:// or twin://.
  • Do not add a Rust special case for a particular rover, lesson, or asset.
  • Do not hand-edit generated or cached assets; author the source and let the pipeline produce the result.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: This glossary defines the terms as they are used in this document. Where a term has a broader meaning in another standard, the definition here is the LunCoSim-specific one.

docs.title: A–C
docs.text:
Asset address. A logical URI that names bytes managed by the asset system. lunco:// addresses the installed engine library; twin:// addresses a file inside the open Twin. Authored files should not use physical cache paths.

Authority. The right to write a control input or structural fact. Selection is not authority. A session must claim an endpoint before its input reaches it.

Avian. The rigid-body physics engine used by the LunCoSim runtime. Avian integrates bodies and joints; it is not where a particular rover or mission is authored.

Build. The perspective used to compose the live scene from assemblies and entities. It edits the running world, not an isolated document.

Communication point. A simulation time at which Modelica participants exchange inputs and outputs. Values are held between communication points.

Composition arc. A USD relationship that combines layers or prims: subLayers, references, payloads, inherits, specializes, and variants.

Connection. An authored USD relationship that carries a value from an outputs: property to an inputs: property. The runtime derives a SimConnection from it.

Cosimulation. Running two or more participants together on a shared clock, exchanging values at communication points. LunCoSim uses the term for the Modelica-to-physics loop and for the broader participant fabric.

docs.title: D–H
docs.text:
Default prim. The root prim a USD stage declares as its reference target. LunCoSim uses it as a stable root for composition and projection.

Dock panel. A workbench panel placed in a dock rectangle. Runtime UI surfaces can align to a dock panel but do not own the dock tree.

Editor. The perspective that opens one explicit USD document in an isolated preview. Saving and undo apply to that document, not to the live scene.

Entity. A runtime object projected from the composed scene. An entity has a stable identity, a name, components, and possibly ports. The entity tree is a runtime view, not the authored prim hierarchy.

Exposure. A typed, named snapshot published by an engine producer for presentation consumers. Runtime UI templates and API readers consume exposures; they do not query ECS state directly.

Fixed step. A simulation update at a deterministic interval. The task kernel, physics, and realtime-safe Modelica programs advance on fixed steps.

FMU. A Functional Mock-up Unit packaged for FMI. LunCoSim can import FMI 3.0 Co-Simulation FMUs with scalar Float64 ports on desktop builds.

glTF. An external mesh and scene format. A .gltf or .glb file is referenced from a USD payload or reference and loaded by the glTF importer; it is not a USD layer.

HUD. A heads-up display surface over the viewport. LunCoSim has both workbench HUDs (graphs, performance, input overlay) and authored runtime surfaces (rover, camera, terrain progress).

docs.title: I–M
docs.text:
Input hold. A live value written to a port by a session. It overrides the authored source until released. SetPorts creates a hold; ReleasePort and ReleaseControl remove it.

Lunica. The Modelica perspective and workbench. It provides the model browser, diagram, text editor, compile and run controls, plots, and experiments.

Manifest. twin.toml, the file that makes a folder a Twin. It declares the project identity, entry scene, source roots, and settings.

Modelica participant. A compiled Modelica class admitted into the running simulation. It has typed inputs and outputs and advances at communication points.

Modelica source root. A directory declared in [modelica].paths where the compiler looks for .mo sources.

docs.title: N–R
docs.text:
OpenUSD. The scene description and composition standard used for the world. LunCoSim uses standard USD physics schemas and a small set of LunCoSim schema extensions.

Perspective. A task layout over the same Twin. The five main layouts are View, Build, Analyze, Editor, and Lunica.

Port. A typed scalar input or output at a component boundary. A port has a name, direction, kind, and owner. Ports are the vocabulary of the connection fabric.

Prim. A node in a USD stage. A prim can carry schemas, attributes, relationships, and children.

Program. A Modelica model or Rhai scenario attached to a prim through LunCoProgramAPI. The program is a child prim, so deleting the prim removes the behavior.

Projection. The runtime process that turns a composed USD stage into live entities, components, physics bodies, and renderable objects.

Realtime-safe. A declaration (lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true) that a program may drive force or torque ports on a client-predicted body. It is a promise that the program is fixed-step deterministic, not a quality rating.

Rhai. The embedded scripting language used for scenario policy, tutorial flow, and authored tests.

Rumoca. The Modelica compiler and runtime used by LunCoSim. It parses, type-checks, compiles, and integrates the authored models.

docs.title: S–Z
docs.text:
Scene test. A headless, deterministic run of an authored Rhai observer against a scene. The exit code is the verdict: 0 pass, 1 fail, 2 no verdict.

Shader look. A material intent that names a WESL source, parameter values, and texture layers. It is projected from an authored USD material or created by a tool.

SimConnection. The runtime representation of an authored USD connection. It carries a typed value from a producer to a consumer at a communication point.

Stage. A composed USD scene. The stage is inert until the runtime projects it.

SysML. The requirements and systems-modeling language used for optional requirement and verification mappings. Support is bounded to scalar constraints and authored observations.

Texture layer. A named raster role a shader can sample: Height, Albedo, Mineral, Surface, Normal, ShadowCache, and related roles. Texture slots are the scarce resource; scalar layers should usually share a packed channel.

Twin. A project folder containing twin.toml. It is the unit of saving, versioning, sharing, and opening.

Typed command. A write operation with a reflected name and validated parameters. The UI, Rhai, and HTTP API use the same command surface.

Typed query. A read operation with a reflected name and typed result. A missing value is not silently replaced with zero.

USD. See OpenUSD.

Verdict. The typed result a test scenario publishes. A test that ends without a verdict is not a pass.

WESL. The shader source language used for LunCoSim materials. A WESL material declares its parameters in a struct Material block.

World hold. A runtime state in which simulation advancement is paused because required preparation is incomplete. A world hold is not a slow world.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
LunCoSim separates what the system is from how it behaves and what the operation does. Each layer has a standard format and a clear owner. The runtime composes those layers into one live world and gives every participant the same clock, identity, and command surface.

The authored layers and the runtime. The arrows indicate ownership and projection, not a one-way build pipeline.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
Layer Owns Does not own twin.toml Project identity, entry scene, search roots, settings Physical equations USD Parts, transforms, variants, materials, physics schemas, typed ports, connections Modelica state integration Modelica Continuous equations, energy and state balance, solved outputs Scene traversal or mission sequencing Rhai Events, commands, sequencing, authored test verdicts Continuous dynamics Assets.toml Declarations for external bytes: libraries, rasters, models, fonts Scene structure or runtime state Rust / Avian Generic projection, physics, scheduling, and engine mechanics A particular rover, mission, or lesson

The important rule is one fact, one owner. A wheel's position belongs in USD. A motor's torque curve belongs in Modelica. A waypoint mission belongs in Rhai. A downloaded terrain DEM belongs in Assets.toml and the asset cache.

docs.title: Runtime flow
docs.text:
The runtime loop. The UI observes and commands; it does not own domain state.

The sequence is easier to understand as a series of boundaries than as a pipeline:

  1. The Twin opens. twin.toml selects the default USD scene and the Modelica and SysML source roots.
  2. USD composition resolves sublayers, references, payloads, and variants into one composed stage.
  3. The runtime projects the composed stage into the live entity world: scene hierarchy, transforms, physics bodies, colliders, lights, cameras, and program attachments.
  4. Modelica participants are admitted. The fixed master clock advances them; outputs cross SimConnections at declared communication points.
  5. Physics applies forces and integrates the rigid bodies. Rhai scenarios receive events and issue typed commands through the same command and query API as the UI and HTTP API.
  6. The UI renders the current state. The UI does not mutate domain state directly; it sends commands to the owning layer.

A composed USD stage by itself is inert. It does not launch Modelica, run Rhai, apply physics, or render. The runtime is what projects the authored documents into a live world.

docs.title: A rover, layer by layer
docs.text:
A single vehicle demonstrates the division better than an abstract diagram. Consider a rover with a chassis, six wheels, a drive controller, and a waypoint mission.

Question File What it contains Where is the chassis, where are the wheels, how do they attach? USD Xform hierarchy, references, UsdPhysics bodies and joints What is the controller law? Modelica .mo equations for drive, steering, motor, or thermal behavior What should the mission do? Rhai task, mission, on_event, waypoints, commands, verdicts Where does the terrain DEM come from? Assets.toml URL, dest, optional sha256 and processing recipe Which scene opens? twin.toml [usd] default_scene

A complete drive loop can look like this:

USD                  Modelica                 Physics
wheels + joints  →   drive law + motor   →   forces + motion
      ↑                                           │
      └──────────── typed USD connections ─────────┘
                           │
                        Rhai policy
                 mission events and commands

The arrows are not a dataflow that the author programs. They are the consequence of the authored topology. The wheel joint is a USD fact. The motor equation is a Modelica fact. The connection is a USD fact. The runtime derives the scheduling order from the composed graph.

docs.title: Why the boundaries matter
docs.text:
The boundaries are not bureaucratic. Each one prevents a class of defect.

A single clock. Modelica participants, physics, and Rhai tasks advance on the same simulation timeline. If a script kept its own timer, two parts of the mission would disagree about when "ten seconds" had passed.

A single identity. A prim path, an entity id, and a port owner are related but not interchangeable. The runtime keeps the mapping explicit so a command cannot accidentally target a different rover after a scene reload.

A single authority. Selection, camera control, and input authority are separate. A script that holds a vehicle and a user who clicks Take control are resolved by the same authority rules, not by whichever system wrote last.

A single evidence trail. A scene test runs the authored observer against the production runtime. A parse check runs the same loaders without a window. A live lint sees the composed stage. Each layer reports what it can see and does not pretend to see more.

docs.title: What stays out of each layer
docs.text:
• Do not put mission decisions or timers in Modelica.
  • Do not integrate physics or reimplement a controller in Rhai.
  • Do not encode equations in USD attributes.
  • Do not add a Rust special case for a specific rover, lesson, or asset.
  • Do not hand-edit generated or cached assets; author the source and let the owning pipeline produce the result.
  • Do not duplicate a route, a limit, or a tuning constant in a lesson when the value is already authored in USD or Modelica.

docs.title: A worked boundary decision
docs.text:
Suppose a rover tips over on a slope. There are several tempting places to "fix" the behavior:

  • Lower the center of mass in the USD asset. This is a physical change and belongs in USD if the design is wrong.
  • Change the suspension spring in the USD suspension schema or the joint drive. This is also a physical change.
  • Reduce the speed in the Rhai mission. This is a policy change and belongs in Rhai if the mission should approach the slope more slowly.
  • Loosen the test's tilt limit. This changes the evidence, not the system. It is appropriate only when the original limit was wrong and the new limit is justified.

The correct fix depends on the question being asked. The layer boundaries do not choose the answer; they make it clear which answer is being changed.

docs.text:

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The supported way to use LunCoSim is the packaged desktop application. Build from source only if you are developing the engine or need the newest unreleased code. The packaged build includes the application, the installed asset library, and the updater.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
Get the current installer from the LunCoSim releases page.

Platform Package Launch Windows x86_64 LunCoSim-Windows-x86_64-Setup.exe Start-menu or desktop shortcut macOS Apple Silicon LunCoSim-macOS-Apple-Silicon.pkg Installed LunCoSim.app macOS Intel LunCoSim-macOS-Intel.pkg Installed LunCoSim.app Linux x86_64 LunCoSim-Linux-x86_64.AppImage The same AppImage from a writable location

Do not launch Setup.exe again to use the app, and do not launch a copied .app binary or a source-build executable if you want the updater to work. Use the installed shortcut or the same AppImage you originally placed on disk.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Run LunCoSim-Windows-x86_64-Setup.exe and follow the installer. Launch LunCoSim from the Start menu or the desktop shortcut. The installer records the installation so the built-in updater can replace it later.

If Windows SmartScreen shows a warning for an unsigned development build, verify the download against the release notes before choosing to run it.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: Open the .pkg and install LunCoSim.app where the installer offers. Launch the installed application from Finder or Launchpad. The installed app bundle is the update target; running a copy from a disk image or a build directory is not an installed build.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
The Linux package is an AppImage. Place it somewhere writable, make it executable, and run it:

chmod +x LunCoSim-Linux-x86_64.AppImage
./LunCoSim-Linux-x86_64.AppImage

There is no system-wide installation step. Keep the AppImage in a location where you can replace it, because the built-in updater replaces that file. If the AppImage fails to start because of a missing FUSE library, install the distribution's FUSE compatibility package or run the AppImage with the documented extraction option for your distribution.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
LunCoSim may check the release feed once at startup. If an update is available, the status bar shows a clickable notice. Choose Download update, then Install and restart when the package is ready.

The application is ready when the main window shows the 3D viewport and the perspective tabs. The first launch does not automatically load a sandbox; open a scene or a lesson explicitly. Continue with First run.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text: Source builds are for contributors and for running the newest unreleased code. Packaged users do not need Rust or LLVM.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Rust toolchain selected by the repository (rust-toolchain.toml)
  • LLVM/libclang for the FMI import dependency
  • The native windowing and audio development libraries used by Bevy

On Debian/Ubuntu, the CI build installs:

sudo apt-get install -y \
  libasound2-dev libudev-dev \
  libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev \
  libx11-dev xorg-dev

On macOS, the Xcode Command Line Tools provide libclang. On Windows, install the MSVC C++ Build Tools and Windows SDK, then install LLVM:

winget install --exact --id LLVM.LLVM --architecture x64

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/LunCoSim/lunco-sim.git
cd lunco-sim
cargo build -p lunco-luncosim --bin luncosim -j 4
target/debug/luncosim --api 4101

Run from the repository root so the application can find its bundled assets. The --api flag is optional, but an explicit free port is useful for scripts, screenshots, and inspection. Do not reuse a port that another LunCoSim session is already using.

If the build reports Unable to find libclang, verify that LLVM contains libclang and that LIBCLANG_PATH points to its containing directory if it is not in the default location.

docs.title: Build profiles
docs.text: A debug build is the normal development build. It keeps development checks and is slower than a release build. Use a release build when measuring frame time or running a long experiment; do not compare a debug frame rate with a release frame rate.

docs.title: The updater
docs.text:
Automatic updates only work from a supported installed package:

  • the Windows Setup.exe installation;
  • the installed macOS app;
  • the same Linux AppImage you originally launched.

A source build and an ordinary extracted archive correctly report NotInstalled. Reinstall from the current release to restore update support. Do not move an installed application after the updater has recorded its location unless you reinstall it.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text: Use the platform's normal uninstall flow for the installed package. Project folders are not removed by uninstalling the application. User settings and the asset cache live outside the application directory; remove them separately only if you intend to reset the application state.

docs.title: Integrate your stack
docs.text:
LunCoSim is designed to sit beside existing tools, not replace them. The integration boundary is made of two things:

  • Authored files in a Twin: USD, Modelica, Rhai, SysML, and the TOML manifests.
  • A typed runtime surface of commands and queries, available to Rhai and over HTTP.

That boundary is deliberately narrow. A scene graph, a solver, a mission script, and an operator console keep their own owners instead of being copied into a second integration layer.

docs.title: What you can keep
docs.text:
Existing stack What you keep What changes Status USD scenes and assets Geometry, materials, physics schemas, typed ports, composition Reference through lunco:// or twin://; no second scene graph Available glTF mesh or scene The .gltf or .glb asset and its materials Reference it from a USD payload or reference; choose scene or mesh mode Available Modelica source .mo classes and package structure Declare a Twin source root; recompile after edits Available; see the package note below FMI 3.0 Co-Simulation FMU The binary FMU Load with LoadFmu; expose scalar Float64 ports Native import only ROS 2 nodes and topics Your ROS 2 graph Add a sidecar that translates ROS 2 traffic to the HTTP API No bridge shipped URDF, SDF, or MJCF robot The source robot description Convert it to USD first No direct importer Python, C++, or Julia tools Your process and libraries Call the HTTP command/query API HTTP only; no SDK YAMCS, Open MCT, or Grafana Your operator tool Add an adapter that reads telemetry and sends commands No bundled adapter SysML v2 requirements .sysml and .kerml source Mount a Twin source set and map verification cases Bounded support Rhai mission logic Scenario intent and event policy Use LunCoSim's Rhai surface and typed commands Native

A missing adapter is not a missing runtime capability. The command and query surface is available today; an adapter is a small external process that speaks your protocol on one side and the documented HTTP envelope on the other.

docs.title: The integration boundary
docs.text:
Use the same path as the UI and the authored tests:

your tool
   │  HTTP/JSON or Rhai
   ▼
typed command / query
   │
   ▼
USD, Modelica, Rhai, physics, telemetry

The HTTP envelope is documented in HTTP API. The JSON is an external wire format only; inside the application, values cross through typed contracts. Do not build a sidecar that parses internal structures or writes domain state behind the owning document.

For live control, use ClaimControl/ReleaseControlClaim for authority and SetPorts/ReleasePort for input holds. See Mission control.

docs.title: Modelica packages
docs.text:
Keep the package structure and its within declarations. Add the package directory to the Twin manifest:

[modelica]
paths = ["models"]
externals = [
  { name = "BundledModelicaLibraries", path = "@bundled:source-bundle" },
]

paths tells the compiler where the source roots are. externals adds a library outside the Twin. Use @bundled:source-bundle for the installed Modelica source bundle.

Opening a single package.mo does not recursively import every .mo file in its folder. For a multi-file package, open the directory as a workspace or Twin root and declare it in [modelica].paths. In the browser build, a single-file pick remains a single document; the current package-loading limitation is tracked in issue #49.

docs.title: FMI
docs.text:
Native FMI 3 Co-Simulation import is available on desktop builds through LoadFmu. It is an explicit Co-Simulation profile with these limits:

  • FMI 3.0 Co-Simulation only; FMI 2 and Model Exchange are not accepted.
  • Unclocked scalar Float64 input and output ports only. Arrays, other port types, Scheduled Execution clocks, and external execution tools are rejected.
  • Fixed internal FMU steps must divide the admitted communication interval.
  • Inputs are held across each communication interval. Implicit master iteration is not implemented.
  • A native initialization failure is terminal and stops shared simulation advancement; it is not retried silently.

The browser build cannot load native FMU binaries and does not register LoadFmu. FMU export and SSP packaging are not shipped.

Do not confuse "the port fabric follows FMI/SSP vocabulary" with "every model is an FMU." The internal Modelica backend is not a packaged FMU. A reference FMU can be run beside it through the native import path.

docs.title: ROS 2 and robot descriptions
docs.text:
There is no ROS 2 bridge in the shipped runtime. Issue #57 tracks the request. A ROS 2 integration therefore has the same shape as any other operator adapter:

  1. Keep the ROS 2 graph outside LunCoSim.
  2. Translate its command topics or services into ClaimControl and SetPorts.
  3. Translate port reads or telemetry into ROS 2 publications.
  4. Release the claim and input holds when the ROS 2 session disconnects.

LunCoSim does not import URDF, SDF, or MJCF directly. Convert the robot to USD, preserve the authored joint and collider structure, and validate the result before wiring behavior. A converter load test is backlog work, not a supported importer.

glTF is the supported path for mesh content from a content tool. Export the model as .gltf or .glb, reference it from a USD payload or reference, and keep the USD prim as the scene identity. See Addresses and assets.

docs.title: A practical adoption path
docs.text:
1. Put the project in a Twin. Add twin.toml, the default USD scene, the Modelica roots, and the Rhai scenarios. See Create a Twin and twin.toml.
  2. Keep USD as the scene fact. Ports and wires are authored inputs: and outputs: properties. Do not add a parallel configuration file for the same facts.
  3. Put continuous behavior in Modelica. Keep mission sequencing and operator policy in Rhai.
  4. Add an authored acceptance test. A scene test is the production behavior gate. See Validation.
  5. Connect the external surface. Use the HTTP API for a process, a test driver, or an operator adapter. Use ClaimControl for authority and SetPorts for a live input hold.
  6. Compare against a reference. A passing test proves the authored contract; it does not prove physical accuracy for your mission. Record the reference data, tolerances, solver settings, and build version.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not expose the command API directly to an untrusted network. It is loopback-only and executes powerful commands.
  • Do not treat SetPorts as permanent wiring. It is a live input hold; released inputs return to their authored source.
  • Do not edit authored USD text from a sidecar. Use the document tools or the typed operations so identity, undo, and journaling stay coherent.
  • Do not create a second scene graph in the adapter. The composed USD stage is the scene fact.
  • Do not claim ROS 2, URDF, FMU export, or a ground-system adapter works until the adapter exists and its own test passes.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
LunCoSim is an open-source space mission workbench. It is used to assemble a vehicle and its environment, connect continuous models to the assembled physics, script an operation, and observe the result in one running simulation. The application is built on Rust and Bevy, with Avian for rigid body physics and an embedded Modelica toolchain built on the Rumoca compiler.

The project is not a CAD program, a general-purpose game engine, or a certified flight-dynamics package. It is a place where a scene, a set of equations, and a mission policy can be authored in standard formats and then run together with a shared notion of time, identity, and authority.

docs.title: The problem the workbench addresses
docs.text:
A space mission study usually spans several tools. Geometry lives in a 3D content tool, equations live in a modeling environment, mission logic lives in a scripting or ground-system tool, and the results are compared in yet another application. The interfaces between those tools are often files, spreadsheets, or hand-copied constants. The copies drift, and the drift is hard to see because each tool is internally consistent.

LunCoSim takes a different position: keep the domain formats, but give them explicit ownership and one runtime that composes them. A USD stage is still a USD stage. A Modelica class is still a Modelica class. A Rhai script is still a Rhai script. The workbench adds the project manifest, the asset addressing scheme, the typed connection fabric, and the runtime that makes the combination observable.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
The following principles explain most of the behavior described in this document.

One fact, one owner. Geometry, mass, and joint topology belong in USD. Continuous equations belong in Modelica. Mission decisions belong in Rhai. Project configuration belongs in TOML. The runtime projects these facts; it does not maintain a second editable copy of them.

Compose, do not duplicate. A reusable rover is referenced into a scene, not copied into it. A variant selects an authored alternative, not a second hand-maintained assembly. A route is composed from ordered USD prims, not pasted into every lesson script.

The authored document is the source of truth. The runtime does not rewrite authored USD to hide a problem. An editor preview is a preview; saving goes through the document owner and its journal. Generated or cached assets are products of a pipeline, not files to hand-edit.

Continuous and discrete behavior are different. Modelica advances equations at communication points. Rhai reacts to events and advances a task tree. A per-tick script loop is not a substitute for a solver, and a Modelica model is not a mission sequencer.

Evidence is layered. A parse check, a live lint, a scene test, a requirement verification, and a physical accuracy claim answer different questions. The application reports what it actually observed and does not upgrade a green check into a certificate.

docs.title: What the workbench contains
docs.text:
The desktop application combines five task layouts over one project:

  • View operates the running mission.
  • Build composes the live scene from assemblies and entities.
  • Analyze reads telemetry, ports, and graphs.
  • Editor edits one explicit USD document in isolation.
  • Lunica develops, compiles, and runs Modelica models.

The same Twin can be opened in any of these layouts without reloading the world. A lesson can pin the layout its steps depend on, and a Twin can declare an initial layout in its manifest. The Perspectives section describes each task in detail.

docs.title: Relationship to standards
docs.text:
LunCoSim uses standard formats wherever a standard exists:

Standard Use in LunCoSim OpenUSD Scene description, composition, physics schemas, shader networks, and typed ports glTF 2.0 External mesh and scene assets referenced from USD payloads Modelica Continuous and discrete-equation models, packages, and acausal connectors FMI 3.0 Co-Simulation Optional native import of scalar Float64 FMUs on desktop builds SysML v2 / KerML Requirements and verification mappings, with bounded support WESL Shader source assets and material parameter declarations TOML Project and asset manifests

The workbench adds conventions on top of these standards, but it does not replace their syntax. A .mo file remains usable in another Modelica tool, and a .usda file remains readable in another USD application, provided the LunCoSim-specific schemas and asset addresses are available.

docs.title: What LunCoSim is not
docs.text:
• It is not a CAD replacement. Use a content tool to author detailed geometry, then bring the result in as USD or as a glTF payload referenced from USD.
  • It is not a certified flight-dynamics or thermal-analysis package. Model coverage and numerical fidelity vary by domain.
  • It is not a mission-control system. It exposes a typed API that an operator adapter can drive; it does not ship a ground-segment product.
  • It is not a general game engine. The runtime is specialized for engineered systems, authored documents, and evidence.
  • It is not a converter for every robot description. URDF, SDF, and MJCF are not imported directly; convert them to USD first.

docs.title: Development status
docs.text:
LunCoSim is under active development. The core authoring loop, the USD projection, the Rhai task kernel, and the Modelica cosimulation path are implemented and exercised by authored tests. Other areas are partial or platform-specific. Native FMI import is desktop-only. The browser build does not load native FMU binaries. ROS 2, URDF, and ground-system adapters are not bundled.

The documentation states these limits where they matter. When a workflow depends on a capability that is not shipped, the text says so rather than describing an intended future feature as if it were available.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Continue with How it fits together for the runtime flow, or read Formats for a side-by-side comparison of the authored layers. A reader who wants to start using the application should go to Installation.

docs.title: Perspectives
docs.text:
A perspective is a task layout over the same Twin. Switching from View to Build, Analyze, Editor, or ∿ Lunica does not reload the scene, reset the simulation, or duplicate your project. It changes which tools are docked and what the center of the window is for.

The title bar pins the five main tasks. View → Perspectives lists those tasks plus specialist presets such as Terrain and Keybindings, and any tasks contributed by the Twin.

  • ◉ View

    Operate and present the running Twin.

    Open View

  • ↗ Analyze

    Compare signals and inspect live port values.

    Open Analyze

  • ⚒ Build

    Compose and tune the live scene.

    Open Build

  • ✎ Editor

    Edit one explicit USD document in isolation.

    Open Editor

  • ∿ Lunica

    Develop, compile, and run Modelica models.

    Open Lunica

  • ↻ Switch layouts

    Preserve the Twin, documents, and simulation.

    Switch and recover

Analyze is the built-in label for analytics work; there is no separate Analytics tab.

docs.title: Switch and recover a layout
docs.text:
Select a title-bar tab, or choose View → Perspectives and pick a task. Compact windows collapse the tabs into a picker. Switching perspectives preserves the Twin and the simulation; layout changes stay with their task. Switching does not start or stop the simulation; the title-bar transport and simulation state remain global.

Open document tabs stay open when you switch, including documents with unsaved edits. The active task and each task layout are remembered per Twin. A Twin can declare its initial task with default_perspective in twin.toml; once you choose a task yourself, that choice takes precedence when you reopen the Twin.

  • View → Reset Layout reapplies the authored default for the current perspective.
  • Help → Perspective help explains what the current perspective is for.
  • The View menu also has task submenus (Build, Analyze, Editor, Lunica, and General) that open optional panels.
  • The Graphs menu action switches to Analyze when that workflow is available.

A guided lesson can temporarily pin the perspective its steps rely on. When the lesson completes or is skipped, normal perspective switching resumes.

docs.title: View: operate the mission
docs.text:
View gives the live scene the whole window. It is the perspective to use when the task is to watch, drive, fly, or demonstrate rather than author.

The viewport keeps selection, control, and camera targets separate. Selecting an object does not give you its controls, and moving the camera does not change what is selected.

The View perspective leaves the live scene full-window. Open optional panels from View when you need them.

To use it:

  1. Open a scene or lesson and let the scene finish preparing.
  2. Click an object to select it, or click an input endpoint to take control of a vehicle or mechanism. In a lesson, use the Take control action when the card offers it.
  3. Drive with the displayed bindings. The lesson card and the active input map always show the keys configured on your machine.
  4. Right-drag to orbit and scroll to zoom. The camera keeps its own target.
  5. Use the transport controls or P to pause when you need to inspect a moment without stopping the app.

Release control with G when you are done; selecting another object does not transfer control. Use View for operating and presenting a Twin. Switch to Build when you need to add or edit scene objects, and to Analyze when you need the signal data behind what you see.

docs.title: Analyze: read the signals
docs.text:
Analyze is the telemetry and plotting perspective. The live scene remains in the center, Telemetry sits above Entities on the left, Ports is on the right, and Graphs occupies the bottom dock.

Analyze brings the live scene, Telemetry, Ports, and Graphs together. Graphs records simulation samples, not rendered frames.

To compare signals:

  1. Switch to Analyze. If no scene is mounted, Graphs opens in the center.
  2. Select an entity in Entities, or choose it in Telemetry, to narrow the channel list.
  3. Check a channel, or drag it into the active plot in Graphs. Add more channels to the same plot to compare them on one time axis.
  4. Use Ports to read current values and to write manual inputs while the model is running. Use the port's direction and kind: write inputs, read outputs.
  5. Pause the simulation to inspect the latest sample. The graph keeps the samples it already recorded; it does not replay rendered frames.

Use New in the Graphs toolbar to open a separate plot with its own signal set. If Graphs is hidden, use the Graphs menu or open the optional View → Analyze panels. Graphs is the canonical analysis surface; the same data is also available through the HTTP API when you need to script a check.

docs.title: Build: compose the live scene
docs.text:
Build is the scene-composition perspective. Entities sits above the Twin file browser on the left, the live scene is in the center, and Inspector and Environment sit above the Spawn palette on the right.

Build places the scene tree, Twin files, Inspector, Environment, and Spawn palette around the live scene.

To assemble a scene:

  1. Open the Twin or scene you want to edit. Build edits the live scene, so the simulation keeps running while you work.
  2. Select an object in Entities to inspect it, or choose an assembly in the Spawn palette.
  3. Place the new object, then adjust its transform and properties in Inspector or with the viewport transform gizmo.
  4. Use Environment for scene-wide settings such as lighting and the environment profile.
  5. Save the scene document to keep the change in the authored USD stage.

Build is for composing the world from assemblies and entities. When you need to edit the internals of a reusable assembly, open that USD document in Editor. When you need the signal behind a behavior, use Analyze.

docs.title: Editor: edit one USD document
docs.text:
Editor is the focused USD authoring perspective, also used as the assembly editor for reusable USD components. Twin and Prims are on the left, the document preview is in the center, and Inspector, Requirements, and Change History are on the right. The center stays empty until you open a document or tool.

Editor opens one USD document in an isolated preview. Selecting a prim drives the Inspector; save and undo apply to that document.

To edit a document:

  1. Choose a USD file in Twin, or use File → Open. The file opens as an editing preview; it does not replace the live scene.
  2. Select a prim in Prims or click it in the preview. The Inspector shows the selected prim's properties.
  3. Edit the value in the Inspector, or switch between Visual and Text to inspect the rendered stage or its USD text.
  4. Left-drag to pan, right-drag to orbit, middle-drag to pan, and use the wheel to zoom. The transform gizmo edits the selected prim directly.
  5. Review the journal in Change History. Save and Undo apply to the active document, not to the live scene.

Opening a scene through Scenarios is a world load; opening a USD file in Editor is a document edit. To find a prim's file in the Twin browser, right-click the prim and choose Reveal in Twin.

Editor is the right place for reusable assembly internals, prim hierarchy, materials, and authored properties. It deliberately does not show the live Entity list or Spawn palette; use Build for the composed world.

docs.title: Lunica: engineer a Modelica model
docs.text:
∿ Lunica is the Modelica perspective. The Twin browser is on the left, and the center holds the Welcome page or the model views you open. Models open in their own document tabs; inside a model, switch between Text, Diagram, Icon, and Docs.

Lunica opens Modelica sources from the Twin. Compile the model, run it live, or use Fast Run for a batch experiment.

To work on a model:

  1. Switch to ∿ Lunica, then choose the Modelica section in the Twin browser to browse packages and classes. Open a class to create a model tab.
  2. Work in Diagram for the schematic, or Text for the equations.
  3. Choose Compile to build the model. A successful compile leaves the model ready and paused.
  4. Choose Run to start live simulation, then pause, reset, or restart from the same toolbar. Use Fast Run when you want a batch run that does not need to play in real time.
  5. Open View → Lunica → Experiments to revisit completed runs and compare their variables. For signals from the running Twin, use Analyze instead.

Lunica edits and runs Modelica; it does not replace the USD scene or the Rhai scenario. Use it to develop the continuous model, then wire that model into the Twin and observe the coupled behavior in Analyze or View.

docs.title: Choose the right task
docs.text:
You want to… Use Start with Drive, fly, or present the running mission View Click an input endpoint, or Take control in a lesson Compare telemetry and inspect port values Analyze Select an entity, then check a channel in Telemetry Add, place, or tune objects in the live scene Build Pick an assembly in Spawn Edit the prims and properties inside a USD document Editor Open the USD file in Twin Develop, compile, and run a Modelica model Lunica Open a .mo file, then Compile

Additional task presets, such as Terrain and Keybindings, appear under View → Perspectives but are not pinned to the title bar. A Twin can also add its own perspectives; they appear beside the built-in tasks.

Switching perspectives is part of normal work, not a reset. If a layout feels wrong, use View → Reset Layout for the current task, or open Help → Perspective help to confirm what that task is meant to do.

Continue with First mission for a guided flow. For the full keyboard and camera reference, see Controls.

docs.title: Twins
docs.text:
A Twin is a project folder for one engineered system: a lunar base, a rover test rig, a lander, a power subsystem, or a whole mission. It is the unit of saving, versioning, sharing, and opening in LunCoSim.

A folder becomes a Twin when it contains twin.toml. That manifest is the only required file.

A typical Twin layout. The manifest selects the entry scene and the source roots; the other files remain ordinary domain files.

docs.title: A minimal Twin
docs.text:
my-rover-twin/
├── twin.toml
├── scene.usda
├── models/
│   └── Drive.mo
├── scenarios/
│   └── drive.rhai
└── .lunco/              # session state, not project content

twin.toml declares the project name, version, entry scene, and search roots. The other files are ordinary domain files:

File Role scene.usda The USD scene that becomes the active world models/Drive.mo A Modelica source file scenarios/drive.rhai A Rhai scenario or test policy .lunco/ Local session and workspace state; normally gitignored

docs.title: Standard files, tool-specific manifest
docs.text:
A Twin deliberately separates tool configuration from system modeling:

  • USD owns geometry, composition, materials, physics, and connections.
  • Modelica owns equations and continuous state.
  • SysML owns requirements and system structure, when the Twin uses them.
  • Rhai owns scenario and test policy.
  • TOML owns tool configuration: twin.toml and Assets.toml.

The domain files stay in their standard syntax. A .mo file is still a normal Modelica file, a .usda file is still normal USD, and a .sysml file is still normal SysML. LunCoSim-specific configuration lives in twin.toml, so those files remain usable in other tools.

docs.title: File, folder, or Twin
docs.text:
LunCoSim supports three levels of structure:

Mode What you open What you get File One .usda, .mo, or other document Edit that file; no project-level discovery Folder A folder without twin.toml Browse and edit files; no manifest, no Twin search roots Twin A folder with twin.toml Full project discovery, default scene, libraries, and Twin settings

You can promote a folder to a Twin at any time by adding a twin.toml or by using Save as Twin…. The files do not move.

docs.title: The manifest is read at open
docs.text:
The manifest is not watched for structural changes. If you edit default_scene, the Modelica source roots, or the SysML roots, reopen the Twin before expecting the change to take effect. The parser rejects unknown fields, so a typo fails visibly instead of being silently ignored.

The [settings] table is different: it is a live, namespaced scalar map that Rhai and the Twin settings panel can read and write. See twin.toml for the field reference.

docs.title: Nested Twins
docs.text:
A Twin can compose child Twins:

[[children]]
name = "engine"
path = "engine"

Opening the parent loads local children eagerly. A child can be a complete project in its own right, which is useful for an engine, a comm stack, or a science payload that is also developed separately.

Remote URL children are reserved for future remote-Twin support; they are listed in the manifest but are not followed today.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Opening and closing a Twin is a real lifecycle boundary. When a Twin closes, its documents, Modelica participants, scripts, timelines, and scene-owned state are retired before another Twin can use those names. If you switch projects, expect a fresh load rather than a reuse of the previous session's state.

This is why a Twin is a better unit than a loose collection of tabs: the project owns its resources and can shut them down as one system.

The boundary also applies to runtime UI. A Twin can provide its own presentation manifest; closing the Twin restores the shared application surfaces. See Runtime UI.

docs.title: Create or open a Twin
docs.text:
• File → New Twin… creates a manifest and opens the new project.
  • File → Open Twin… opens an existing folder with twin.toml.
  • Save as Twin… promotes the current document or scene into a new project folder.

Once the Twin is open, the Twin panel shows its files. The declared default scene is loaded into the viewport; other USD files remain a referenceable asset library until a scene references them.

docs.title: What belongs in the project
docs.text:
A Twin should contain the files that define the system and the policy that travels with it. A useful test is: if a colleague opened this folder on another machine, would they need this file to reproduce the authored system?

Belongs in the Twin Does not belong in the Twin USD scenes, assemblies, and variants Downloaded cache bytes Modelica sources and package structure Generated solver artifacts Rhai scenarios, tutorials, and tests Screenshots and scratch recordings Assets.toml declarations Absolute machine paths twin.toml and project settings User-global preferences SysML requirements and verification mappings Secrets or private tokens

External bytes are declared, not copied. Use Assets.toml to name the source, destination, and optional hash. The asset system resolves the logical address to the local cache.

docs.title: Sharing a Twin
docs.text:
A Twin is an ordinary folder. You can version it with Git, zip it, or hand it to a colleague. Before sharing:

  1. Remove local session state and any large generated artifacts.
  2. Confirm that every external asset is declared in Assets.toml.
  3. Confirm that the default scene opens on a clean machine.
  4. Run the authored validation and scene test.
  5. Record the LunCoSim build and any reference data used for an accuracy claim.

The Validate and share tutorial walks through the complete handoff.

docs.title: Modelica
docs.text:
Modelica is LunCoSim's language for continuous behavior: motion, power, thermal flow, fluid systems, and control laws. A .mo file contains equations, not a sequence of commands. The solver advances the equations over time.

LunCoSim uses Rumoca, a Modelica compiler and interactive solver, as its Modelica runtime. The compiler is strict: an unsupported construct fails at compile time rather than being silently approximated.

docs.title: What Modelica owns
docs.text:
Fact Authored as Consumed by Differential and algebraic equations equation sections Rumoca solver Continuous state Variables with der(...) Solver and observables Parameters parameter declarations Instance configuration Acausal connections connect(...) between connectors Equation system Inputs and outputs input / output declarations USD port interface Events and discrete state when, if, pre(...) Solver event handling Experiments Bounds, overrides, tolerance Batch runner

Modelica does not own scene traversal, mission sequencing, or user input. Those belong to USD and Rhai.

docs.title: A small model
docs.text:
within MyRover;

model Drive
  input Real throttle;
  output Real speed;
  parameter Real timeConstant = 1.0;

initial equation
  speed = 0.0;

equation
  der(speed) = (max(-1.0, min(1.0, throttle)) - speed) / timeConstant;
end Drive;

The pieces:

Keyword Meaning within MyRover; The package namespace for this class model Drive A reusable model class input Real throttle A value supplied by the surrounding system output Real speed A value exposed to the surrounding system parameter Real timeConstant A tunable value that is constant during a run initial equation The initial condition equation The continuous relationship der(speed) The time derivative of speed

This model turns a throttle command into a first-order speed response. It does not find prims, read the scene, or decide when a mission is complete.

docs.title: Attaching a model to USD
docs.text:
A Modelica class becomes a simulation participant when a USD prim carries LunCoProgramAPI and names the source:

def Scope "Controller" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
) {
    uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover/models/Drive.mo@
    uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true
}

Use @twin://...@ for a model inside the open Twin. Use @lunco://models/...@ for a model shipped in the installed asset library.

The program prim's inputs: and outputs: properties are the external contract. They must match the compiled interface. A model output becomes connectable only when the component prim declares the matching outputs:<name> property.

docs.title: How cosimulation works
docs.text:
When a Modelica model drives a physical body, LunCoSim runs the two sides together:

  1. The fixed master clock reaches a communication point.
  2. Model outputs are sampled.
  3. The values cross the authored USD connections as SimConnections.
  4. Physics applies the resulting forces or reads the new state.
  5. The new state becomes the next input sample.

Outputs are held between communication points. A script does not step this loop; the wiring and the runtime do. This is why a component must declare its outputs:<name> ports in USD before another component can consume them.

The rule of thumb:

  • Modelica owns the condition. A model computes low_fuel = 1 when its state crosses a threshold.
  • USD owns the wire. A LunCoEvent prim connects that output to a named event.
  • Rhai owns the response. A scenario listens for lander_low_fuel and displays a warning.

docs.title: The Lunica workbench
docs.text:
Open the ∿ Lunica perspective to work on Modelica directly. It provides the Twin browser's Modelica section, text, diagram, icon and documentation views, parameter editing, compilation, run controls, plots, and experiments. See Perspectives for the layout and workflow.

Use it to:

  • inspect a model before attaching it to a scene;
  • change parameters and compare runs;
  • run a model in real time or as a fast batch;
  • plot and compare experiment results.

The simulator embeds the same workbench, so you do not need a separate application to edit a model used by a Twin.
