docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
LunCoSim exposes a small HTTP API for automation, inspection, tests, and screenshots. It is the same typed command/query surface used by the UI and by Rhai, not a second control path.

Launch with an explicit free port:

luncosim --api 4101

The command endpoint is loopback-only. Do not expose it to an untrusted network.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Method Path Purpose POST /api/commands Execute a command or query GET /api/commands/schema Discover command names and field types GET /api/health Liveness; does not read the world GET /api/ready Readiness, scene hold, and pending work GET /api/diagnostics Co-simulation wiring and connection health

docs.title: Request envelope
docs.text:
Every write and query uses the same JSON envelope:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "type": "ExecuteCommand",
        "command": "SetPorts",
        "params": {
          "target": 42,
          "producer_id": 4812,
          "writes": [["throttle", 0.4], ["steer", 0.0], ["brake", 0.0]],
          "seq": 0,
          "tick": 0
        }
      }'

The successful response wraps the owner's result:

{
  "data": {
    "accepted": true
  }
}

An error response is terminal. Do not retry a rejected command blindly; read the error, inspect the target, and fix the input.

ListEntities can also be sent as a shorthand request:

{"type": "ListEntities"}

docs.title: Discover the surface
docs.text:
Never guess a command name from memory:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands/schema" | python3 -m json.tool

The schema is derived from the running application's reflected command and query types. It grows with the features actually registered in that build.

docs.title: Readiness
docs.text:
Before controlling a scene, wait for readiness:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/ready"

Continue only when ready is true, world_hold is false, and pending_count is zero. A faulted world is not a slow world; inspect the readiness detail and /api/diagnostics.

docs.title: Commands and queries
docs.text:
The API has both write commands and read queries. They share ExecuteCommand for transport, but their contract differs:

  • A write command has side effects and returns an acceptance/result.
  • A query reads state and returns typed data.
  • A rejected command does not partially apply a multi-target write.
  • A missing value is not silently replaced with a zero.

Common discovery/read examples:

# Entities, including their stable api_id
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ListEntities"}'

# Ports on one entity
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "ListPorts",
       "params": {"api_id": 42}}'

docs.title: Driving from a script
docs.text:
A Python or shell client only needs an HTTP request. There is no SDK and no handshake:

import json
import urllib.request

def execute(command, params=None):
    body = json.dumps({
        "type": "ExecuteCommand",
        "command": command,
        "params": params or {},
    }).encode()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands",
        data=body,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
        payload = json.load(response)
    if "error" in payload:
        raise RuntimeError(payload["error"])
    return payload["data"]

entities = execute("ListEntities")["entities"]

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
• The API is a transport. Domain state is still owned by USD, Modelica, Rhai, and the native runtime.
  • Use LoadScene, not direct file writes, to mount a scene.
  • Use SetPorts for a live input hold; use ReleaseControl or ReleasePort to return the input to its authored source.
  • Use CaptureScreenshot for visual evidence; do not infer a rendered result from a numeric query alone.
  • Run scene tests through the production binary (luncosim test), not through a private HTTP loop that skips the authored verdict.

For live values, see Telemetry. For the operator lifecycle, including authority claims, telemetry, and safe release, see Mission control. For supported asset and tool boundaries, see Integrate your stack. For command-line flags, see CLI.

docs.title: Mission control
docs.text:
LunCoSim is a simulation workbench, not a mission-control system. It exposes a typed command and query API that a ground-segment or operator adapter can drive. No YAMCS, Open MCT, or Grafana adapter is bundled in this build.

The integration shape is simple:

operator tool  ──►  adapter  ──►  POST /api/commands  ──►  LunCoSim
                               ◄──  telemetry queries  ◄──

The adapter owns protocol translation, authentication policy, and operator workflow. LunCoSim owns the scene, simulation state, authority, and typed results.

docs.title: What is available
docs.text:
Need Surface Discover entities and ports ListEntities, ListPorts Claim an endpoint ClaimControl Write live inputs SetPorts, SetPortsBatch Release an input or claim ReleasePort, ReleaseControl, ReleaseControlClaim Read current values ReadPorts, ReadPortsBatch, ReadActuatorStatus Read telemetry ListTelemetryChannels, QueryTelemetryHistory, ExportTelemetryRecording Check health GET /api/ready, GET /api/diagnostics Inspect coupling CosimStatus, GetBrokenConnections, CausalTrace Capture admitted inputs StartSessionInputCapture, StopSessionInputCapture, ExportSessionInputCapture

Not shipped:

  • YAMCS, Open MCT, or Grafana adapters.
  • CCSDS or XTCE translation.
  • A ROS 2 bridge (issue #57).
  • Whole-session deterministic replay.

Use the absence of an adapter as an adapter task, not as a missing runtime control surface.

docs.title: Start with readiness
docs.text:
Launch with an explicit, free API port and keep the API on loopback:

luncosim --api 4101

Do not expose the command endpoint to an untrusted network. It executes powerful authoring and control commands and has no general-purpose remote authentication layer.

Wait until the scene is admitted:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/ready"

Proceed only when ready is true, world_hold is false, and pending_count is zero. A faulted world is not a slow world; read /api/diagnostics and the readiness detail instead of retrying commands.

docs.title: A minimal operator adapter
docs.text:
The following Python example shows the lifecycle. It assumes the endpoint is a rover and that its declared input names are throttle, steer, and brake.

import json
import time
import urllib.request

PORT = 4101
BASE = f"http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}"
PRODUCER = 4812  # stable for this adapter session; nonzero


def post(command, params=None):
    body = json.dumps({
        "type": "ExecuteCommand",
        "command": command,
        "params": params or {},
    }).encode()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE}/api/commands",
        data=body,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
        payload = json.load(response)
    if "error" in payload:
        raise RuntimeError(payload["error"])
    return payload["data"]


def find_endpoint(name):
    for entity in post("ListEntities")["entities"]:
        if entity["name"] == name:
            return entity["api_id"]
    raise LookupError(f"no entity named {name}")


endpoint = find_endpoint("Rover")
post("ClaimControl", {"target": endpoint})

try:
    for _ in range(100):
        post("SetPorts", {
            "target": endpoint,
            "writes": [["throttle", 0.2], ["steer", 0.0], ["brake", 0.0]],
            "seq": 0,
            "tick": 0,
            "producer_id": PRODUCER,
        })
        time.sleep(0.05)
finally:
    # Release the hold, then relinquish the endpoint.
    post("ReleaseControl", {
        "target": endpoint,
        "seq": 0,
        "tick": 0,
        "producer_id": PRODUCER,
    })
    post("ReleaseControlClaim", {"target": endpoint})

Replace the input names with the names returned by ListPorts. A write to a port that the endpoint does not declare is rejected; it is not silently mapped to a default.

docs.title: Authority rules
docs.text:
• ClaimControl claims a stable endpoint for the originating session. AcquireControl is the UI-oriented variant that also binds the local camera.
  • Use ReleaseControlClaim on disconnect. Do not rely on timeout cleanup.
  • SetPorts is a live input hold. ReleaseControl and ReleasePort return the input to its authored wiring; they do not write a stop value. If the safe state requires a specific setpoint, write it explicitly before releasing.
  • Keep one stable, nonzero producer_id per operator or adapter session. The ID records provenance; it is not an authorization credential.
  • A claim is exclusive per endpoint. A successful ClaimControl releases the previous owner's claim when RBAC and claim policy allow the takeover; do not write through another session's claim without claiming first.
  • SetPortsBatch is atomic on an authoritative host or local embodiment. Shared clients and authenticated network sessions should use single-target SetPorts, ReleasePort, and ReleaseControl.
  • A rejected command is terminal. Read the error and fix the target, port, or value; do not retry the same request blindly.

docs.title: Read telemetry
docs.text:
Discover the retained channels first:

channels = post("ListTelemetryChannels")["channels"]
key = channels[0]["key"]

history = post("QueryTelemetryHistory", {
    "key": key,
    "limit": 200,
})

Each sample has a simulation time t and a value v; the response also carries epoch_jd when a mission epoch is available. A missing value is a hole, not a zero.

For a recording that can be compared with an experiment or external tool:

recording = post("ExportTelemetryRecording", {
    "keys": [key],
})

The recording has a union time grid and null for channels that did not report at a given time. It deliberately does not interpolate.

For the current wiring boundary, use ListPorts and then ReadPorts or ReadPortsBatch. ReadPortsBatch returns one shared sim_tick, so values from different endpoints can be compared at the same simulation moment. Use ReadActuatorStatus when the question is whether a commanded actuator has settled within a tolerance.

docs.title: Audit and replay
docs.text:
StartSessionInputCapture records a bounded slice of admitted session inputs. StopSessionInputCapture refuses while an admitted input is still waiting for its fixed-tick commit. On a native host, ExportSessionInputCapture writes a durable .lcsin archive; ReadSessionInputArchiveExport reports its status.

That archive is an input record, not a complete replay package. It does not contain a baseline manifest or a playback consumer, and not every command is in the input slice. CausalTrace ties an admitted input to its producer, tick, and sequence, which is useful evidence for an operator action.

Do not claim bit-reproducible mission replay from this build. Deterministic replay is a separate engineering track.

docs.title: ROS 2 and other protocols
docs.text:
There is no shipped ROS 2 bridge. Keep ROS 2 outside the simulator and translate its command and telemetry topics into ClaimControl, SetPorts, and the telemetry queries above. The same pattern applies to YAMCS, Open MCT, Grafana, or a custom ground tool.

The adapter should:

  1. Wait for readiness.
  2. Discover the exact entity and port names.
  3. Claim the endpoint before writing.
  4. Send finite values at a controlled cadence.
  5. Read telemetry or ports for feedback.
  6. Release the hold and claim on shutdown.
  7. Expose a clear failure when the API rejects an input.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The API is bound to a loopback or otherwise private interface.
  • [ ] The scene is ready before the first write.
  • [ ] The adapter uses stable entity identities, not display names.
  • [ ] The adapter knows the declared port names and directions.
  • [ ] One operator owns the endpoint claim.
  • [ ] The safe condition is written before releasing an input, when required.
  • [ ] The adapter releases its claim on every exit path.
  • [ ] Rejections are visible to the operator, not retried silently.
  • [ ] Telemetry uses a single tick for comparisons.
  • [ ] The test includes a negative case and a real verdict.

docs.text:

  • Telemetry — live values, history, and graphs

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with the visible owner: the status bar, the lesson card, the readiness endpoint, or the terminal that launched the app. A log line is evidence only when it names the same failure.

docs.title: The app does not start
docs.text:
--api port is already in use

Choose a different free port:

luncosim --api 4102

Do not reuse a port owned by another LunCoSim session. Stop only your own session through its API, then relaunch.

The window does not appear

Check that the machine has a working display and GPU driver. For a headless or remote run, use the documented headless/recording options rather than expecting a window.

A source build fails on libclang

Install LLVM. On Windows:

winget install --exact --id LLVM.LLVM --architecture x64

On Debian/Ubuntu, install libclang-dev or the matching LLVM package. If libclang is not in a default location, set LIBCLANG_PATH to the directory that contains it.

Linux build fails on a missing system library

Install the windowing and audio development headers:

sudo apt-get install -y \
  libasound2-dev libudev-dev \
  libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev \
  libx11-dev xorg-dev

docs.title: The scene is empty or the Twin opens as files
docs.text:
A Twin only mounts a scene when twin.toml declares it:

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

The path is relative to the Twin root. If it is missing or wrong, the Twin opens as a file browser. Check that the file exists and that the manifest has no unknown-field typo; the parser rejects unknown fields.

If the scene loads but the ground is missing, a terrain asset is probably not installed. See Assets below.

docs.title: The vehicle ignores input
docs.text:
1. Click Take control or use possess. Selection is not control.
  2. Confirm the vehicle is not held by another session or producer.
  3. Check that the input binding is actually mapped. The lesson hint resolves the current binding; a label of unbound means the action has no key.
  4. If a script holds the vehicle, release that claim before taking manual control.

docs.title: An asset is missing
docs.text:
LunCoSim does not download external data silently at launch. When a declared asset is missing:

  1. Open Settings → Data & libraries or the Twin's assets view.
  2. Confirm the entry exists in Assets.toml with a valid url and dest.
  3. Start the download explicitly and watch its status.
  4. If a hash is declared, a mismatch rejects the download. Remove the bad cache artifact only after confirming the source, then retry.

The cache lives at:

Platform Path Linux ~/.cache/lunco/ macOS ~/Library/Caches/lunco/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\lunco\

Set LUNCOSIM_CACHE to use a different root. Do not hardcode a cache path in a USD file; use lunco:// or twin:// addresses instead.

docs.title: The rover does not move
docs.text:
Check the whole chain, not just the script:

  1. Does the scenario attach to the entity that should act?
  2. Does the drive model compile and report a running participant?
  3. Does the component declare the outputs: port that the connection targets?
  4. Is the target input actually wired to a source?
  5. Is a higher-priority control hold keeping the input at another value?

A missing port is not a zero. Inspect it with ListPorts and the wiring diagnostics rather than assuming a default.

docs.title: Modelica does not run
docs.text:
• Check that the .mo file parses and compiles in the Lunica perspective.
  • Confirm the Twin's [modelica].paths includes the model's root.
  • Confirm the USD program prim names the exact source asset.
  • Check that required external libraries are installed and declared.
  • Read the participant status and cosim diagnostics; a model that stopped is not a model that is still advancing.

docs.title: Telemetry shows no value
docs.text:
• Wait for readiness; a port can be absent while its model is compiling.
  • Run ListPorts before ReadPorts; reads require explicit port names.
  • For solver state, use SnapshotVariables, not only the port surface.
  • If a value was valid earlier and then vanished, check whether the owning entity or scene was replaced.

docs.title: The API rejects a request
docs.text:
• Read the error. Unknown fields and malformed nested values are rejected, not ignored.
  • Confirm the command name with GET /api/commands/schema.
  • Confirm IDs are the stable api_id, not a display name or a local index.
  • For a multi-target write, fix the whole batch; a rejection means no partial writes were admitted.
  • Do not retry a rejected input with the same value and expect a different result.

docs.title: The updater says NotInstalled
docs.text:
Automatic updates only work from a supported installed package:

  • the Windows Setup.exe installation
  • the installed macOS app
  • the same Linux AppImage you originally launched

A source build and an ordinary extracted archive correctly report NotInstalled. Reinstall from the current release to restore update support.

docs.title: What to include in a report
docs.text:
Include:

  • the LunCoSim version and platform
  • whether it is a packaged build or a source build
  • the exact scene or Twin path
  • the exact command or input that failed
  • the readiness/diagnostic response
  • a screenshot when the failure is visual
  • the first error, not only the last log line

Never include secrets, tokens, or private asset URLs in a public report.

docs.title: twin.toml
docs.text: twin.toml is the only file required for a folder to be a Twin. It identifies the project, selects the entry scene, and declares where the domain sources live. It does not contain physical equations or scene geometry.

docs.title: Minimal manifest
docs.text:
name = "my-rover-twin"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A minimal rover project"

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

The current format uses top-level name, version, and description. Unknown fields are rejected, so a typo fails visibly instead of being silently ignored.

docs.title: A fuller manifest
docs.text:
name = "Lunar Rover Lab"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Classroom practice project"

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"
scenes = ["scenes/*.usda", "scenes/tests/*.usda"]

[modelica]
paths = ["models"]
externals = [
  { name = "BundledModelicaLibraries", path = "@bundled:source-bundle" },
]

[sysml]
root = "requirements.sysml"
paths = ["."]

[settings]
"ui.lunar_map" = false

[[children]]
name = "engine"
path = "engine"

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning name Human-readable project name version Manifest/project version description Optional long description uuid Optional stable scenario identity used by networking default_perspective Optional authored initial task layout [usd].default_scene Twin-relative path to the stage opened when the Twin opens [usd].scenes Globs for scenes offered by the Scenarios menu [modelica].paths Twin-relative Modelica search roots; defaults to ["."] [modelica].externals Additional Modelica libraries, including @bundled:source-bundle [sysml].root Optional entry-point .sysml or .kerml file [sysml].paths Twin-relative SysML source roots; defaults to ["."] [settings] Scalar project settings read and written by Rhai policy [[children]] Nested Twins composed into this project [journal].persist Persist the edit journal across sessions; off by default

[[components]], [verification], and [[native_plugins]] are advanced project contracts. Most user Twins do not need them.

docs.title: How default_scene is chosen
docs.text:
The Twin does not guess a starting scene from a folder of .usda files. If default_scene is present, that exact Twin-relative stage becomes the active world when the Twin opens. If it is absent, the Twin opens like a folder: files are indexed, but no scene is auto-loaded.

Other .usda files in the Twin remain a referenceable library. Only the declared stage is mounted automatically. A scene can still reference them through normal USD composition.

[usd].scenes controls which files appear as loadable scenes in the Scenarios menu. If omitted, LunCoSim falls back to the conventional scenes/** and sim/scenes/** layouts. Declaring the globs explicitly is safer for a project that organizes scenes differently.

docs.title: Modelica and SysML roots
docs.text:
[modelica].paths tells the compiler where to look for .mo sources. A path may be "." to make the Twin root a search root. externals adds libraries outside the Twin, such as the bundled source library or a sibling folder.

[sysml] is optional. When present, root selects the entry-point source and paths narrows the source-set discovery. SysML files remain ordinary Twin files; the section does not embed model text or duplicate requirements.

docs.title: Twin settings
docs.text:
[settings] is a flat table of scalar values. Keys are namespaced strings:

[settings]
"ui.lunar_map" = false
"my_mission.max_speed" = 1.5

Rhai reads and writes them through get_twin_setting(...) and set_twin_setting(...). Use this for project policy and preferences, not for large structured data.

docs.title: Children and journal
docs.text:
[[children]] composes local child Twins. A child is opened as part of the parent, and a child can itself have a twin.toml.

[journal].persist = true writes the edit history to <twin>/history/journal.json. It is off by default; opening a folder should not start writing history into it unless the project asks for it.

docs.text:
• Twin — the project folder and lifecycle
  • Assets.toml — external bytes used by the Twin
  • Create a Twin — a hands-on walkthrough

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Validation is layered. Each layer answers a different question, and a clean result at one layer does not imply a clean result at the next. Use the lightest layer that can answer your question, then keep the evidence with the project.

docs.title: What are you trying to prove?
docs.text:
Question Evidence What it does not prove Do the authored files parse and compose? luncosim --validate, ValidateAsset That the scene runs or behaves correctly Does the Twin resolve its names and assets? ValidateTwin That a runtime owner does not collide Is the loaded scene structurally sound? RunLint That the behavior matches a requirement Does the authored scenario meet its verdict? luncosim test --scene That the model is physically accurate Does a SysML requirement pass? --verification with a Twin registry entry That every requirement is covered Is the live runtime healthy? /api/ready, CosimStatus, GetBrokenConnections That the authored design is correct Does it look right? Screenshot or recording That the numbers are right Is it accurate for my mission? Comparison with reference data and documented assumptions That it is accurate outside that evidence

LunCoSim provides a test and evidence harness. It does not issue a generic accuracy certificate.

docs.title: Preflight the files
docs.text:
luncosim --validate \
  path/to/twin/scene.usda \
  path/to/twin/models/Drive.mo \
  path/to/twin/scenarios/drive.rhai

Supported inputs are .mo, .usda, .sysml/.kerml, .wesl, and .rhai. The command runs without a window, GPU, or application instance. It exits 0 when every report is valid and 1 when any report fails.

--validate is parse- and loader-oriented. It catches syntax errors, broken references, invalid Modelica declarations, missing authored wheel attributes, and unparsable Rhai. It does not execute the scenario, run the solver, or prove that a value is physically correct.

From a running session, the same file-level checks are available as the ValidateAsset query. It admits one operation and returns an operation ID; poll that ID until the report is ready. Use ValidateTwin when the question spans a whole Twin folder and its resolver closure. ValidateTwin reports namespace collisions; use policy: "error" when a collision should fail the check.

docs.title: Lint the loaded scene
docs.text:
A file check cannot see entities spawned at runtime or edits made after load. After loading and editing a scene, run the explicit live lint:

{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "RunLint", "params": {}}

Then poll GetDiagnostics until the report is complete before treating it as clean. Loaded-stage lint can see runtime-owned ports that file validation cannot. It remains an explicit check; nothing lints automatically on load or on a physics tick.

Use RunLint when you need to know whether the scene as composed will behave correctly, not merely whether its files parse.

docs.title: Run the authored behavior test
docs.text:
luncosim test --scene path/to/twin/tests/drive.usda

The scene test runs the authored Rhai observer with manual, fixed-step time advancement. The exit code is the verdict:

Exit Meaning 0 PASS 1 FAIL 2 No verdict was produced

A passing test must come from a real verdict, not from the absence of a failure. A test that exhausts its tick budget without a verdict is exit 2. Keep a negative fixture for the behavior you are guarding; a test that cannot fail is not evidence.

Useful selectors:

Option Use --list Discover test scenes and their execution kind --verdict-channel NAME Accept the verdict only from a named channel --verification QUALIFIED_NAME Bind the run to a Twin SysML verification case --max-ticks N Bound cumulative simulated steps; default 20000 --tick-hz HZ Select the manual update rate; default 60 --readiness-timeout SECS Bound scene preparation time; default 420 --determinism-reference PATH Load a typed state reference for comparison

A component suite can use:

luncosim test-component --twin path/to/twin --component rover.wheels

The component manifest owns the scene and observer, so the test and its fixture stay together. Run scene tests through the production luncosim binary; do not substitute a private harness or --validate.

docs.title: Verify requirements with SysML
docs.text:
A Twin can keep its requirements in .sysml/.kerml source and map a verification case to a scene and Rhai observer:

[verification]
[[verification.cases]]
name = "Project::VerifyDrive"
scene = "tests/drive.usda"
script = "scenarios/tests/drive.rhai"
verdict_channel = "DRIVE_REQUIREMENTS"

Run the mapped case:

luncosim test --scene path/to/twin/tests/drive.usda \
  --verification Project::VerifyDrive

ValidateSysml checks source validity and structural policy. AnalyzeSysml returns typed facts for Rhai policy. --verification checks that the qualified name, scene, observer, and verdict channel match the Twin registry before the run starts.

This is a bounded subset: scalar constraints and authored observations are supported; full KerML execution and automatic requirement-to-USD projection are not. Keep the requirement text and limits in SysML, and keep provider selection and runtime observations in the Twin's Rhai observer.

docs.title: Read runtime evidence
docs.text:
Before treating a live value as final, check readiness:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/ready"

Require ready: true, world_hold: false, and pending_count: 0. A missing port is not a zero; it can mean the owner is still preparing.

For the coupled chain, read:

  • CosimStatus for per-entity model timing, status, and propagated values.
  • GetBrokenConnections for rejected wires and dropped writes.
  • CausalTrace for an admitted input edge and its producer identity.
  • ListTelemetryChannels then QueryTelemetryHistory for retained samples.
  • ExportTelemetryRecording for a columnar times/series export.

A single sample proves a moment; a history query proves a trend. Use one ReadPortsBatch response when comparing values from the same simulation tick. The telemetry t value is simulation seconds; epoch_jd gives the absolute mission frame when one is authored.

docs.title: Make an accuracy claim
docs.text:
Separate three questions before saying a model is accurate:

  1. Model form. What equations, assumptions, and neglected effects define the model?
  2. Numerical verification. Which solver, step size, tolerances, units, and initial conditions were used? Did refinement change the answer?
  3. Validation. What reference data was used, over what range, with what tolerance, and on which build?

Record the answer with the run. Compare the exported telemetry against a reference run or an external tool. A reference FMU can be run through native FMI import when you need an independent implementation, but that is a comparison setup, not an automatic equivalence proof.

A useful evidence record contains:

  • the Twin revision and luncosim build;
  • the exact scene and scenario paths;
  • the passed requirements and verdict channels;
  • the reference data source and tolerance;
  • the readiness and cosim diagnostics;
  • a screenshot when the claim includes presentation.

Do not use a render screenshot as numerical evidence, and do not use a green scene test as an accuracy certificate.

docs.title: A practical gate
docs.text: Stage Run While authoring luncosim --validate on every changed asset Before opening a Twin ValidateTwin and RunLint Before sharing a behavior luncosim test --scene … Before claiming a requirement is met luncosim test --verification … Before publishing a result Reference comparison, versioned evidence, and a saved recording or screenshot

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text: Trap Better check Treating --validate as a runtime test Run the authored scene test Treating a missing port as 0.0 Check readiness and ListPorts Accepting a test with no verdict Require exit 0, not merely no failure Comparing samples from different ticks Use one batch read Calling a screenshot "validation" Pair it with numeric evidence Claiming FMI conformance from one imported FMU State the exact FMI profile and tested limits

docs.title: Rhai
docs.text:
Rhai is LunCoSim's language for scenario policy. A scenario is a persistent program attached to an entity. It observes the simulation, reacts to events, and issues typed commands. It does not integrate physics, solve equations, or replace a Modelica model.

Rhai is small, sandboxed, and implemented in Rust. The same scripts run on the desktop and in the browser build. The engine exposes a deliberately narrow host surface; most convenience comes from an editable prelude written in Rhai itself.

docs.title: What Rhai owns
docs.text:
Fact Authored as Consumed by Mission phases and objectives task, mission, on_event Scenario runtime Waypoint selection and sequencing Task-tree constructors Native behavior kernel Reactions to events on_event and wait_for Event bus User-facing hints and tutorial flow HUD prelude helpers Workbench UI Test assertions and verdicts Authored test scenarios luncosim test Policy that should change without a rebuild .rhai assets and tool libraries Hot-reload pipeline

Rhai does not own continuous equations, direct scene-graph mutation outside the command surface, a second implementation of a Modelica controller, or per-tick polling that should be an event or a task predicate.

docs.title: A scenario is attached, not global
docs.text:
A scenario is a prim applying LunCoProgramAPI — usually a child Scope — or a program started against a specific entity:

def Scope "Mission" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
) {
    uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover/scenarios/drive.rhai@
}

The asset source is loaded and hot-replaced by the asset layer. In the editor and API workflows you can also run a scenario directly against an entity with RunScenario, or run a file-backed asset with RunScenarioAsset.

The program prim is the authored attachment point, but the runtime binds me to its immediate owning prim. Use name(me) for the vessel or mission host that owns the program; parent(me) refers to the scene hierarchy above that owner and is not a replacement for the program host.

docs.title: Lifecycle at a glance
The command/query bridge
docs.text:
Scripts use the same public surface as the UI and HTTP API:

let result = cmd("SetPorts", #{ target: rover, writes: [["throttle", 0.4]] });
let state = query("QueryPhysicsState", #{ id: rover });
let rover = find("Rover");
  • cmd(name, params) performs a write with side effects.
  • query(name, params) reads state; no-data is (), failure is an error map.
  • emit(name, value) produces a telemetry event delivered to on_event.
  • Prelude helpers such as drive, brake, nav_to, possess, and input_hint compose common behavior.

The full command surface is generated by the running app and is intentionally larger than this chapter. Use the app's command reference or discover it over the HTTP API when you need an exact name.

docs.title: Events, not polling
docs.text: Production scenarios should react to events or task predicates. A fixed-tick on_tick loop is reserved for test sampling and verdicts. The kernel already advances tasks, waits, and event leaves; re-implementing that in a polling loop duplicates the runtime and makes the scenario less deterministic.

docs.title: Determinism and ownership
docs.text:
Scenarios run in a defined owner scope and clock. Twin, application, and core policy are distinct. A script must not assume it can mutate another owner's state on an arbitrary thread.

Directives can select the execution target and timing:

// @peer host
// @timing simulation

host includes the standalone authoritative process. simulation is the default; presentation runs on application frames and may submit typed domain commands, but not direct structural world writes. Use these only when the behavior genuinely needs that scope.

docs.title: Reading this chapter
docs.text: Section Question it answers Lifecycle When does each hook run, and what state does it own? Tasks How is a mission expressed as a task tree? Commands and queries How does a script read and change the world? Events How do scripts coordinate without calling each other? Testing How does a scenario produce a PASS or FAIL verdict? Patterns What do real mission and controller scripts look like? Tooling How do the prelude, tool libraries, and authoring tools fit together?

docs.title: Practical rules
docs.text:
• Put equations and state in Modelica; put sequencing and decisions in Rhai.
  • Attach the scenario to the entity that owns the behavior.
  • Use task for progression and on_event for external reactions.
  • Use cmd for operations with side effects and set only for tuning writes.
  • Release control, stop actuators, and clear owned state in on_stop.
  • Keep scenario state in this; keep source files hot-reloadable.
  • Test the public command and query result, not a private script detail.

docs.title: Commands and queries
docs.text:
A script touches the world through the same typed command and query surface as the UI, HTTP API, and MCP. It does not receive a private scene-graph pointer and it does not call Rust functions directly. That restriction is what keeps a scenario portable, auditable, and safe to hot-reload.

The bridge has two directions:

Direction Verb Contract Write with side effects cmd(name, params) Fires a registered command; returns an acknowledgement Read state query(name, params) Calls a read-only provider; returns data, (), or an error map Tuning write set(id, path, value) Writes a reflected field or scalar port; not replicated Tuning read get(id, path) Reads a reflected component field Resource write set_setting(path, value) Writes a reflected resource field Resource read get_setting(path) Reads a reflected resource field

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
let result = cmd("SetPorts", #{
    target: rover,
    writes: [["throttle", 0.4], ["steer", -0.1]],
});

if result.ok != true {
    print("command failed: " + result.error);
}

cmd returns a map with id, ok, data, and error. The id is the correlation id for a deferred result and for causal tracing. data carries command-specific result data, such as a spawned entity id.

Commands are the right channel for an operation that must be authoritative, replicated, undoable, or observed by another subsystem. Examples include SetPorts, ReleasePort, ReleaseControl, LoadScene, SpawnEntity, SetObjectProperty, ApplyUsdOp, CompileModel, SetModelInput, TeleportToSurface, RunScenario, RegisterTimeline, and CaptureFromCamera.

Use command_result(id) when a command is admitted asynchronously:

let pending = cmd("LoadScene", #{ path: "twin://my-twin/scenes/yard.usda" });
let result = command_result(pending.id);

command_result accepts native unsigned command ids and non-negative integer literals. A negative id is an evaluation error.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
let hit = query("Raycast", #{ origin: [0.0, 1.0, 0.0], direction: [0.0, -1.0, 0.0] });
let nearest = query("Nearest", #{ position: world_pos(me), radius: 25.0 });

A successful query returns its data directly. A successful query with no data returns (). A failure returns a map with ok: false and an error field, so a script can distinguish "nothing there" from "the provider rejected the call".

Useful providers include Raycast, Nearest, GroundHeight, CausalTrace, ListSpawnCatalog, ValidateTwin, SensorOccupants, Links, InspectSelection, ListOpenDocuments, ListDatasets, and ListToolLibraries. The exact provider list belongs to the running app; a scenario should discover rather than assume an optional provider exists.

docs.title: Reads and writes by reflected path
docs.text:
get and set address a reflected component field by name:

let battery = get(rover, "Battery.level");
set(rover, "Battery.level", 0.8);

Vectors are returned as [x, y, z] and quaternions as [x, y, z, w]. Structs are returned as maps. A missing field or an unsupported type returns (), and set returns false on a bad path or type.

get_setting and set_setting use the same path shape for reflected resources:

let samples = get_setting("RendererSettings.samples_per_pixel");
set_setting("RendererSettings.samples_per_pixel", 256);

These are host-side tuning writes. They are not replicated, undoable, or a persistent port hold. A client-targeted script cannot use them because there is no prediction or forwarding path.

docs.title: Ports and control
docs.text:
set may fall through to a canonical scalar co-simulation port, but that is a raw write. Use commands when the value must persist until an explicit release:

cmd("SetPorts", #{ target: rover, writes: [["throttle", 0.5]] });
cmd("ReleasePort", #{ target: rover, name: "throttle" });
cmd("ReleaseControl", #{ target: rover });

ReleaseControl returns every local input hold to authored wiring without writing replacement values. Send an explicit SetPorts value if a safe setpoint is required.

Control authority is a separate concern:

claim_control(me);
drive(me, 0.5, 0.0);
release_control_claim(me);

ClaimControl and ReleaseControlClaim update the session authority table. AcquireControl composes the same transition with an avatar ControlLink and optional camera binding. An unpossessed vessel can still fly its own guidance; it discards external stick writes.

For discrete controls, use an atomic semantic edge instead of two ordered held writes:

intent_pulse(lander, "release");

intent_edge(target, intent, edge) accepts pressed, released, or pulse. The controller publishes intent.edge; authored Twin policy decides what the edge means and which ports it writes. Use SetPorts or SimulateIntent for level-triggered and continuous control.

docs.title: Identity and hierarchy
docs.text:
Verb Returns Use find(name) Entity id, or -1 Lookup by canonical Name name(id) Presentation label Human-readable text, not identity usd_path(id) Projected USD prim path Identity-only lookup, safe during dependency planning parent(id) Parent id or () Hierarchy traversal children(id) Child id array Hierarchy traversal list_entities() Entity records Enumerate the live world owner_of(id) Session id or () Which session owns the entity controller(id) Session role or () Controlling role, if any is_controlled(id) Boolean Whether any session owns it

list_entities() returns records with id, name, type, catalog_id, input_surface, control_bound, celestial_body, and pos. name is the human-readable presentation label; type is the projected USD kind, not a control-component heuristic. input_surface is the authoritative InputPorts readiness bit.

find is a name lookup, not a path lookup. Use an explicit USD path or a relationship when identity must be stable across renames.

docs.title: Pose and spatial values
Settings and Twin policy
docs.text:
let speed = get_twin_setting("mission.cruise_speed");
set_twin_setting("mission.cruise_speed", 1.4);

get_twin_setting reads a scalar from the active Twin manifest's generic [settings] table. set_twin_setting persists a scalar through the generic SetTwinSetting command. There is no per-setting Rust binding.

twin_name() returns the current twin:// mount authority from the asset registry; it is empty only when no Twin is active. Reopening a Twin assigns a fresh authority, so use this value for Twin source queries rather than reconstructing it from the manifest name.

get_exposure("namespace", "property") reads one raw value from the generic engine exposure registry. Rhai owns selection and presentation policy.

docs.title: Clock and execution context
docs.text:
Verb Meaning sim_tick() Current fixed simulation tick dt() Configured physics timestep elapsed_seconds() Simulation seconds execution_context() Owner scope, cycle, phase, clock sample, sequence, and producer stamp

These calls reject use outside the simulation cycle as a Rhai invocation error. A wrong-cycle call does not fault the simulation or another runtime cycle. dt() reads the configured physics timestep; pause and rate changes do not rescale it.

execution_context() is read-only. It reports the stable Twin id when the scenario is Twin-owned, the scene generation when one is committed, and the event producer stamp for an on_event pass. Scope, Twin id, cycle, and generation are unit when no owner route exists.

docs.title: Deterministic randomness
docs.text: rand(), rand_range(lo, hi), and rand_int(lo, hi) use deterministic per-hook seeding. The seed is derived from the entity, the event producer or cycle sequence, and the hook. A re-run with the same inputs produces the same sequence, so a script does not need to seed explicitly.

docs.title: Structural operations
docs.text:
add(id, "Comp", #{fields}) inserts or replaces a reflected component. remove(id, "Comp") strips one. despawn(id) despawns an entity and its children. These are structural operations and replicate on a host.

Spawning uses the catalog command rather than a generic constructor:

let spawned = cmd("SpawnEntity", #{
    entry_id: "skid_rover",
    position: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
});

Actorless Rhai callers of raw-file scenes also pass a stable nonzero producer_id.

docs.title: Structural invalidation
docs.text:
Policy that reads USD topology on a fixed tick should use the owning document's generation as its invalidation clock:

let generation = usd_document_generation(doc_id);

The native bridge reads the document host's generation directly. A policy may cache a route, component, or relationship snapshot and refresh it only when the generation changes. Runtime transforms, sensor values, and actuation stay on their live per-tick paths because they are state, not structural invalidation.

docs.title: Assets and JSON
docs.text:
asset_source_relative_uri(document, relative) resolves a safe document-relative asset while preserving its registered source authority. It is URI algebra only and performs no filesystem read.

parse_json(text) returns native maps, arrays, and scalars, or () for JSON null. Malformed JSON and integers outside Rhai's signed integer range are errors.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Events are the coordination mechanism between scenarios. A script does not call another script directly; it emits a named telemetry event, and interested scenarios receive it through on_event or a task event leaf. This keeps the scripts isolated, replayable, and independent of entity iteration order.

docs.title: Emitting
docs.text:
emit("MARKER_REACHED", #{ marker: 3, position: world_pos(me) });

emit reuses the shared TelemetryEvent bus. The name is the YAMCS mnemonic; the value is a typed scalar, array, or map. External clients receive the same event through SubscribeTelemetry.

Emitting is not a synchronous call into another script. The event is queued and delivered on the receiver's next eligible pass.

docs.title: Receiving
docs.text:
fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "MARKER_REACHED" {
        this.reached = true;
        notify_kind("Marker reached", "success");
    }
}

evt is a map with name, source (the emitter gid), value, severity, timestamp, sim_secs, and sim_tick. ctx carries the scenario parameters and execution context of the receiving pass.

A task can wait for an event instead of handling it in on_event:

fn task(me, ctx) {
    seq([
        once(|m| notify("Waiting for the sample")),
        wait_for("SAMPLE_READY"),
        once(|m| notify("Sample is ready")),
    ])
}

Use wait_for_from(event, src) when the event must come from a specific entity or path. act_until_event(act, event, src) keeps an action running until the scoped event arrives.

docs.title: Delivery and ordering
docs.text:
• A running simulation releases events whose recorded tick precedes the current SimTick after SimTickSet.
  • While paused, the next Update pass delivers discrete events without advancing the fixed tick.
  • Events emitted while a pass is delivering its current batch remain queued for the following pass. A lifecycle hook can publish a readiness edge without losing it at the dispatch boundary.
  • Every event carries the simulator's sim_secs and sim_tick stamp. The absolute timestamp is only the derived TDB epoch label.
  • While the scene-readiness lifecycle gate is closed, events are not buffered because no scenario can consume them and the gated driver cannot drain them.
  • Scene transitions clear pending events from the outgoing scene.
  • A new or restarted program does not receive events accumulated before its on_start. Query current state instead of relying on history.

Events emitted by on_start retain their producer stamp for the next eligible scenario pass. Inter-script interaction is bus-only because each scenario runs in an isolated VM.

docs.title: Coordinator and workers
docs.text:
A single coordinator owns assignment; workers own local execution. The coordinator reacts to worker readiness and publishes one assignment per worker:

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "WORKER_READY" {
        let worker = evt.value.worker;
        cmd("SetPorts", #{ target: worker, writes: [["assigned", 1.0]] });
        emit("ASSIGNMENT", #{ worker: worker, task: "survey" });
    }
}

The workers never address each other. They emit readiness and completion, and the coordinator decides what happens next.

docs.title: Phase transitions
docs.text:
A mission can use events as durable phase boundaries:

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "DESCENT_COMPLETE" && this.phase == "descent" {
        this.phase = "surface";
        mission_checkpoint(me, mission_document(me), "@root@", "phase", "surface");
        notify("Surface phase");
    }
}

The checkpoint writes through the explicit USD document path, so a hot reload can resume the phase instead of restarting the mission.

docs.title: Sensor and collision events
docs.text:
Generic sensor and collision events carry the identities a scenario needs to decide what happened:

Event family Payload use SENSOR_ENTER / SENSOR_EXIT Sensor and moving-body identity COLLISION_START / COLLISION_END Collision pair intent.edge Target, intent, edge, correlation id intent.hold Held intent with producer and input-order stamp

The prelude wraps the collision family with collision_pair, collision_other, entered, and exited.

TriggerZone labels additionally provide named geofence events. A route program can advance on the matching named sensor enter without re-creating distance checks.

docs.title: Model events
docs.text:
A Modelica condition becomes an event through USD, not through a script polling the model:

  1. Express the condition in Modelica as a 0/1 output.
  2. Connect it to a def LunCoEvent prim through inputs:trigger.connect.
  3. Author the bus-facing lunco:event:name and lunco:event:severity on the event prim.
  4. Receive the event in on_event on a later eligible pass.

Physical thresholds and hysteresis stay in the model. USD owns the wire. Rhai owns the response.

docs.title: Event names are protocol
docs.text:
Event names are authored strings, not an enum. Treat them as a stable protocol between the producer and every consumer:

  • Keep names uppercase and specific: DESCENT_COMPLETE, not DONE.
  • Put structured data in the value map instead of encoding it in the name.
  • Do not rename an event without updating every consumer and test.
  • Prefer one meaningful event over a stream of per-tick telemetry when the consumer only needs the transition.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: A scenario is compiled once, initialized once, and then advanced by the owner that invoked it. The lifecycle separates dependency planning, module initialization, the ready callback, steady-state progression, event reactions, and teardown. Keeping those stages distinct prevents a script from reading a participant that has not been admitted or from running two copies of the same mutable state.

docs.title: The hook sequence
docs.text:
Stage Hook or body Runs Allowed work Admission plan simulation_dependencies(me, ctx) Before mutable initialization Read stable identities and declare required inputs Module body Top-level statements Once per instance, after declared inputs are ready Construct per-instance state in this Ready callback on_start(me, ctx) Once at the ready boundary Setup that needs the live owner Progression task(me, ctx) Tree built once; advanced each fixed step Actions, predicates, waits, event leaves Objectives mission(me, ctx) Declared once; evaluated by the runtime Objective state and completion conditions Reaction on_event(me, evt, ctx) Next eligible pass after an event arrives Discrete policy and state updates Sampling on_tick(me, ctx) Each authored cadence tick Test sampling only Teardown on_stop(me, ctx) Hot reload, detach, despawn, scene teardown Release control and stop actuators

A script may define any subset. The runtime treats a missing hook as absent; it does not invent a default task or a default teardown.

docs.title: Initialization and readiness
docs.text:
Scenario admission waits until all world and entity readiness holds clear, because a program can reference entities outside its own hierarchy. After admission, a later entity hold idles scenarios attached in that subtree and release resumes them without restarting.

simulation_dependencies is the place to declare what the scenario needs. It runs before mutable initialization and may use only stable identities, parameters, and its declared read surface. It must not read facts from the inputs it requires before they are admitted.

The top-level module body then initializes per-instance scope with its stable scenario identity. Declared query_reads work during initialization as well as in later hooks. on_start follows before the activation pass advances its task or tick hook.

on_start is the ready boundary. It runs after applicable scene admission and after the owner's required inputs are ready. A new or restarted program does not receive events accumulated before its on_start; startup policy queries current state instead of relying on history. For sensors, use SensorOccupants in on_start when the initial occupancy matters.

docs.title: Scenario parameters
docs.text:
One source can serve many entities. Pass one natural typed object as params:

{
  "type": "ExecuteCommand",
  "command": "RunScenario",
  "params": {
    "target": 4869542932533563,
    "source": "<rhai source text>",
    "params": { "speed": 1.5 }
  }
}

fn task(me, ctx) {
    let speed = if ctx.speed == () { 0.6 } else { ctx.speed };
    forever(once(|m| drive(m, speed, 0.0)))
}

Omitting params means an empty map. Rhai owns the default for each key, so a scenario chooses the default that fits its policy. The command boundary rejects a scalar, array, null, non-finite number, or a value outside the shared telemetry range. Rust validates and transfers the typed map once per program instance.

param(id, key, default) is a separate helper: it reads a lunco:param:<key> attribute authored on the prim and does not read launch parameters.

docs.title: Owner scope and clocks
docs.text:
The runtime assigns persistent scenario hooks to the cycles owned by the selected application plugins. The script does not choose its Core, Application, or Twin owner; Rust assigns that owner and the schedules that invoke it.

Use directives to select the network peer and the cadence:

// @peer host|client|both
// @timing simulation|presentation

host includes the standalone authoritative process. Omitted timing is simulation. A presentation program runs the same task interpreter on application frames with presentation-clock waits, including while the simulation is paused or manually held. It submits typed domain commands and cannot perform direct reflection or structural world writes.

An unsupported target or timing value, or an unknown metadata directive, disables only that scenario and publishes a document diagnostic for that source revision. Editing the source reparses its directives before the new program runs. Timing metadata does not install schedules, and it does not choose the script's owner.

A standalone Twin presentation program can start and handle navigation without a scene. Its Twin lease and its own declared inputs remain mandatory. Scene-owned programs retain the scene readiness gate.

docs.title: Presentation preparation
docs.text:
on_visualization(me, ctx) runs once in PreUpdate, after lifecycle, document, and terrain admission scans and time-spine projection, but before the first fixed tick. Scene-dependent programs wait for scene, reference, document, and terrain preparation holds; Modelica holds do not block this visual path. Independent presentation programs do not require scene admission.

Its context uses presentation time and has no simulation tick, so it can prepare disposable visual state while Modelica participants are loading. Rhai blocks world writes and events in this phase; only ApplyUsdTransientOps can update the disposable USD view.

docs.title: Hot reload and teardown
docs.text:
Rhai is designed for a fast edit-run loop:

  • The native app loads the prelude and authored scripts from disk.
  • Editing a file-backed scenario can reload it without rebuilding Rust.
  • The outgoing program's on_stop runs before the new one starts.
  • On Twin close or scene replacement, the owner retires its scripts and state.

Always release control, stop actuators, and clear owned state in on_stop when the script acquired them:

fn on_stop(me, ctx) {
    brake(me);
    release_control_claim(me);
}

An inline RunScenario source has no file to watch. Re-issue the command with the updated text to hot-reload it. A file-backed program is replaced by the asset pipeline.

docs.title: Failure and diagnostics
docs.text:
Runtime errors stay visible through the script diagnostics and do not become successful no-ops. A compile error or runtime fault is reported through ScriptStatus with file, line, and column where available. ScriptInspect shows the live this map, defined hooks, generation, and paused/running state.

A malformed directive or an invalid parameter disables only the affected scenario. It does not fault the simulation or another runtime cycle.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: The patterns below are compositions of the same small surface: a task tree, an event reaction, a query, and a typed command. They are policy, not engine features. Copy the shape, then put the vehicle-specific numbers in the Twin.

docs.title: Route following
docs.text:
A route is an ordered set of USD points plus a sibling program. The program resolves its subject, reads the point poses, and advances only when the matching sensor event arrives:

fn task(me, ctx) {
    let points = ctx.points;
    let steps = [];
    for point in points {
        steps.push(step(
            |m| nav_to(m, point, 1.0, 2.0),
            |m| arrived(m, point, 2.0),
        ));
    }
    seq(steps)
}

A file-backed route program resolves its ordered point scope from USD and passes the poses into the same task shape. The reusable route_follow policy records only the next unvisited point in USD order. Out-of-order arrivals do not mark later points. A visited point is turned gray through the transient USD view; the authored route_point.usda marker owns the standard translucent, unlit, shadowless visual.

Route points are not stored on a vessel-owned list. The scene owns the route, and the program owns the traversal policy.

docs.title: Coordinator and workers
docs.text:
Use one coordinator when several workers must not race for assignments:

// Coordinator
fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "WORKER_READY" {
        let worker = evt.value.worker;
        emit("ASSIGNMENT", #{ worker: worker, task: this.next_task });
        this.next_task += 1;
    }
}

// Worker
fn on_start(me, ctx) {
    emit("WORKER_READY", #{ worker: me });
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "ASSIGNMENT" && evt.value.worker == me {
        this.task = evt.value.task;
    }
}

The workers never call each other. They publish readiness and completion, and the coordinator owns the assignment order. This is the multi-robot mission pattern used by the example coordinator and worker scenarios.

docs.title: Reactive obstacle avoidance
docs.text:
A reactive selector prefers avoidance while an obstacle is present and falls back to the route:

fn task(me, ctx) {
    reactive_sel([
        seq([
            check(|m| obstacle_ahead(m, 8.0, 50.0)),
            once(|m| brake(m)),
        ]),
        forever(step(
            |m| nav_to(m, [120.0, 0.0, 50.0], 0.7, 3.0),
            |m| false,
        )),
    ])
}

obstacle_ahead is a sensing helper, not a native autopilot. The policy decides whether to brake, steer, or wait. Continuous steering remains in the authored drive law.

docs.title: Phases and durable checkpoints
docs.text:
Keep the phase in this for the current run and checkpoint it in USD when the mission must survive a reload:

fn on_start(me, ctx) {
    this.phase = mission_checkpoint_read(me, "phase");
    if this.phase == () { this.phase = "descent"; }
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "TOUCHDOWN" && this.phase == "descent" {
        this.phase = "surface";
        mission_checkpoint(me, mission_document(me), "@root@", "phase", "surface");
    }
}

mission_document(me) returns the explicit document id supplied by ListOpenDocuments. The checkpoint helper writes a lunco:mission:checkpoint: attribute through ApplyUsdOp; it does not invent a second persistence file.

docs.title: Controller claim
docs.text:
A vessel that drives itself through an authored program has three layers:

  • the control law in Modelica;
  • the mission logic in Rhai;
  • the structure and authority in USD.

Claim authority before commanding a vessel that expects an external pilot:

fn on_start(me, ctx) {
    claim_control(me);
}

fn on_stop(me, ctx) {
    brake(me);
    release_control_claim(me);
}

AcquireControl composes the claim with an avatar ControlLink and optional camera binding. ClaimControl updates the session authority table without an avatar, which is what a headless run needs.

Control authority is the wired piloted signal. An unpossessed vessel can still fly its own guidance; it discards external stick writes. If a vehicle "ignores throttle and just falls", check authority before debugging the command.

docs.title: Tutorial flow
docs.text:
A tutorial is a scenario. The HUD prelude exposes the presentation primitives:

Helper Presents hint(msg) / clear_hint() A sticky instruction objectives_hud(list) An objective list; mission auto-publishes guided_hud_actions(tool, hook, actions) Persistent semantic buttons spotlight(anchor, caption) A dimmed, ringed workbench widget focus_panel(id) Opens a singleton workbench panel coach_step(steps, i) One coach-mark tour step

Tutorial progression is authored in the lesson's on_event, where it matches raw public event names such as cmd:<Name>, key:<Name>, and authored simulation events. coach_step only presents a step; it does not advance the cursor.

Keep lesson-specific runtime checks in Rhai observers under assets/scenarios/tests/ and run them through luncosim test, so changing a tutorial script does not require rebuilding Rust.

docs.title: Tool libraries
docs.text:
Put reusable policy in a tool library rather than copying it into every scenario:

let plan = formation::line(leader, 4, 12.0);

A tool is a named bundle callable as libname::fn(...) from any hook. Tools can import other registered tools with ordinary Rhai syntax. A tool that must be available before the first lifecycle hook should be imported by its explicit lunco:// asset URI, because a namespace call does not declare an asset dependency.

Use a tool for geometry, formation, survey, or authoring policy that several Twin scenarios share. Keep vehicle-specific limits and mission text in the Twin.

docs.title: Script-first authoring
docs.text:
A scenario can build or inspect a USD assembly through explicit document ids:

let context = model_authoring::model_context(doc, root, "@root@");
let ready = model_authoring::readiness_report(doc, root, "@root@", policy);
let recipe = model_authoring::scene_recipe(doc, "@root@", scene, context.generation);

The sequence is inspect → plan → apply → checkpoint. Keep the identity tuple from the document read: document, root path, edit target, generation. Apply through assembly_edit::batch or the normal proposal/review/commit flow, then re-read the new generation. Do not write USDA text directly.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text: Pattern Problem Use instead on_tick control loop in production Duplicates the kernel and hurts determinism task, wait_until, on_event while true inside a hook Blocks the owner and never yields A task tree with waits Polling a value every tick Wastes work and hides the real transition A predicate or event leaf Direct writes from a client script No prediction or forwarding path A typed command One scenario for every entity Shared state and unclear ownership One program per owner, events between them Hardcoded scene paths Breaks when the Twin moves twin:// and lunco:// addresses Copying a prelude helper Drifts from the shared contract A tool library

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A mission is a task tree. task(me, ctx) returns pure data once, and the native behavior kernel advances one deterministic step per fixed tick. The kernel owns the cursor, dwell timestamps, event delivery, and terminal status. The script owns which actions, predicates, event names, and compositions the mission requests.

This split is the reason a production scenario does not need a fixed-tick loop. A hand-written on_tick cursor duplicates the kernel and makes the mission less deterministic.

docs.title: One explicit node schema
docs.text:
Every node is a map with a required string kind. There is no inference from which fields happen to be present, no default leaf, and no fallback spelling. The prelude constructors are the authoring API. Handwritten maps are useful for tests and generated policy only when they obey the same schema.

kind Required fields Runtime meaning once act Call the action once, then succeed step act, done Call the action while the predicate is false act_for act, secs Call the action while the simulation dwell is active act_until_event act, event, src Call the action until the named event arrives from the specified gid or path wait secs Succeed after the simulation dwell wait_until done Succeed when the predicate returns true wait_for event Succeed when any emitter produces the event name wait_for_from event, src Succeed for the event from the specified gid or path check check Return success or failure immediately from the predicate seq, sel, all, race, reactive_seq, reactive_sel items Compose child nodes repeat, retry n, body Repeat a child by count or retry failures forever, invert, force_ok, force_fail body Apply a decorator to one child

Unknown kinds, missing required fields, wrong field types, and fields belonging to another kind are compile errors. __bt is reserved runtime bookkeeping on the root map and is not authored policy.

The words in kind are schema discriminators, not mission text. Event names such as "GO" and emitted telemetry names remain authored protocol strings.

docs.title: Leaf callbacks
docs.text:
Action and predicate fields accept either an anonymous Rhai closure with one positional argument (|me| ...) or a named script function pointer (Fn("name"), declared as fn name(me)). me is the host entity id. Both forms access the persistent scenario-state map as the driver-bound this.

The native task driver borrows that map directly and owns progression for both forms. Callback errors propagate as script diagnostics; state mutations already performed remain in the bound map, as they do for lifecycle hooks.

Rhai maps passed to helper functions are value or copy-on-write values. Assigning a field in a helper does not update the caller's this. A helper that changes task state must return the updated map or an explicit result, and the lifecycle callback must assign it back to this.

fn task(me, ctx) {
    seq([
        once(|m| drive(m, 1.0, 0.0)),
        wait_until(|m| arrived(m, [10.0, 0.0, 0.0], 2.0)),
        wait_for("SAMPLE_READY"),
    ])
}

docs.title: Constructors
docs.text:
The prelude in tasks.rhai exposes the readable constructors:

Constructor Composes once(act) One action, then success step(act, done) Drive until a predicate is true act_for(act, secs) Run an action for a simulation dwell act_until_event(act, event, src) Run an action until a scoped event wait(secs) A simulation dwell wait_until(done) A predicate wait wait_for(event) An unscoped event wait wait_for_from(event, src) An event wait scoped to a source check(pred) An immediate pass/fail predicate seq(items) Run children in order sel(items) Select the first child that succeeds par_all(items) Run children in parallel; all must succeed par_race(items) Run children in parallel; the first terminal result wins reactive_seq(items) Re-evaluate children reactively in sequence reactive_sel(items) Re-evaluate children reactively for selection repeat(n, body) Repeat a child a fixed number of times forever(body) Repeat a child indefinitely retry(n, body) Retry a failing child invert(body) Invert success and failure force_ok(body) Treat any result as success force_fail(body) Treat any result as failure

The kernel emits TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED for the native task root.

docs.title: A route mission
docs.text:
fn task(me, ctx) {
    let goals = [[12.0, 0.0, 0.0], [12.0, 0.0, 25.0]];
    let steps = [];
    for i in 0..goals.len() {
        let goal = goals[i];
        steps.push(step(
            |m| nav_to(m, goal, 1.0, 2.0),
            |m| arrived(m, goal, 2.0),
        ));
    }
    steps.push(wait_for("MISSION_RELEASE"));
    seq(steps)
}

nav_to publishes a waypoint to the authored drive law; it does not integrate motion itself. arrived reads the authoritative pose and checks the radius.

docs.title: Reactive selection
docs.text:
A reactive tree can prefer an avoidance branch while an obstacle is present and otherwise follow the route:

fn task(me, ctx) {
    reactive_sel([
        seq([
            check(|m| obstacle_ahead(m, 8.0, 50.0)),
            once(|m| brake(m)),
        ]),
        forever(step(
            |m| nav_to(m, [120.0, 0.0, 50.0], 0.7, 3.0),
            |m| false,
        )),
    ])
}

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
mission(me, ctx) is separate from task. It declares objective state and completion conditions that the runtime can display and evaluate:

fn mission(me, ctx) {
    let goal = [12.0, 0.0, 8.0];
    [
        objective("reach_marker", #{
            text: "Drive to the marker",
            done: |m| arrived(m, goal, 2.0),
        }),
    ]
}

An objective is policy, not a second progression engine. The task tree still owns the actions and waits that move the mission forward.

docs.title: Timelines
docs.text:
A timeline is a mission expressed as pure data. Each step contains exactly one explicit operation word and only that operation's fields:

Operation Meaning move_to Drive to a world position move_to_entity Drive to another entity possess Acquire control of a subject brake Stop a subject cmd Issue a typed command emit Publish a telemetry event wait Dwell for simulation seconds wait_event Wait for a named event

Common fields such as subject, speed, radius, secs, params, and value are validated against the selected operation at the command boundary.

compile_timeline lowers a timeline onto the same task-tree contract. A timeline is serializable, so it can run inline with RunTimeline or be stored and run with RunStoredTimeline. Stored timelines live under <twin>/timelines/*.json and are discovered with ListTimelines and GetTimeline.

Timelines do not create a second progression engine. They lower into the same task(me, ctx) contract.

docs.title: Task state and durability
docs.text:
Use this for ordinary per-instance task state. For a mission that must resume after a hot reload or restart, author phase state on the host prim through the explicit USD document path:

fn mission_document(me) {
    // Return the document id supplied by ListOpenDocuments.
    42
}

mission_checkpoint and mission_checkpoint_read write and read USD string attributes at objective or phase boundaries. This keeps durable state in USD rather than in a second persistence mechanism.

docs.title: Authoring rules
docs.text:
• Return a tree from task(me, ctx); do not implement a fixed-tick loop.
  • Use wait_for and wait_until instead of polling in on_tick.
  • Keep event names stable; they are the authored protocol between scripts.
  • Keep leaf callbacks pure where possible; return state changes explicitly.
  • Prefer an existing composite or decorator before adding a new mechanism.
  • Use on_tick only in authored tests that sample state and publish a verdict.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: A scenario can be a test. The same Rhai runtime that drives a mission can sample live state, assert a property, and publish a typed verdict. The production scene-test runner consumes that verdict and turns it into a process exit code. No private Rust harness and no rebuilt simulator are required.

docs.title: The verdict contract
docs.text:
A test scenario emits a telemetry event on a named channel:

fn on_start(me, ctx) {
    this.start = world_pos3(me);
    this.reported = false;
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name != "MARKER_REACHED" { return; }
    if this.reported { return; }
    this.reported = true;

    let pos = world_pos3(me);
    let distance = if pos == () || this.start == () {
        ()
    } else {
        vlen(vsub(pos, this.start))
    };

    let fails = [];
    fails.push(t_present(pos, "rover position"));
    fails.push(t_moved(distance, 3.0, "rover travel"));
    report_verdict(fails, "DRIVE TEST", "DRIVE_TEST");
}

report_verdict(fails, title, channel) prints the failures, emits a typed verdict on channel, and raises a notification. The runner reads the channel and returns:

Exit Meaning 0 PASS 1 FAIL 2 No verdict was produced

A test that exhausts its tick budget without a verdict is exit 2. That is a failure of the test, not a pass by default.

docs.title: Assertion helpers
docs.text:
The auto_tests.rhai prelude provides checks that return an empty string on success and a self-describing message on failure. The caller collects them into an array, so every check runs and the report names all failures.

Helper Checks t_range(v, lo, hi, what) A value lies inside an inclusive range t_max(v, limit, what) An absolute value does not exceed a bound t_true(cond, what) A plain predicate t_present(v, what) A value was measured at all t_rel(a, b, tol_pct, what) Two values agree within a relative tolerance t_bounded(pos, radius_m, what) A body remains at a finite position inside the scene t_moved(distance_m, min_m, what) Something actually moved

A silent pass is not a pass. A hook that never fires, a find that returned -1, and a phase that never advanced all look like a clean run. Pair a measurement check with t_present, and pair a stationary check with t_moved, so a dead command surface cannot produce a meaningless match.

report_structured_verdict(report, title, channel) accepts a structured requirement report with pass, fail, inconclusive, error, or unverified evidence. A report with no checks and no results is inconclusive, not a pass.

docs.title: Negative fixtures
docs.text:
A test that cannot fail is not evidence. Keep a fixture that reproduces the defect the test is guarding against:

  • expect_fault(port) declares a deliberately dangling port in a lint fixture. The runner asserts that the declared port really dangles.
  • expect_runtime_fault(kind) declares the terminal runtime fault a negative production fixture must reproduce.
  • expect_scene_load_failure(path, detail_contains) asserts that a later load_scene(path) fails with the specified terminal detail.

These helpers assert, they do not mute. A fixture that quietly stops reproducing its defect fails the scene.

docs.title: Where tests live
docs.text:
A production scene test keeps the fixture and the observer in the authored asset tree:

assets/
├── scenes/tests/
│   └── rover_drive.usda
└── scenarios/tests/
    └── rover_drive.rhai

The fixture scene carries the geometry, physics, and program attachments. The observer scenario is attached to a host prim and publishes the verdict. Assert the public command or query result, not a private script detail.

Do not embed a large USDA string in a Rust test when the behavior can be observed through the production scene runner. Rust tests remain for low-level parsing, serialization, lowering, and generic engine seams that Rhai cannot observe.

docs.title: Running a scene test
docs.text:
luncosim test --scene assets/scenes/tests/rover_drive.usda
luncosim test --list
Option Meaning --list List discovered test scenes and their execution kind --verdict-channel NAME Accept the verdict only from this channel --verification QUALIFIED_NAME Require a Twin manifest SysML verification mapping --max-ticks N Bound cumulative fixed steps; default 20000 --tick-hz HZ Manual update rate; default 60 --readiness-timeout SECS Bound scene and participant preparation; default 420 --determinism-reference PATH Load a typed JSON state reference for Rhai comparisons --threads N Compute-pool width; 1 is the gate profile --jitter FRAC / --seed U64 Exercise seeded fractional-dt pacing

The scene runner defaults to four independent headless production processes. -j/--jobs N changes that bound without changing each gate process's deterministic --threads 1 --jitter 0. Use -j 1 when diagnosing ordering or resource interactions. Graphics assertions remain a separate serial offscreen pass.

--validate is not a substitute. It proves that files parse and declarations are structurally valid; it does not prove that a body moved, a joint held, or a mission completed. See Validation for the evidence layers.

docs.title: One-shot checks
docs.text:
For a standalone Rhai assertion that needs a live USD world, keep one API session open and run the source through RunRhai:

luncosim rhai --api 4101 -f scripts/check.rhai

The REPL and the evaluator are deliberately separate. The running host owns the Rhai engine and the reflected RunRhai command; the terminal client only sends the generic API envelope and formats the result. That means the terminal path uses the same command path as every other external client.

RunRhai is a one-shot evaluation with full world access in a bounded FIFO cycle. It does not attach a persistent scenario. Use RunScenario for a persistent per-entity observer and RunRhai for a quick verdict or inspection.

docs.title: Debugging a test
docs.text:
• print(...) lands in the console and in the test output.
  • ScriptStatus { target } reports compile and runtime health, including located errors.
  • ScriptInspect { target } shows the live this map, defined hooks, generation, and paused/running state.
  • report_verdict prints TESTS_OK or TESTS_FAIL and the human title.
{
  "type": "ExecuteCommand",
  "command": "ScriptStatus",
  "params": { "target": 4869542932533563 }
}

A function pointer in live state is represented as a read-only map with kind: "function", name, anonymous, and curried_argument_count. The API exposes its identity for diagnosis; it does not expose callable function values.

docs.title: Sampling with on_tick
docs.text:
on_tick is reserved for authored tests. It samples state on the authored cadence and publishes a bounded verdict:

fn on_tick(me, ctx) {
    if sim_tick() < 120 { return; }
    if this.reported { return; }
    this.reported = true;

    let fails = [];
    fails.push(t_range(get(me, "Battery.level"), 0.0, 1.0, "battery level"));
    report_verdict(fails, "BATTERY SAMPLE", "BATTERY_SAMPLE");
}

Production missions use task, wait_until, and on_event instead. A hand-written tick loop duplicates the kernel and makes the mission less deterministic.

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text: A test should produce the same result from the same inputs. Use the fixed clock (sim_tick, dt, elapsed_seconds) for timing, and use the deterministic rand helpers rather than an external entropy source. When a test needs a stored state reference, load it with --determinism-reference and compare typed values rather than formatted strings.
