docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: The Rhai runtime is deliberately small. Most authoring convenience comes from three editable layers: the prelude, tool libraries, and authoring tools. All three are Rhai policy over the same command and query bridge, and all three can change without rebuilding the engine.

docs.title: The prelude
docs.text:
The prelude is a directory of .rhai files, one per topic. It provides vector math, navigation, sensing, task constructors, mission helpers, HUD helpers, input automation, and control wrappers:

assets/scripting/prelude/
├── nav.rhai
├── sensing.rhai
├── control.rhai
├── tasks.rhai
├── mission.rhai
├── science.rhai
├── links.rhai
├── math.rhai
├── select.rhai
├── hud.rhai
├── coordinates.rhai
├── ports.rhai
├── vessel.rhai
├── input.rhai
├── authoring.rhai
├── recording.rhai
├── auto_tests.rhai
└── …

On native, the prelude is read from the runtime asset tree at startup. Edit a helper and restart the app; no rebuild is required. A missing or unreadable directory is reported as an error; the runtime does not substitute a compiled snapshot. On wasm, the normal Bevy asset pipeline fills the same script-source registry. A parse error is reported and the app does not silently run stale helpers.

The prelude is part of each scenario's compiled AST. A changed prelude invalidates compiled scenarios; a static tool-module rebinding does not.

docs.title: Tool libraries
docs.text:
A tool library is a named bundle of reusable policy, callable as libname::fn(...) from any hook:

let plan = formation::line(leader, 4, 12.0);

Author one by dropping a .rhai file in assets/scripting/tools/, or register it at runtime:

cmd("RegisterToolLibrary", #{ name: "survey", source: source });
Command or query Purpose RegisterToolLibrary { name, source } Install or replace a tool library ListToolLibraries Discover registered libraries and their scope GetToolLibrary { name } Read one library's source and metadata

A library may lazily import another registered tool with ordinary Rhai syntax. The resolver uses the registry and does not read dependency files. A scenario that needs a source-defined tool before its first lifecycle hook should import the explicit lunco:// asset URI instead, because a namespace call does not declare an asset dependency.

Each result includes the winning standard, core, application, or twin:<id> scope. A Twin can replace an application tool without restarting Core or Application scenario state. A changed authored prelude still invalidates compiled scenarios.

Registered libraries are mirrored to <twin>/tools/*.rhai. On Twin mount, twin.lifecycle selects indexed tool files and requests their loading through typed commands.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
ScriptingCatalog aggregates the full callable surface: verbs, hooks, prelude, tools, commands, and queries. A full catalog value can exceed the shared sandbox size limit, so Rhai callers use a bounded query:

let matches = query("ScriptComplete", #{ prefix: "Set", limit: 20 });

The same catalog is available to external authoring clients. Use it instead of guessing a command name from a version of the documentation.

docs.title: Structured UI tools
docs.text:
A Rhai tool can be invoked by a pointer or menu action through RunRhaiTool { tool, args }. The tool receives typed arguments and runs its on_click(context) entry point:

fn on_click(context) {
    if pointer_intent(context, "route.add_point") {
        return add_route_point(context);
    }
}

A scene context includes the picked point, the diagnostic button (primary, secondary, or middle), and pointer_intents derived from the active keymap. Use pointer_intent(context, name) rather than matching raw modifier chords; the binding stays remappable.

RunRhaiToolHook { tool, hook, args } invokes a persistent callback through an explicit binding. The runtime pins the committed scene generation and retires queued calls on reload, scene transition, or Twin close.

Continuous pointer-move hooks are opt-in through SetScenePointerMoveHook { doc_id, interaction_id, tool, hook, context } and cleared with ClearScenePointerMoveHook { doc_id, interaction_id }. One interaction owns a document at a time.

docs.title: Input automation
docs.text:
Rhai can drive the actual application input path through InjectWindowInput and the helpers in input.rhai:

input_key_press("AltLeft");
input_click("primary", 960.0, 540.0);
input_key_release("AltLeft");

The helpers emit the same aggregate window events and typed Bevy messages that the native backend produces. Egui, picking, focus, key bindings, and authored tools all observe one canonical path. Rhai owns the gesture sequence; Rust owns event validation and fan-out.

Use input_pointer_move, input_pointer_press, input_pointer_release, and input_scroll for drag and viewport workflows. Coordinates are logical pixels in the primary window. The command does not warp the OS pointer.

A frame wait is not a gesture-duration guarantee. Slow rendering can stretch a held press beyond egui's click limit. Split press and release across frames when the held state matters.

docs.title: Authoring tools
docs.text:
The authoring libraries are policy over the explicit document commands. They do not parse USDA, maintain a second document, or write ECS state directly.

Library Purpose assembly_builder Semantic frames, shapes, placement, alignment, collision clearance, and body/joint plans assembly_edit Explicit-document USD edits, components, programs, and connections model_authoring Assembly context, readiness reports, scene recipes, and port graphs modelica_editor Generation-checked AST, diagram, and text batches sysml_editor Source-range edits and semantic checkpoints rhai_editor Generation-checked script source edits authoring_session Cross-domain capability discovery, dry plan, grouped apply, checkpoint, undo, redo editor_workflow Inspect/projection/lint checkpoints and opt-in autosave physics_acceptance Contact, motion, settling, joint, and runtime-evidence checks

The common editing contract is:

let state = authoring_session::inspect("sysml", sysml_doc);
let dry = authoring_session::plan("sysml", ops, "update contract", state.generation);
let applied = authoring_session::apply(
    "sysml", sysml_doc, ops, dry.label, dry.parent_generation);
let checked = authoring_session::checkpoint("sysml", sysml_doc);

plan is pure. apply sends one reviewed group to the format owner and never chooses an active tab or writes a source file directly. checkpoint reads the owner's current generation and diagnostics. undo and redo use the same explicit document id.

USD, Modelica, SysML/KerML, and Rhai each provide a thin typed adapter for their parser or projection semantics. WESL remains renderer-owned until it receives the same document adapter; generic tools must not write shader files directly.

docs.title: Inspection and diagnostics
docs.text:
Query Answers ScriptStatus { target } Is the scenario healthy? Compile and runtime diagnostics ScriptInspect { target } What is it doing? Live this, hooks, generation, paused/running ScriptingCatalog What can be called? The full surface for external clients ScriptComplete { prefix, limit } Bounded completion over the same owner

print(...) lands in the console. A compile error includes file, line, and column where available. Runtime errors remain visible and do not become successful no-ops.

docs.title: Running a scenario
docs.text:
Transport How Scene asset LunCoProgramAPI with info:sourceAsset HTTP API ExecuteCommand with RunScenario MCP The run_scenario tool One-shot eval RunRhai { code } Structured click tool RunRhaiTool { tool, args } Control SetScenarioPaused, StopScenario

RunScenario.source is Rhai source text, not a filesystem path. For a file-backed script, read the file into the request body. RunScenarioAsset accepts an asset address and rejects empty or whitespace-only source input before URI conversion, asset loading, or pending-host publication.

The terminal client is a thin API consumer:

luncosim rhai --api 4101
luncosim rhai --api 4101 -e 'print(find("Rover"))'
luncosim rhai --api 4101 -f scripts/check.rhai

The REPL evaluates against the live app. Authored tests belong in a scene test, not in the REPL.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text:
A shader look in LunCoSim is data, not a Rust material type. A WESL source asset declares a parameter block and, optionally, a set of named texture layers. A USD material selects that source and authors its inputs. The renderer reflects the source, packs the parameters, binds the textures, and builds the pipeline.

This is why a new look is usually a new .wesl file and a material network, not a new engine feature. Rust hardcodes no parameter names, ranges, or defaults.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
What it is Where it lives Capacity Parameter A scalar or vector uniform the shader reads One opaque 512-byte uniform block 128 f32 scalars or 32 vec4s, subject to layout alignment Texture layer A raster the shader samples A bind-group entry 13 named roles

Parameters are cheap and open-ended. Texture slots are the scarce resource. Most "I need another layer" instincts should be spent on a packed channel before a new slot.

docs.title: The data flow
docs.text:
1. A UsdShade network binds a material to a prim.
  2. The material's Shader prim names a WESL fragment source and, optionally, a vertex source.
  3. The WESL source declares struct Material at @group(2) @binding(0) and //!@ annotations.
  4. The renderer reflects the struct into a ParamSchema and the annotations into Inspector metadata.
  5. The USD projection publishes a ShaderLook with the source paths, parameter values, and texture handles.
  6. The render binder validates the stage contract, packs the parameter block, binds the textures, and caches the material by look key.

A material is rejected visibly if the source is missing, the stage contract is invalid, or a texture cannot load. Rust does not substitute StandardMaterial or a guessed shader.

docs.title: What a shader owns
docs.text:
Fact Authored as Consumed by Surface appearance WESL fragment entry point Render pipeline Parameter set struct Material and annotations Reflection and Inspector Texture roles Declared bindings Material binder Vertex deformation Optional WESL vertex entry point Mesh and shadow passes Material selection USD UsdShade network USD projection Parameter values USD inputs:<name> ShaderLook Renderer budgets RenderingQualitySettings All GPU-backed views

A shader does not own scene composition, physics, mission policy, or the renderer-wide quality preset.

docs.title: Sharing
docs.text:
Identical looks share one material and one bind group. The binder caches by the look key, which quantises floats so a rounding error cannot mint a second material. Vary a parameter per instance and you get a material per instance: a draw call and a bind group each. If instances must differ, bucket the value first.

Per-tile quality is a natural exception: terrain tiles carry their own look and texture handles, so a near tile can use a larger albedo than a far tile. Tiles at the same quality still share a material.

docs.title: Reading this chapter
docs.text: Section Question it answers Parameters How does a shader declare and receive its uniforms? Texture layers Which named rasters can a shader sample? USD materials How does a material bind a source and its inputs? Terrain How does the layered terrain material work? Quality Which renderer budgets change with the quality preset? Authoring How do I write, validate, and debug a shader look?

docs.title: Practical rules
docs.text:
• Declare every parameter in struct Material; do not rely on undeclared uniforms.
  • Use //!@ui, //!@default, and //!@engine to make the schema readable.
  • Keep the vertex stage's Material layout identical to the fragment stage's.
  • Pack scalar layers into channels before consuming another texture slot.
  • Bind textures and parameters through the composed UsdShade network.
  • Treat a rejected material as an authoring error, not as a reason to add a fallback.
  • Measure rendering cost separately from a deterministic recording run.

docs.title: Authoring
docs.text: A shader look is authored in two files: a WESL source and a USD material. The source declares the parameter block and texture bindings; the material selects the source and authors the inputs. The runtime reflects the rest.

docs.title: Create the source
docs.text:
Put the source inside the Twin when it belongs to the Twin:

my-rover-twin/
└── shaders/
    └── dusty_surface.wesl

Use @twin://my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface.wesl@ to address it. A source shipped with the engine uses @lunco://shaders/...@.

A minimal fragment source:

//!@ui      dust_density 0 1      "Dust density"
//!@default dust_density 0.35
//!@ui      clump_scale  0 64     "Clump scale (/m)"
//!@default clump_scale  8
//!@ui      tint         color    "Tint"
//!@default tint         0.62,0.62,0.64,1.0

struct Material {
    dust_density: f32,
    clump_scale: f32,
    tint: vec4<f32>,
}

@group(2) @binding(0) var<uniform> material: Material;

@fragment
fn fragment(in: VertexOutput) -> @location(0) vec4<f32> {
    // Sample the base colour and apply the authored parameters.
    // ...
}

The exact imports and entry-point signature depend on the Bevy/WESL pipeline you are extending. Copy the structure of a shipped shader that already targets the pass you need.

docs.title: Declare the contract
docs.text:
Every field must use a supported type and be reflected in struct Material:

  • f32, i32, u32, vec2<f32>, vec3<f32>, vec4<f32>
  • std140 alignment, total block at most 512 bytes
  • @group(2) @binding(0) for the material uniform
  • //!@ui for the Inspector presentation
  • //!@default for the authored default
  • //!@engine for runtime-filled fields

A name that is not in the schema is dropped at pack time with a warning. A struct that exceeds 512 bytes is clipped with a warning. Both are authoring errors in practice, not silent feature extensions.

If the shader needs a second stage, declare the same Material fields, order, and types in the vertex source. Both stages read the same block; the fragment schema is the layout that gets packed.

docs.title: Bind the source in USD
docs.text:
def Material "DustyMaterial"
{
    token outputs:surface.connect = </World/Looks/DustyMaterial/Shader.outputs:surface>

    def Shader "Shader"
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface.wesl@

        float inputs:dust_density = 0.35
        float inputs:clump_scale = 8.0
        color4f inputs:tint = (0.62, 0.62, 0.64, 1.0)
    }
}

Add info:wesl:vertexAsset only when the default mesh vertex stage is not sufficient. Add info:wesl:interface only when the shader declares a named ABI such as the lunar-surface continuation contract.

Texture inputs are asset-typed properties:

asset inputs:albedo_map = @twin://my-rover-twin/terrain/albedo.png@
asset inputs:normal_map = @twin://my-rover-twin/terrain/normals.png@

docs.title: Bind the material
docs.text:
def Xform "Rover" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["MaterialBindingAPI"]
)
{
    rel material:binding = </World/Looks/DustyMaterial>
}

The editor and SetObjectProperty follow the composed binding network. A parameter edit authors a typed UsdOp on the bound UsdShade.Shader prim's inputs:<name> attribute.

Use material:binding:physics for a physics-purpose material. A purpose-specific binding wins over the all-purpose binding for that purpose.

docs.title: Validate before running
docs.text:
luncosim --validate path/to/my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface.wesl

--validate checks source syntax and material facts. It is preflight evidence, not a GPU compile. The renderer still owns pipeline specialization and GPU validation.

A graphics gate must reject shader compilation errors in the process log as well as domain runtime diagnostics. A captured image can retain stale pixels after a failed submission, so an image alone is not proof that the shader compiled.

docs.title: Reload and inspect
docs.text:
The native desktop asset watcher reloads a changed .wesl source without relaunching the application. The render binder waits for prepared sources and refreshes affected looks on asset events.

To inspect the result:

  1. Select the prim in Build or Editor.
  2. Open the Inspector.
  3. Find the material parameters. Slider bounds and labels come from the reflected schema, not a hand-written list.
  4. Change a value and observe the viewport.

If the shader fails to compile, the owning material is rejected and a structured runtime diagnostic is published. Fix the source and reload; do not hide the error by switching to a different material.

docs.title: Keep the look shared
docs.text:
Identical looks share one material and one bind group. The binder caches by the look key, which quantises floats so a rounding error cannot mint a second material.

Vary a parameter per instance and you get a material per instance. If instances must differ, bucket the value first. For per-place texture quality, give tiles different rasters rather than a different scalar for every tile.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Material rejected No callable fragment entry point Declare @fragment or correct the source role Vertex stage fails Its Material layout differs from the fragment stage Use the same fields, order, and types Parameter missing from Inspector Field is not in Material or has an unsupported type Add the field with a supported type and annotation Parameter change does nothing Input name does not match the reflected field Author inputs:<name> with the canonical snake-case name Parameter silently ignored Name is not in the schema Check the struct and the pack warning Shader compiles but looks wrong Texture role missing or mis-bound Check the material's texture inputs and the role Two instances create many materials A per-instance float varies the look key Bucket the value or share the look Overlay drag causes a stall An overlay was baked into a texture Derive the view in the shader from a data layer

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Use one Material per appearance, not one per prim.
  • Prefer sourceAsset over inline shader text.
  • Declare every parameter in the Material block; do not rely on undeclared uniforms.
  • Mark engine-filled fields with //!@engine.
  • Pack scalar layers into channels before adding a texture role.
  • Keep the vertex ABI identical to the fragment ABI.
  • Treat a rejected material as an authoring error, not as a reason to add a fallback.
  • Validate syntax, then verify the GPU pipeline in a graphics gate.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: A dynamic shader declares its own material parameters. The engine reads the layout out of the WESL source, so no parameter names, ranges, or defaults are hardcoded in Rust. Adding a parameter means editing a .wesl file. It never means editing the renderer.

docs.title: The material block
docs.text:
A shader declares a struct named exactly Material at @group(2) @binding(0):

//!@ui      dust_density 0 1      "Dust density"
//!@default dust_density 0.35
//!@ui      clump_scale  0 64     "Clump scale (/m)"
//!@default clump_scale  8
//!@ui      tint         color    "Tint"
//!@default tint         0.6,0.6,0.62,1.0
//!@engine  sun_dir
//!@default sun_dir      0,1,0

struct Material {
    dust_density: f32,
    clump_scale: f32,
    tint: vec4<f32>,
    sun_dir: vec3<f32>,
}

@group(2) @binding(0) var<uniform> material: Material;

The struct field order and WESL types define the layout. The annotations are metadata for the Inspector and the runtime; they do not change the GPU layout.

docs.title: Annotation vocabulary
docs.text:
Annotations are //!@ comments outside the struct, one per field:

Annotation Form Meaning //!@ui name min max "Label" Floating-point slider bounds and label //!@ui name color "Label" Color picker //!@ui name int min max "Label" Integer field bounds //!@default name value Value used when the author sets none //!@engine name Field is filled by the engine, not authored //!@interface identifier Shader ABI identifier, such as a continuation contract //!@capability identifier Optional shader feature declaration

A field with no //!@ui annotation gets a default presentation from its type: f32 becomes a 0..1 slider, integer types become 0..32, vec3/vec4 become a color picker, and vec2 is free-form.

//!@engine is a statement of ownership, not a hidden default. A field marked engine-filled is written by the runtime; authoring it from USD would fight the engine writer.

docs.title: Supported types and layout
docs.text:
WESL type Size Alignment Rhai/USD shape f32 4 4 Number i32 4 4 Integer u32 4 4 Unsigned integer vec2<f32> 8 8 Two-number array vec3<f32> 12 16 Three-number array vec4<f32> 16 16 Four-number array or color

Offsets follow std140 / WESL uniform rules: a field starts at the next multiple of its alignment, and the total size is rounded up to 16 bytes. A vec3 occupies 12 bytes but aligns to 16.

The packed block is 512 bytes, or 32 vec4 lanes. A struct that reflects past that size logs a warning and clips the extra fields. Split a large material into a smaller parameter set or move data into a texture instead of relying on clipping.

A type outside the supported set prevents the struct from reflecting as a parameter schema. Keep the block to the scalar and vector types above.

docs.title: Packing and naming
docs.text:
Values are stored by name and packed at their reflected offsets. A name that is not in the schema is dropped at pack time with a warning; it is never silently mis-packed into a neighbouring field.

Parameter spelling is normalized by the shared to_snake_case rule used by USD projection, live authoring, and the render binder. Runtime ports use the exact keys published by ListPorts; geometry connections and commands must use those WESL keys so wiring, holds, and admission retain one input identity.

A USD-backed parameter edit belongs to the bound Shader prim's inputs:<name> attribute:

float inputs:dust_density = 0.35
float inputs:clump_scale = 8.0
color4f inputs:tint = (0.6, 0.6, 0.62, 1.0)

The editor and SetObjectProperty follow the composed material:binding network, use the composed typeName without collapsing roles or array shape, validate the USDA literal, and author a typed UsdOp.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
//!@default supplies the value used when the author does not set an input. A default is part of the shader contract, not a renderer fallback. If a parameter must have a meaningful value, declare a default and document its units in the label.

A missing default for a field leaves the packed lane at zero. Prefer an explicit default for every authored parameter; a zero that means "off" is different from a zero that means "unset".

docs.title: Vertex stages share the ABI
docs.text:
An optional vertex shader is a second stage of the same material, not a second parameter block. Both stages read @binding(0) from the one 512-byte block. The fragment stage's reflected schema is the layout that gets packed, so the vertex stage must declare the same Material fields, order, and WESL types.

// terrain_geomorph.wesl — vertex-only stage
struct Material {
    // Same fields, order, and types as terrain_layered.wesl.
    // ...
}

The terrain pair (terrain_layered.wesl plus terrain_geomorph.wesl) uses one canonical fragment layout and a vertex-only geomorph stage. A cross-shader contract test guards the required ABI at that boundary.

A portable material can keep both entry points in one source asset and use that same asset for both projected stages.

docs.title: Engine-filled fields
docs.text:
Terrain materials expose fields the runtime fills every frame:

Field family Filled from sun_dir, sun_dir_world, sun_tan_radius Active sun and body frame hf_size, hf_res Shadow heightfield extent and resolution csm_far, shadow_cache_on, horizon_march_steps Shadow configuration morph_start, morph_end, stitch_edges CDLOD morph and edge stitching site_* Site-local continuation and photometry facts map_texel_size_m, derived_*_on, authored_*_on Active map and source state

Mark these with //!@engine so the Inspector does not present them as editable authoring knobs.

docs.title: Live parameters
docs.text:
A ShaderLook carries an open set of parameter values. Identical looks share one material; the binder caches by a key that quantises floats to 1e-4.

A parameter that is globally uniform and continuously tuned can be excluded from the material identity so changing it reuses the same material and writes the new value in place. This is appropriate only when every look that could share the material carries the same value, such as a global overlay slider. A per-entity value belongs in the ordinary parameter set.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
Rendering quality is a budget choice, not a shader-identity switch. The RenderingQualitySettings resource owns budgets that affect all GPU-backed views. USD remains the authority for the scene's ShaderLook and authored WESL source.

A scene can therefore keep its authored lunar terrain and starfield shaders while the High preset supplies the largest renderer budgets around them.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Preset Intent Low Lowest-cost shadow and lighting budgets Balanced The default interactive balance High Largest shipped shadow, lighting, derived-map, rock, and tessellation budgets

The stable policy keys are low, balanced, and high. The Graphics settings menu presents the same three choices. The CLI can select one for a process:

luncosim --render-quality high

The setting is persisted with the other graphics settings. It is not a per-material property and it does not replace the shader authored by the scene.

docs.title: What the preset budgets
docs.text:
RenderingQualitySettings covers:

Family Examples Shadow maps Directional, point, and spot map sizes; cascade count; caster limits; shadow storage budget Shadow filtering Hardware 2×2 or Gaussian 5×5 Horizon cache Enablement, sun-angle invalidation threshold, march steps, bake supersampling Camera MSAA, tone mapping, exposure, bloom Sky Dome cubemap face size Terrain LOD Tile resolution, pixel error, maximum depth, tile budget, bake cadence, hysteresis, morph band Terrain derived maps Roughness/AO/normal resolution, AO directions and steps, anisotropy Terrain rocks Maximum instances, mesh buckets, LOD fade distances Geometry Sphere, cylinder, capsule, NURBS, and curve tessellation Editor preview Preview key light, local-light defaults, render-failure recovery

The exact numeric values belong to the shipped profile and may change between releases. Read the current settings in Settings → Graphics rather than copying a table from a version of the documentation.

docs.title: Shadow filtering
docs.text:
The Graphics settings expose two shadow filters:

Filter Character Hardware 2×2 Four comparison samples with hardware filtering; lower cost Gaussian 5×5 A wider nine-sample footprint; highest quality without temporal anti-aliasing

The default is Gaussian. The terrain material's normal bias is scaled by the shadow texel size so grazing-angle terrain does not sample its own surface inside the filter footprint.

docs.title: Terrain quality
docs.text:
The High preset keeps the interactive terrain CDLOD envelope at the proven Balanced bound: 49-vertex tiles, depth 8, a 768-tile cover, and the corresponding sampling and bake cadence. High increases the surrounding lighting, derived-map, rock, and tessellation budgets; it does not double terrain cover merely to spend the frame budget on duplicate geometry.

Per-tile texture quality is authored separately. A near tile can use a 2048² albedo and a far tile a 256² one, with the same roles and different images. This is the right way to spend quality where the camera actually looks.

docs.title: Quality does not change material identity
docs.text:
The quality preset does not rewrite a ShaderLook. It changes renderer budgets around the authored material. A material that is invalid at Low is still invalid at High; a shader that fails to compile is a shader error, not a quality setting.

Likewise, changing a quality setting does not repair a missing texture or a malformed parameter. Those are authoring errors and remain visible.

docs.title: Measuring cost
docs.text:
A deterministic recording run is not a profiling run. Use a separate session when measuring frame time:

luncosim --no-vsync --no-throttle --log-diag

--log-diag reports FPS, frame time, and physics diagnostics. Compare presets in the same scene, camera, and resolution; a different view invalidates the comparison.

For a headless gate, keep the deterministic --threads 1 --jitter 0 profile. Graphics assertions are a separate serial offscreen pass because GPU state and driver behavior are not part of the fixed-step determinism contract.

docs.title: Material sharing and quality
docs.text:
Identical looks share one material and one bind group. The look key includes texture handles, so two tiles at different texture resolutions correctly get two materials, while tiles at the same quality share one.

Varying a scalar per instance mints a material per instance. If a quality choice must vary continuously, bucket it into a small set of values rather than giving every instance a unique float.

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text: Terrain is the largest authored shader surface in LunCoSim. It combines measured DEM geometry, procedural regolith detail, georeferenced raster layers, lunar photometry, and sun visibility in one material contract. It is not a separate renderer and it is not one shader per layer.

docs.title: The canonical sources
docs.text:
Path Role Contract assets/shaders/terrain_layered.wesl Authored DEM fragment The single canonical DEM material: albedo, layers, DEM relief, filtered detail, lunar photometry, and self-shadow assets/shaders/terrain_geomorph.wesl Optional streamed DEM vertex stage CDLOD morphing and crack-free edge stitching; no fragment entry point and no second appearance law assets/shaders/terrain_shadow.wesl Explicit non-authored terrain material Plain authored/display albedo, scene PBR, and heightfield sun visibility assets/shaders/regolith.wesl General mesh material Ordinary regolith meshes, not a terrain source selection assets/shaders/terrain_debug.wesl Diagnostic material Analysis and debug views outside the production material contract

USD selects the fragment source and may select the vertex source on the same Shader prim. The terrain runtime consumes that projected look; it does not choose a shader filename.

terrain_shadow.wesl may be selected by an authored Rhai or tool policy for a terrain with no authored material. Rust never installs it to hide a missing or invalid authored source.

docs.title: USD authoring
docs.text:
An authored terrain material uses standard UsdShade stage metadata:

def Material "LunarTerrain"
{
    token outputs:surface.connect = </World/Looks/LunarTerrain/Shader.outputs:surface>

    def Shader "Shader"
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @lunco://shaders/terrain_layered.wesl@
        uniform asset info:wesl:vertexAsset = @lunco://shaders/terrain_geomorph.wesl@
        uniform token info:wesl:interface = "lunco.lunar-surface-continuation.v1"

        float inputs:weight_albedo = 1.0
        float inputs:weight_normal = 1.0
        float inputs:weight_rough = 1.0
        float inputs:weight_ao = 1.0

        asset inputs:albedo_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/albedo.png@
        asset inputs:normal_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/normals.png@
        asset inputs:surface_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/surface.png@
    }
}

sourceAsset is the canonical fragment and material contract. vertexAsset is optional: omit it for a static or ordinary mesh vertex path, and use it for streamed CDLOD geometry. The explicit SpawnDemTerrain command is a generic tool API and requires its caller to provide a look.

docs.title: One appearance, two delivery paths
docs.text:
Static and streamed terrain differ only in geometry delivery. A static mesh is effectively the non-morphing root LOD of the same appearance contract. The streamed ECS quadtree may still manage residency, colliders, and LOD selection independently.

Both paths use the same material law, the same layer weights, and the same distance rules. They must not choose different physical surface laws or distance-dependent colour and normal rules.

The optional vertex stage runs in the main, depth/normal, and native shadow passes. It selects Bevy's forward or prepass output interface using PREPASS_PIPELINE; the material group remains bound in depth-only passes so the same morph uniforms are available. CDLOD distance uses the viewing camera's origin, shared with its shadow cascades. Edge stitching and morph interpolation therefore describe the same surface in every pass.

docs.title: The layer stack
docs.text:
The procedural regolith is the floor. Even where a layer map is low-resolution or absent, the rover camera still sees real close-range detail. On top ride UV-registered raster layers, each blended by a reflected weight_* knob:

Weight Layer weight_albedo Body-wide colour raster weight_mineral Classification or analysis overlay, composited unlit weight_rough Packed surface roughness weight_ao Packed ambient occlusion weight_normal DEM-derived meso-scale normal

A weight_* = 0 layer contributes nothing. Maps are sampled by the planar UV the horizon bake establishes, under @if(VERTEX_UVS_A); without UVs the material is procedural.

Mineral is composited unlit after lighting and shadowing, so an analysis overlay stays readable in shadow. It is data, not a material tint.

The packed surface map's G channel is ambient occlusion. Both terrain paths resolve it through the shared terrain-surface helper and apply it to indirect diffuse light only. AO is not an albedo term and must not be multiplied into the authored colour raster or direct sunlight.

docs.title: Physical-scale detail
docs.text:
The canonical DEM material can combine georeferenced site rasters with optional repeatable material scans:

Input Role inputs:detail_albedo_map Repeatable colour detail inputs:detail_normal_map Repeatable tangent-space normal detail inputs:detail_surface_map Repeatable packed roughness and AO

detail_tile_size_m defines one repeat in terrain-local metres. Coordinates remain stable as tiles and the camera move; explicit gradients select mip levels across wrap boundaries.

Detail normals use +X/-Z tangent axes and perturb the existing DEM or procedural normal, fading below the resolved pixel footprint. They never replace the DEM normal map or change height queries and colliders.

Colour detail multiplies the site albedo by scan luminance relative to the USD-authored detail_albedo_mean in linear light. This preserves the site's broad tone while adding photographed variation. All detail weights default to zero, so an existing scene does not request detail maps or change appearance.

docs.title: DEM-to-globe continuation
docs.text:
A measured DEM covers a site, not the whole body. The exterior smoothing preserves the first native posting and filters only the continuation in its preparation worker. Geometry and material fades multiply the two axial weights, keeping corner diagonals smooth.

The generated collar has two independent scene inputs: the DEM prim supplies the crop dimensions and local map images, while the celestial body's composed UsdShade binding selects the surface appearance. The collar clones the body's current ShaderLook and adds the DEM material base colour, cropped albedo, and packed surface images in the dedicated continuation roles.

A body fragment shader that accepts these local roles declares //!@interface lunco.lunar-surface-continuation.v1 and authors the same identifier as info:wesl:interface. The required Rhai hook terrain.lunar_surface_continuation receives the declaration and reflected interface and returns compose, wait, or hold.

This composition is visualization only. It never resamples, blends, edits, or replaces DEM heights, terrain queries, or colliders.

docs.title: Sun visibility
docs.text:
Terrain uses two sun-visibility paths:

  • A live horizon ray march against the heightfield.
  • A pre-baked ShadowCache sampled once in the fragment shader.

The quality preset chooses whether the cache is available and how many march steps are allowed. shadow_cache_on selects the path in the material. The cache is refreshed when the sun direction changes beyond the configured threshold.

Height is a non-filterable R32Float world-height raster used by the march. ShadowCache is an R8Unorm visibility raster. Neither is authorable from USD; both are engine-filled by the horizon system.

The High profile's Gaussian shadow filter uses a normal bias scaled by each cascade's shadow texel size to keep grazing-angle terrain from sampling its own surface inside the filter footprint.

docs.title: Quality and budgets
docs.text:
The renderer-wide quality preset owns terrain LOD and cache budgets, derived-map resolution, rock budgets, and tessellation. It does not choose the terrain shader. A scene can keep its authored lunar material while the preset supplies larger budgets around it.

Per-tile quality is a separate, authored choice: give a near tile a larger albedo and a far tile a smaller one. The same roles are used; only the images differ. Tiles at the same quality still share one material.

See Quality for the preset categories and profiling guidance.

docs.title: Texture layers
docs.text: A texture layer is a raster the shader samples. The engine exposes a fixed set of 13 named roles. A shader opts in by declaring the binding; a shader that does not declare it is unaffected by that layer being set. One role set serves every shader, so a new look does not create a new material type.

docs.title: The roles
docs.text:
Role Content Typical format Height World heights for ray-marched sun shadows R32Float, non-filterable Albedo Body-wide colour raster, such as a lunar mosaic RGBA8, linear light Mineral Class-id or composition raster, tinted through a palette LUT RGBA8 Surface Packed scalars: R roughness, G ambient occlusion, B rock density, A hazard RGBA8 Normal Tangent- or world-space normals from DEM relief RGBA8 ShadowCache Pre-baked sun visibility R8Unorm ContinuationAlbedo Site-local albedo for a lunar-surface continuation shader RGBA8 ContinuationSurface Site-local packed roughness/AO for a continuation shader RGBA8 SurfaceAnnotations Sparse terrain-local vector annotations, read with textureLoad Typed DetailAlbedo Repeatable colour detail, independent of the georeferenced raster RGBA8 DetailNormal Repeatable tangent-space normal detail RGBA8 DetailSurface Repeatable packed scalars: R roughness, G ambient occlusion RGBA8 Displacement Authored scalar displacement, separate from the runtime shadow heightfield Scalar

Height is a slot precisely because R32Float is non-filterable and cannot be packed with filterable colour data. ShadowCache is a separate slot because it has its own single-channel format and refresh cadence.

docs.title: Authorable inputs
docs.text:
A USD material addresses the authorable roles through asset-typed inputs: properties:

USD input Role inputs:albedo_map Albedo inputs:mineral_map Mineral inputs:surface_map Surface inputs:normal_map Normal inputs:detail_albedo_map DetailAlbedo inputs:detail_normal_map DetailNormal inputs:detail_surface_map DetailSurface inputs:displacement_map Displacement

height_map and shadow_cache are deliberately not addressable from USD. They are engine-filled by the horizon-shadow system; authoring them would fight the engine writer.

ContinuationAlbedo, ContinuationSurface, and SurfaceAnnotations are also runtime-owned. The DEM-to-globe continuation compositor clones the body look and supplies the site-local maps. Terrain annotations publish sparse vector data through the annotation path.

A connected inputs: property is skipped by the texture reader; it is fed by a producer node, not by an authored file.

docs.title: Spend a channel before a slot
docs.text:
Surface is one texture carrying four independent scalar layers:

Channel Layer R Roughness G Ambient occlusion B Rock density A Hazard

A new scalar layer should take a spare channel, not a new slot. Four scalars for one binding is a 4× win on the scarce resource, and it costs one texture fetch instead of four.

DetailSurface follows the same rule for repeatable detail: R is roughness and G is ambient occlusion. A single-channel roughness image requires detail_ao_weight = 0.

Reach for a new slot only when the layer is genuinely not a scalar: a colour, a normal, something with its own format, or something with different filtering rules.

docs.title: Formats and filtering
docs.text:
The role determines the prepared image contract:

Family Filtering Albedo, Mineral, ContinuationAlbedo Linear light, sRGB decode on load Surface, ContinuationSurface, DetailSurface Scalar channels averaged Normal, DetailNormal Vectors averaged and renormalized Height, ShadowCache, SurfaceAnnotations Dedicated native-image access Displacement Authored scalar range

Prepared RGBA8 rasters are filtered inside the native asynchronous asset pipeline. Each role has its own native root type and labeled image identity, so one source file can supply different roles without settings races. Requests use native asset paths and ImageLoaderSettings; decoding stays in Bevy's native loader.

The CPU mip chain follows the GPU extent rule: every axis becomes max(1, floor(previous / 2)). Non-power-of-two authored and derived maps are valid inputs and remain renderable.

docs.title: Albedo is not a grayscale orthophoto
docs.text:
An authored grayscale orthophoto is not intrinsic albedo. Its broad brightness field contains acquisition illumination, and the runtime would light it a second time. The asset pipeline has a distinct kind = "albedo" processor that removes the low-frequency illumination field, anchors the remaining local variation at an authored neutral regolith value, and sRGB-encodes the result.

A generic kind = "map" output is analysis or display data and must not be bound directly as inputs:albedo_map. A calibrated reflectance raster may use the texture pipeline when its colour-space contract is declared by the asset.

docs.title: Detail maps
docs.text:
The canonical DEM material can combine georeferenced site rasters with optional repeatable material scans:

  • detail_albedo_map multiplies the site albedo by scan luminance relative to detail_albedo_mean in linear light.
  • detail_normal_map perturbs the existing DEM or procedural normal. It uses +X/-Z tangent axes and fades below the resolved pixel footprint.
  • detail_surface_map supplies independent roughness and ambient-occlusion weights.

detail_tile_size_m defines one repeat in terrain-local metres. Coordinates remain stable as tiles and the camera move, and explicit gradients select mip levels across wrap boundaries. Detail maps never replace the DEM normal map or change height queries and colliders.

All detail weights default to zero, so an existing scene does not request detail maps or change appearance.

docs.title: Continuation roles
docs.text:
A body fragment shader that accepts site-local maps declares:

//!@interface lunco.lunar-surface-continuation.v1

and the USD Shader prim authors the same identifier as info:wesl:interface. The DEM collar supplies ContinuationAlbedo and ContinuationSurface while the body-wide Albedo and Surface remain the globe appearance. The exterior composes the site base colour with its authored raster weight before fading to the body appearance.

This is visualization only. It never resamples, blends, edits, or replaces DEM heights, terrain queries, or colliders.

docs.title: Per-tile quality
docs.text:
Terrain is tiled, and each tile carries its own ShaderLook, hence its own texture handles. Per-place quality is therefore a matter of giving the near tile a larger albedo and the far tile a smaller one. The same roles are used; only the images differ. Tiles at the same quality still share one material.

This is the answer for "higher quality near the rover" and for "this landing site has a real orbital raster, the rest of the Moon does not."

docs.title: When 13 roles are not enough
docs.text:
In order of cost:

  1. Channel-pack. Almost always the right answer for a scalar.
  2. Add a role. The set is a conservative choice, not a hardware wall. A new role is a change to TextureLayer plus a binding in the material; every existing shader ignores it unless it declares the binding.
  3. Use a texture_2d_array. One binding, N layers of the same kind and format. This converts the budget from per-layer to per-kind.
  4. Virtual texturing or a clipmap. A fixed physical cache plus an indirection table. This is a serious streaming and eviction project; do not reach for it until the simpler options are exhausted.

Thirteen sampled roles remain within the portable sixteen-texture limit. Check the actual binding budget before adding a role that must run on every target.

docs.title: Do not bake overlays into a texture
docs.text:
Bake the data. Derive the view.

Normals, heights, and DEM-derived slope are expensive and do not change when a user drags a slider: bake them. Hazard colours, traversability bands, and science-zone tints are views: derive them in the shader from a data layer, gated by uniforms.

Baking an overlay makes a slider drag a multi-second re-bake of every resident tile. It also freezes a presentation choice into the data, so the same raster cannot be re-interpreted for a different analysis.

docs.title: USD materials
docs.text: A material is the authored answer to "what does this surface look like?" The renderer does not choose a shader by prim name or folder. A UsdShade network selects a WESL source, the source declares its parameters, and the runtime projects that into a ShaderLook.

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
def Material "DustyMaterial"
{
    token outputs:surface.connect = </World/Looks/DustyMaterial/Shader.outputs:surface>

    def Shader "Shader"
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface.wesl@

        float inputs:dust_density = 0.35
        float inputs:clump_scale = 8.0
        color4f inputs:tint = (0.62, 0.62, 0.64, 1.0)
    }
}

Bind it to a prim:

def Mesh "Hull" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["MaterialBindingAPI"]
)
{
    rel material:binding = </World/Looks/DustyMaterial>
}
Element Meaning Material The bindable material prim outputs:surface The material's surface terminal Shader A source-backed shader node info:implementationSource Selects a source asset rather than inline text info:wesl:sourceAsset The WESL fragment stage info:wesl:vertexAsset Optional WESL vertex stage info:wesl:interface Optional declared shader ABI inputs:<name> Authored parameter or texture input material:binding The all-purpose visual binding

docs.title: Source selection
docs.text:
info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset" is the standard UsdShade selector. info:wesl:sourceAsset follows the standard source-type convention; vertexAsset is a LunCo renderer extension because UsdShade has no second stage selector.

A source used as sourceAsset must declare a callable @fragment entry point. An optional vertexAsset must declare a callable @vertex entry point. One module may declare both and is valid for either role.

A portable material can keep both entry points in one source asset and use that same asset for both projected stages. The terrain pair uses separate files:

uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @lunco://shaders/terrain_layered.wesl@
uniform asset info:wesl:vertexAsset = @lunco://shaders/terrain_geomorph.wesl@

The render binder validates the requested stage after the asset loads. An invalid contract rejects the owning material and publishes a structured RuntimeDiagnostics error. Rust does not substitute StandardMaterial, a guessed terrain shader, or another guessed source.

docs.title: Interface declaration
docs.text:
A shader may declare an ABI identifier:

//!@interface lunco.lunar-surface-continuation.v1

The USD Shader prim authors the same identifier:

uniform token info:wesl:interface = "lunco.lunar-surface-continuation.v1"

This is validation metadata. It names a shader ABI, never a shader asset; the asset path remains wholly selected by the composed UsdShade binding. The identifier does not change GPU material identity.

docs.title: Parameter inputs
docs.text:
A USD-backed parameter edit belongs to the bound Shader prim's inputs:<name> attribute. The editor and SetObjectProperty share the bound-Shader resolver: it follows the composed material:binding network, uses the composed typeName without collapsing USD roles or array shape, validates the USDA literal, and authors a typed UsdOp.

The input name must match the WESL field after the shared snake-case normalization. A name that is not in the reflected schema is dropped at pack time with a warning; it is never silently mis-packed into a neighbouring field.

Geometry primvars: are reserved for standard UsdGeom primvars such as primvars:displayColor. They are not a generic shader-parameter namespace.

docs.title: Texture inputs
docs.text:
Texture inputs are asset-typed inputs: properties:

asset inputs:albedo_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/albedo.png@
asset inputs:normal_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/normals.png@
asset inputs:surface_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/surface.png@

The projection maps the authored role to the named TextureLayer the shader declares. The authorable set is albedo_map, mineral_map, surface_map, normal_map, detail_albedo_map, detail_normal_map, detail_surface_map, and displacement_map.

height_map and shadow_cache are engine-filled and deliberately not addressable from USD. Continuation and annotation roles are runtime-owned.

A connected input is skipped by the texture reader because it is fed by a producer node, not by an authored file.

docs.title: Binding strength and purpose
docs.text:
material:binding is the all-purpose visual binding. material:binding:physics is the physics-purpose binding. A purpose-specific binding wins over the all-purpose binding for that purpose; the fallback lets a single material serve both.

Bindings compose through references like any other relationship. An instance can override the material without editing the referenced asset:

def Xform "RoverB" (
    prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
)
{
    over "Chassis" {
        rel material:binding = </Looks/DustyPaint>
    }
}

A resolved binding that targets a missing or non-material prim rejects admission visibly.

docs.title: Display color
docs.text:
primvars:displayColor is a standard UsdGeom primvar, not a shader parameter namespace. It is appropriate for simple unlit markers, debug geometry, and assets that must render without a material network.

Route markers are a good example: their unvisited color is authored in primvars:displayColor and primvars:displayOpacity, and the generic route_follow policy changes the visited state through the transient view layer.

docs.title: Sharing and caching
docs.text:
Identical looks share one material and one bind group. The binder caches by the look key, which quantises floats to 1e-4 so a rounding error cannot mint a second material. Texture handles are part of the key.

Vary a parameter per instance and you get a material per instance. If instances must differ, bucket the value first. A per-tile terrain look is a deliberate exception because the tiles genuinely carry different rasters.

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text:
Failure Result Shader source missing Material rejected, RuntimeDiagnostics error No fragment entry point Material rejected, stage contract error Parameter name not in schema Dropped with a warning at pack time Binding targets a non-material prim Admission rejected Malformed authored literal Typed edit rejected before authoring Unsupported texture format Asset load fails Declared interface does not match Continuation or lint error; the material is not silently accepted

The renderer never repairs a malformed material by guessing. An authored Rhai policy can observe the diagnostic and choose a replacement; that choice is visible policy, not a renderer fallback.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text: The tutorials are guided paths through the workbench. They use the same production runtime as a normal Twin: a lesson is an ordinary file-backed Rhai scenario with an optional authored USD scene. Nothing in a lesson is a simulation shortcut.

docs.title: How lessons work
docs.text:
The authored lesson catalog is under Scenarios → Tutorials. Each entry belongs to a track and is one of three lesson types:

Type Behavior Tour Explains a workflow and advances with Next and Back. A tour does not certify that you performed an action. Exercise Advances only when the simulation observes the requested result. Challenge A longer open-ended task with an authored success condition.

Selecting a lesson loads its scene when the lesson needs one, then starts the lesson's Rhai scenario. A lesson that needs a world names its scene explicitly, so selecting it cannot accidentally keep an unrelated scene from the previous lesson.

Lesson cards identify their type. A tour is the right choice when you want to learn where things are; an exercise is the right choice when you want the simulator to confirm completion.

docs.title: Learning paths
docs.text:
The catalog is organized into tracks. The suggested order is:

  1. Start Here → Lunar Rover Lab — the hands-on workshop: take control, reach a marker, read measured speed, compare two drive runs, move a scene object, and save a personal Twin.
  2. Rover Driving → Moon Driving Basics → Slopes & Tip-Over → Rover Variants — build driving skill, then compare authored tire and motor settings on one shared chassis. The variants lesson is a guided comparison; it does not claim that the rover profiles have different center-of-mass settings.
  3. How It Works → Model Meets Physics, then Sandbox → Lander & Rover Mission — move from the scene and runtime model to a live Modelica/physics connection and then an event-driven mission.
  4. Sandbox → Build a Scene — a guided tour of placement, editing, and saving. The assessed placement exercise is Build a Lunar Base.

docs.title: The catalog
docs.text:
The shipped catalog contains the following tracks and lessons. Durations are estimates from the catalog, not timers that gate progress.

Track Lesson Type Minutes Start Here Lunar Rover Lab (featured) Exercise 30 LunCoSim SysML Requirements Tour 3 LunCoSim Read the Sim UI Tour 3 LunCoSim Authority Handoff Exercise 3 How It Works How Simulation Works Tour 5 How It Works Model Meets Physics Tour 3 Navigation Choose a Perspective Tour 3 Sandbox Sandbox Intro Tour 3 Sandbox First Drive Exercise 5 Sandbox Lander & Rover Mission Exercise 10 Sandbox Build a Scene Tour 3 Sandbox Build a Lunar Base Exercise 8 Sandbox Script a Rover Tour 3 Sandbox Rhai Editor & REPL Tour 3 Sandbox Inspect the Simulation Tour 3 Rover Driving Moon Driving Basics Exercise 7 Rover Driving Slopes & Tip-Over Exercise 8 Rover Driving Rover Variants Tour 3 Rover Driving Join a Team Session Tour 3 Modelica Lunica Overview Tour 3 Modelica Your Workspace Tour 3 Modelica Open & View a Model Tour 3 Modelica Compile & Run Tour 3 Modelica Experiments & Sweeps Tour 3 Modelica Plots & Results Tour 3 Modelica Automate with API + MCP Tour 3

A Twin can contribute its own catalog with the same JSON shape. Its menu is nested under the Twin's name and its quick action is visible only while that Twin is active.

docs.title: The hands-on tutorials in this chapter
docs.text:
The lessons above are shipped with the application. The tutorials in this chapter are longer, authoring-oriented walkthroughs that use the same mechanisms:

Tutorial What it builds First mission A first drive, and the layer model behind it Create a Twin A project folder with a manifest and entry scene Build a scene A composed scene with placed assemblies and saved USD Add a Modelica model A continuous model attached to a USD program prim Script a mission A Rhai task tree, objectives, events, and a verdict Author a shader A WESL material with parameters and texture layers Compose a HUD A runtime-authored surface with bindings and actions Validate and share Preflight, lint, scene test, evidence, and handoff

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need a working LunCoSim installation and a scene to edit. If the application is not installed, start with Installation. If you have never opened the workbench, read First run first.

The tutorials assume that you can create a folder, edit a text file, and open a terminal. They do not assume prior OpenUSD, Modelica, or Rhai experience. Each step states what the file is for before showing the source.

docs.title: Conventions used in the tutorials
docs.text:
• Bold names a UI label or perspective.
  • Monospace names a file, attribute, command, or value.
  • A step that changes a file shows the complete file or the exact fragment to add. Do not paste a fragment into the wrong nesting level.
  • A step that runs a command shows the command from the Twin root unless stated otherwise.
  • A Note explains a constraint. A Warning explains a mistake that is easy to make and hard to diagnose.

docs.title: What the tutorials do not cover
docs.text: The tutorials are an authoring path, not a complete reference. They do not cover every command, every schema, or every Modelica library. When a tutorial uses a feature, it links to the chapter that documents the full contract. The Reference chapter is the place to look up an exact field or flag.

docs.title: Add a Modelica model
docs.text:
Modelica gives a scene continuous behavior: a motor response, a battery discharge, a thermal network, or a control law. This tutorial adds a small drive model to a rover, attaches it to a USD program prim, wires its output to a consumer port, and observes the result.

The example is intentionally simple: a first-order response that demonstrates the contract without pretending to be a realistic rover controller.

docs.title: Write the model
docs.text:
Create a file under the Twin:

my-rover-twin/
└── models/
    └── Drive.mo

A first-order drive response looks like this:

within MyRover;

model Drive
  input Real throttle;
  output Real speed;
  parameter Real timeConstant = 1.0;

initial equation
  speed = 0.0;

equation
  der(speed) = (max(-1.0, min(1.0, throttle)) - speed) / timeConstant;
end Drive;

The pieces are:

Element Meaning within MyRover; The package namespace for this class model Drive A reusable model class input Real throttle A value supplied by the surrounding system output Real speed A value exposed to the surrounding system parameter Real timeConstant A tunable value that is constant during a run initial equation The initial condition equation The continuous relationship der(speed) The time derivative of speed

This model does not find prims, read the scene, or decide when a mission is complete. It turns a throttle command into a first-order speed response.

docs.title: Declare the source root
docs.text:
The compiler must be able to find the model. Add the directory to the Twin manifest:

[modelica]
paths = ["models"]

paths is relative to the Twin root. If the model uses a package structure, keep the within declarations and the directory layout consistent. For a multi-file package, open the directory as a workspace or Twin root; opening a single package.mo does not recursively import every file in its folder.

docs.title: Compile the model
docs.text:
Open the ∿ Lunica perspective, choose the Modelica section in the Twin browser, and open Drive.mo. Choose Compile.

A successful compile leaves the model ready and paused. A failed compile reports a diagnostic with the source location. Fix the source and compile again; the scene runs the compiled artifact.

You can also preflight the file without opening the application:

luncosim --validate path/to/my-rover-twin/models/Drive.mo

--validate proves that the file parses and its declarations are structurally valid. It does not run the model or prove that its behavior is correct.

docs.title: Attach the model to a prim
docs.text:
A Modelica class becomes a simulation participant when a USD prim carries LunCoProgramAPI and names the source:

def Xform "Rover"
{
    def Scope "Controller" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
    )
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/models/Drive.mo@
        uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true
    }
}

Use @twin://...@ for a model inside the open Twin. Use @lunco://models/...@ for a model shipped in the installed asset library.

The program here is a child Scope, so deleting the Scope removes the behavior without deleting the rover. The source path is an asset address, not a relative path from the current working directory.

docs.title: Declare the ports
docs.text:
A model output becomes externally connectable only when the prim carrying LunCoProgramAPI declares the matching outputs:<name> property. A connection target alone does not create a public port.

def Xform "Rover"
{
    def Scope "Controller" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
    )
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/models/Drive.mo@
        uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true

        float inputs:throttle = 0.0
        float outputs:speed
    }
}

The names must match the Modelica declarations exactly. The runtime resolves the typed port through the program and the composed stage; it does not guess a port from a display name.

docs.title: Wire the model to a consumer
docs.text:
A connection is authored on the prim that consumes the value. Here the chassis declares the speed it consumes from the controller:

def Xform "Rover"
{
    def Scope "Controller" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
    )
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/models/Drive.mo@
        uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true

        float inputs:throttle = 0.0
        float outputs:speed
    }

    def Xform "Chassis" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["PhysicsRigidBodyAPI"]
    )
    {
        float inputs:drive_speed.connect = </Rover/Controller.outputs:speed>
    }
}

The composed stage resolves references, payloads, variants, and the connection graph. The runtime derives a SimConnection from the authored wire and samples the output at the declared communication point.

If the model drives a force or torque port on a client-predicted body, it must declare lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true. The runtime rejects that edge at wire-build time when the declaration is missing, because a late or nondeterministic program would diverge from the server.

docs.title: Run and observe
docs.text:
1. Open the Twin and load the scene.
  2. Wait for readiness. A model can be compiling while the scene is already visible.
  3. Switch to Analyze.
  4. Select the rover in Entities or Telemetry.
  5. Add speed and throttle to a graph.
  6. Command a throttle through the UI, a script, or the API.
  7. Watch the speed settle toward the commanded value.

A missing port is not a zero. Use Ports or ListPorts to confirm that the port exists and has the direction and kind you expect.

docs.title: Tune a parameter
docs.text:
Parameters are constant during a run. Change timeConstant in the source and recompile, or override it through an experiment. Do not hide a tuning value in a script when the model owns it; a parameter is a model fact.

Lunica's Experiments panel can override parameters and compare several runs without editing the source. See Experiments.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The model does not appear [modelica].paths does not include its root Add the path and reopen the Twin Compile fails Syntax or type error Read the diagnostic; run --validate The value does not reach the consumer The output is not declared or not connected Declare outputs:speed and author the connection The connection is rejected The target input does not exist Check the exact inputs: name The force edge is rejected Missing realtimeSafe on a predicted body Declare the program realtime-safe or move it off the prediction path The value never changes The model is paused or not admitted Check readiness and the participant status A parameter change has no effect The model was not recompiled Recompile; the scene runs the compiled artifact

docs.title: Author a shader
docs.text:
A shader look is authored as data: a WESL source asset declares its material parameters, and a USD material binds the source and its texture inputs. The renderer reflects the parameter schema and builds the pipeline; Rust does not hardcode the parameter set.

This tutorial adds a simple surface look to a prim and exposes one parameter in the Inspector. It assumes a Twin with a scene and a basic USD material.

docs.title: Create the WESL source
docs.text:
Add a source asset under the Twin:

my-rover-twin/
└── shaders/
    └── dusty_surface.wesl

A material declares its parameters in a struct Material block:

//!@ui      dust_density 0 1      "Dust density"
//!@default dust_density 0.35
//!@ui      clump_scale  0 64     "Clump scale (/m)"
//!@default clump_scale  8
//!@ui      tint         color    "Tint"
//!@default tint         0.6,0.6,0.62,1.0

struct Material {
    dust_density: f32,
    clump_scale: f32,
    tint: vec4<f32>,
};

@group(2) @binding(0) var<uniform> material: Material;

The //!@ annotations are the authoring contract:

Annotation Meaning //!@ui name min max "Label" The slider bounds and label the Inspector uses //!@ui name color "Label" A color picker //!@ui name int min max "Label" Integer bounds //!@default name value The value used when the author does not set one //!@engine name A field filled by the runtime

The uniform block is deliberately opaque. The same 512 bytes are reinterpreted by each shader through its own struct Material. A name that is not in the schema is dropped at pack time with a warning; it is never silently mis-packed into a neighbouring field.

A linked vertex stage shares the same material ABI. Both stages read @binding(0) from the one 512-byte block, and the fragment stage's reflected schema is the layout that gets packed. A vertex shader must declare the same Material fields, order, and WESL types as its fragment shader.

docs.title: Add a texture layer (optional)
docs.text:
A shader can sample named texture roles. The authorable roles are:

Role Content Albedo Colour raster, such as a lunar mosaic Mineral Class-id or composition raster, tinted through a palette LUT Surface Packed scalars: R roughness, G ambient occlusion, B rock density, A hazard Normal Tangent- or world-space normals DetailAlbedo Repeatable colour detail DetailNormal Repeatable tangent-space normal detail DetailSurface Repeatable packed roughness and AO Displacement Authored scalar displacement

Height and ShadowCache are engine-filled and not authorable from USD. Continuation and annotation roles are runtime-owned. See Texture layers for the full role list and channel-packing rules.

A shader that does not declare a binding is unaffected by that layer being set. This is why one slot set serves every shader; a new look does not create a new material type.

Scalar layers should usually share a packed channel rather than consume a new texture slot. Surface is the reference example: four independent scalar layers in one texture fetch.

docs.title: Bind the source in USD
docs.text:
A USD material names the shader source with the standard UsdShade selector and the LunCoSim WESL properties:

def Material "DustyMaterial"
{
    token outputs:surface.connect = </World/Looks/DustyMaterial/Shader.outputs:surface>

    def Shader "Shader"
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface.wesl@

        float inputs:dust_density = 0.35
        float inputs:clump_scale = 8.0
        color4f inputs:tint = (0.62, 0.62, 0.64, 1.0)
    }
}

info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset" is the standard UsdShade selector. info:wesl:sourceAsset follows the standard source-type convention. An optional info:wesl:vertexAsset names a second stage when the default mesh vertex stage is not sufficient:

uniform asset info:wesl:vertexAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface_vertex.wesl@

A portable material can keep both entry points in one source asset and use that same asset for both projected stages.

docs.title: Bind the material to a prim
docs.text:
Bind the material through the standard material:binding relationship:

def Xform "Rover"
{
    rel material:binding = </World/Looks/DustyMaterial>
}

The editor and SetObjectProperty follow the composed binding network. A parameter edit authors a typed UsdOp on the bound UsdShade.Shader prim's inputs:<name> attribute. Geometry primvars: are reserved for standard UsdGeom primvars such as primvars:displayColor; they are not a generic shader-parameter namespace.

docs.title: Reload and inspect
docs.text:
The native desktop asset watcher reloads a changed .wesl source without relaunching the application. The render binder waits for prepared sources and refreshes affected looks on asset events.

To inspect the result:

  1. Select the prim in Build or Editor.
  2. Open the Inspector.
  3. Find the material parameters. The slider bounds and labels come from the reflected schema, not from a hand-written list.
  4. Change a value and observe the viewport.

If the shader fails to compile, the owning material is rejected and a structured runtime diagnostic is published. The renderer does not substitute a StandardMaterial or a guessed shader. Fix the source and reload; do not hide the error by changing the material to a different one.

docs.title: Validate before running
docs.text:
luncosim --validate path/to/my-rover-twin/shaders/dusty_surface.wesl

--validate checks source syntax and material facts. It is preflight evidence, not a GPU compile. The renderer still owns pipeline specialization and GPU validation. A graphics gate must reject shader compilation errors in the process log as well as domain runtime diagnostics.

docs.title: Keep the look shared
docs.text:
Identical looks share one material and one bind group. The binder caches by the look key, which quantises floats so a rounding error cannot mint a second material.

Vary a parameter per instance and you get a material per instance: a draw call and a bind group each. If instances must differ, bucket the value first — snap it to a small set — rather than giving every instance a unique float.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The material is rejected The source has no callable fragment entry point Declare @fragment or correct the source role A parameter is missing from the Inspector It is not in struct Material or has no reflected type Add the field and its annotation A parameter change does nothing The value is not bound to the authored shader input Author inputs:<name> on the bound Shader prim The shader compiles but looks wrong A texture role is missing or mis-bound Check the material's texture inputs and the role Two instances create many materials A per-instance float varies the look key Bucket the value or share the look The vertex stage fails Its Material layout differs from the fragment stage Use the same fields, order, and types
