docs.title: Build a scene
docs.text:
A scene is the USD stage that becomes the live world. Build is the perspective for composing it: placing assemblies, adjusting transforms, inspecting prims, and saving the result into the authored stage. The simulation keeps running while you work, so a change can be observed immediately.

This tutorial assumes that you have a Twin with a default scene. If you do not, complete Create a Twin first.

docs.title: Open the scene in Build
docs.text:
1. Open the Twin. Its default_scene is mounted into the viewport.
  2. Switch to Build from the title bar or View → Perspectives.
  3. Confirm that the Entities tree and the Twin file browser are visible on the left, and Inspector, Environment, and Spawn are on the right.

The Entities tree shows the live runtime objects. The Twin browser shows the authored files. They are related but not identical: an entity can be generated at runtime, and a file can exist in the Twin without being part of the active scene.

docs.title: Place an assembly
docs.text:
1. Open the Spawn palette.
  2. Choose an assembly category, such as a rover, a habitat, or a ground prop.
  3. Click a placement point in the viewport, or drag the assembly into the scene.
  4. The new object appears in Entities and in the viewport.

A spawned assembly is a reference into the scene, not a copy of the source file. The scene stores the placement and any overrides; the reusable asset stays in the installed library or the Twin.

Build places the scene tree, the Twin's files, the Inspector, and the Spawn palette around the live scene.

docs.title: Adjust the transform
docs.text:
Select the object in Entities or click it in the viewport. The Inspector shows the selected prim's properties. Use the transform gizmo or the Inspector fields to set position, rotation, and scale.

The scene placement owns the initial heading. The reusable asset owns its local geometry and its canonical frame. Do not duplicate a heading in the asset, a variant, and a wrapper layer; keep one authoritative placement and let the vehicle controller own later changes.

A prim that can be rotated must declare the rotation op in xformOpOrder. An attribute that is not listed in the order is inert, even if it has a value:

double3 xformOp:translate = (4, 0, 8)
float3 xformOp:rotateXYZ = (0, 35, 0)
uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate", "xformOp:rotateXYZ"]

docs.title: Inspect the prim
docs.text:
The Inspector is a view over the authored prim, not a separate settings store. Editing a value authors a typed USD operation through the document owner. The change appears in the Change History journal when the document is open in Editor.

Useful checks before saving:

Check Why The prim has the expected schema, such as UsdPhysics.RigidBodyAPI A body without the schema will not move A movable child has a joint A nested body without a joint is reported by the scene linter Mass and collision geometry are present A collider without mass or a body without a collider behaves unexpectedly The transform op is listed in xformOpOrder An unlisted op is ignored The asset reference resolves A missing reference composes as an empty prim

docs.title: Scene-wide environment
docs.text:
Environment owns scene-wide settings such as lighting and the environment profile. Use it when the question is about the whole scene rather than one prim: the sun, the sky, the ambient conditions, or the terrain context.

Do not put a per-object light or a per-object material override in the environment panel. Those are prim properties and belong on the object.

docs.title: Save the scene
docs.text:
Use File → Save or Ctrl+S to save the active scene document. The save writes the authored USD stage through the document journal; it does not rewrite unrelated files.

If the scene was opened as a lesson or an installed example, Save as Twin… creates a project copy before you edit it. Saving into the installed library is not the intended workflow.

docs.title: Compose, do not duplicate
docs.text:
A scene can reference a reusable rover and place two instances with different transforms:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "PracticeYard"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
)

def Xform "PracticeYard"
{
    def Xform "RoverA" (
        prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 0, 0)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }

    def Xform "RoverB" (
        prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (8, 0, 4)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }
}

The two rovers share the same source asset. A change to the asset appears in both placements unless the scene overrides the changed property. This is the intended way to keep a scene maintainable.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The object is visible but does not move No rigid body or no collider Add the physics schemas and a collider A mounted part falls away on the first step Nested body without a joint Add the joint or remove the nested body The object is in the wrong place Transform op not listed in xformOpOrder Add the op to the order The scene opens empty default_scene is missing or wrong Fix the manifest and reopen the Twin The change disappeared The scene was not saved Save the document; check Change History A referenced asset is missing The asset address does not resolve Check lunco:// or twin:// and the asset cache

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Continue with Add a Modelica model to give the scene continuous behavior, or Script a mission to add a discrete policy. For the full USD contract, read USD.

docs.title: Compose a HUD
docs.text:
LunCoSim has a small runtime-authored presentation layer for HUDs, telemetry cards, progress overlays, and other Twin-facing surfaces. It looks like HTML and CSS, but it is not a browser: templates become retained Bevy UI entities, and styles become Bevy components through HUI and Flair.

This tutorial adds a mission-status card to a Twin. The card reads a typed exposure, displays two values, and emits a semantic action when a button is pressed.

docs.title: Understand the boundary
docs.text:
A runtime surface may read a named engine capability and emit a semantic action. It cannot inspect ECS state or directly mutate the simulation.

authoritative engine state
        │  change detection + bounded presentation cadence
        ▼
EngineExposures ─────────────► ReadExposures / telemetry / remote clients
        │
        │ named snapshot, revision-gated
        ▼
HUI template properties + Flair CSS custom properties
        │
        ▼
retained Bevy UI tree ───────► WorkbenchEguiHost / window

HTML button ─► HUI callback ─► RuntimeUiAction(action, HookValue map)
          ─► Rhai policy ─► typed command/event

The template owns structure and declared properties. The stylesheet owns appearance and internal layout. The manifest owns the outer rectangle, bindings, actions, gates, and placement. Rhai owns the meaning of an authored action.

docs.title: Create the Twin manifest
docs.text:
A Twin can provide its own JSON manifest with kind: "lunco.runtime-ui-manifest.v1". Normal Twin loading composes it over the application surfaces by stable ID; closing the Twin restores the shared surfaces.

Create a file under the Twin:

my-rover-twin/
└── ui/
    ├── mission.json
    ├── status.html
    └── status.css

A minimal manifest looks like this:

{
  "kind": "lunco.runtime-ui-manifest.v1",
  "surfaces": [
    {
      "id": "mission-status",
      "template": "ui/status.html",
      "stylesheet": "ui/status.css",
      "namespace": "mission-status",
      "bindings": {
        "title": { "source": "title" },
        "state": { "source": "state" }
      },
      "actions": [
        {
          "callback": "runtime_status_pause",
          "action": "mission.pause"
        }
      ],
      "interactive": true,
      "placement": {
        "mode": "window",
        "anchor": "top_right",
        "offset": [-16.0, 16.0],
        "width": 260.0,
        "height": 96.0
      }
    }
  ]
}

Paths in the manifest resolve from the Twin root. A Twin stylesheet can import shared fonts with an explicit logical URI:

@import "lunco://ui/runtime_fonts.css";

docs.title: Write the template
docs.text:
The stable runtime contract uses a deliberately small HUI vocabulary:

<template>
  <property name="title">Mission status</property>
  <property name="state">offline</property>

  <node id="status-root">
    <text id="status-title">{title}</text>
    <text id="status-state">{state}</text>
    <button id="status-pause" on_press="runtime_status_pause">
      <text>Pause</text>
    </button>
  </node>
</template>

Rules that matter:

  • Use <template>, <property>, <node>, <text>, and <button>.
  • Every template, including a keyed collection row, must have one <node> root.
  • Put buttons and text elements beneath that root.
  • A button's visible caption must be a nested <text> node.
  • Use stable id values and #id selectors in the stylesheet.
  • HUI does not turn an HTML class attribute into a ClassList; use id selectors.

A surface callback receives only the pressed entity. The manifest turns it into a RuntimeUiAction; built-ins remain in the host, while a Twin-authored action is forwarded as a typed runtime.ui.action event for Rhai policy.

docs.title: Style the contents
docs.text:
Flair is CSS-like and maps properties to Bevy UI components. The practical subset includes flex layout, limited grid layout, absolute positioning, dimensions, spacing, borders, backgrounds, colours, text properties, #id selectors, custom properties, var(...), transitions, and keyframe animations.

@import "lunco://ui/runtime_fonts.css";

#status-root {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 6px;
  padding: 12px;
  background-color: rgba(8, 20, 32, 0.86);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
  border-radius: 4px;
}

#status-title {
  color: #e8f4f8;
  font-size: 14px;
  font-weight: 700;
}

#status-state {
  color: var(--ui-state-color, #9fd8e4);
  font-size: 12px;
}

#status-pause {
  padding: 4px 8px;
  background-color: #12384d;
  color: #ffffff;
}

The manifest owns the outer rectangle; CSS owns the contents. Authored profiles must fit their contents within the registered size. The runtime pins the root's minimum and maximum size to the resolved rectangle and clips child overflow at that boundary.

docs.title: Publish the values
docs.text:
An engine producer publishes a typed, named snapshot. A Twin's Rhai policy can publish UI-owned values through the generic exposure bridge, or an engine capability can publish them directly. The template never reads ECS state.

A binding with css: true also projects a CSS custom property named --ui-<property-name>; ordinary prose never enters the CSS token stream.

"bindings": {
  "title": { "source": "title" },
  "state": { "source": "state", "css": true }
}

The producer may map exact rendered values such as true, false, or 301 into presentation values. The registry stores typed text, boolean, f64, array, and map values, not CSS or HUI types.

docs.title: Handle the action
docs.text:
A Twin-authored action is delivered to Rhai as a typed event. The policy reads the action and issues a typed command:

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name != "runtime.ui.action" { return; }
    if evt.value.action == "mission.pause" {
        pause();
    }
}

The exact event shape and command name come from the running application. Use GET /api/commands/schema or the app's command reference when you need an exact name.

docs.title: Gate and place the surface
docs.text:
A surface can declare a perspective filter, a named host gate, and a Twin setting:

"visible_in_perspective": "sandbox_view",
"setting": "ui.mission_status",
"setting_default": true

The setting is a namespaced boolean in the active Twin's [settings] table. Omitted keys use the surface's declared default. The setting is project policy, not a user-global preference.

Placement modes:

Mode Use viewport Full-window overlay, useful for HUDs that frame the 3D scene dock_panel Surface aligned to a workbench panel, with an optional inset window Fixed logical-point rectangle anchored at a corner or center

A window surface may declare "draggable": true. Only a descendant tagged tag:ui_drag_handle="true" can move or reset it, so dragging a button does not move the whole panel.

docs.title: Reload and test
docs.text:
On native desktop, the asset watcher reloads runtime UI assets without relaunching:

Edit Result *.html Rebuilds the affected retained surface tree *.css or an imported stylesheet Reapplies Flair styles runtime_surfaces.json or the Twin manifest Replaces registered roots and action mappings runtime_fonts.css Reapplies the font stylesheet

Changing a Rust producer or action observer requires a rebuilt binary.

To inspect a running surface over the API:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"ExecuteCommand","command":"ReadExposures",
       "params":{"surface":"mission-status"}}'

The response contains revision and each surface's state (pending, ready, or failed), error, visible, and typed properties. Wait for ready before reading prepared properties; inspect failed rather than repeating an invalid policy.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Surface absent Wrong namespace, visible false, or a closed gate Check the manifest, exposure, perspective, and placement Blank value Target property is not declared or the source name differs Declare the property and match the binding exactly Button does nothing Callback spelling differs or no action mapping Check the template, manifest, and Rhai handler Tofu glyphs The bundled font is not imported Add @import "lunco://ui/runtime_fonts.css"; Style reverts Rust writes the same style components Let Flair own presentation Surface jumps on resize Placement is being corrected per frame Keep placement in the manifest; use the change-detected boundary

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
This is a minimum native UI language, not full CSS. There is no browser DOM, JavaScript, networking, or browser layout engine. There is one stylesheet per styled subtree; use @import for shared rules. There is no global stylesheet, and !important is detected but ignored. Custom-property fallback values are not supported. calc() is limited by Bevy's Val types. Font support is one explicit @font-face, with no browser-like local or fallback chain. Unsupported web units such as em and features such as text-decoration are not available.

Use the workbench for editors, docking, rich text, large inspectors, and controls that need semantics outside this contract. Use runtime HTML/CSS for Twin-facing presentation that should change without recompiling Rust.

docs.title: Create a Twin
docs.text:
There are two practical ways to start a project:

  • Promote a working scene. Open a lesson or example, then save it as a new Twin. This is the fastest way to get a real scene with physics, models, and scripts.
  • Start empty. Create a new Twin and add your own scene and sources.

Both produce the same artifact: a folder with twin.toml. The difference is how much authored content is already present.

docs.title: Promote a scene into a Twin
docs.text:
1. Launch LunCoSim.
  2. Open Scenarios → Tutorials → Sandbox → First Drive so a working scene is mounted.
  3. Choose File → Save as Twin….
  4. Select or create an empty folder for the project.
  5. Confirm. LunCoSim writes twin.toml and opens the new Twin.

The new folder contains the scene document and the manifest. The scene keeps its normal lunco:// references to the installed library; it is a project that uses the shared asset bundle, not a self-contained copy of every referenced asset.

The Build perspective keeps the scene tree, the Twin's files, the Inspector, and the Spawn palette together while the simulation keeps running.

docs.title: Start from a new Twin
docs.text:
Choose File → New Twin…, select a folder, and provide a name. LunCoSim creates the manifest and opens the project. You can add a scene later.

A minimal manifest looks like this:

name = "my-rover-twin"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "My first LunCoSim project"

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

The folder should look like:

my-rover-twin/
├── twin.toml
├── scene.usda
├── models/
│   └── Drive.mo
├── scenarios/
│   └── drive.rhai
└── .lunco/

default_scene is the important line. It tells LunCoSim which USD stage becomes the active world when the Twin opens. Without it, the Twin opens as a file browser and does not mount a scene.

docs.title: Add a scene
docs.text:
If the Twin was created empty, add a USD file and point default_scene at it. The smallest useful stage declares a default prim and the stage's units:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "MyTwin"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
)

def Xform "MyTwin"
{
    def Xform "Ground"
    {
        def Cube "Pad"
        {
            double size = 10
            double3 xformOp:translate = (0, -0.05, 0)
            uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
        }
    }
}

This stage is inert until the runtime projects it. It has no physics, no behavior, and no mission. That is enough for a first open; add behavior in the next tutorials.

docs.title: Add behavior
docs.text:
• Modelica goes in .mo files under the Twin, then a USD LunCoProgramAPI prim points at it with info:sourceAsset.
  • Rhai goes in .rhai files under the Twin, then a LunCoProgramAPI prim points at the scenario.
  • External assets go in Assets.toml, never as hardcoded cache paths.

The next tutorials build each layer:

  • Build a scene — place and save assemblies.
  • Add a Modelica model — attach and wire continuous behavior.
  • Script a mission — attach a Rhai scenario.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Open the Twin and choose its default scene, or load the scene directly:

luncosim --api 4101 --scene /path/to/my-rover-twin/scene.usda

Use an explicit free API port. Run from the folder containing the Twin if you are using a source build and relative asset paths.

The application does not guess a starting scene from a folder of .usda files. If default_scene is absent or wrong, the Twin opens as a file browser. That behavior is intentional: a project can contain many scenes and only one entry point.

docs.title: Check the manifest
docs.text:
If the Twin does not open the scene you expect:

  1. Confirm default_scene is a path relative to the Twin root.
  2. Confirm the file exists and is a valid .usda.
  3. Reopen the Twin after editing the manifest; the manifest is read at open.
  4. Check that unknown fields are not present — the manifest parser rejects typos.

See twin.toml for the field reference.

docs.title: Version the project
docs.text:
A Twin is an ordinary folder. Initialize a Git repository at the Twin root and commit the authored files, not the local session state:

.lunco/
target/
*.tmp

Do not commit downloaded cache bytes. Declare them in Assets.toml and let the asset system fetch them. A colleague who clones the Twin should be able to open it, accept the declared downloads, and run the same authored scene.

docs.title: First mission
docs.text: The first lesson is a real simulation, not a slideshow. You take control of a rover, drive it with physics, and complete objectives that are checked against the live world. The lesson is the fastest way to see the division between USD, Modelica, Rhai, and the runtime without authoring a project first.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Launch LunCoSim and wait for the workbench to finish opening. You do not need to create a Twin or open a scene manually; the lesson launcher selects the authored scene and starts the lesson's Rhai scenario.

Open Scenarios → Tutorials in the menu bar. The catalog opens with the Start Here track expanded.

docs.title: Option A — Lunar Rover Lab (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Scenarios → Tutorials → Start Here → Lunar Rover Lab

This is the recommended classroom activity. It is an exercise, so each step advances only when the simulation observes the requested result. You will:

  1. Drive to a marker and stop inside it.
  2. Open a speed graph and identify a real motion sample.
  3. Predict the result of changing drive demand, then run two trials.
  4. Explain the measured result.
  5. Move a block into an authoring bay.
  6. Save the result as your own Twin.

The lesson card stays visible across perspectives. Instructor checkpoints let you jump to driving, telemetry, or comparison practice without pretending the earlier tasks were completed. Restart whole lab (discard edits) resets the document through the normal scene restart.

docs.title: Option B — First Drive (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Scenarios → Tutorials → Sandbox → First Drive

Use this when you only want to see the core loop:

  1. Open the lesson.
  2. Click Take control.
  3. Drive to the glowing flag.
  4. Stop inside the marker.

The rover's motion comes from the authored Modelica controller and the native physics engine. The lesson script observes possession, the flag sensor, and the rover's speed; it does not advance from elapsed time.

The lesson card names the current objective and the actions that are valid now. Progress is checked against the live simulation.

docs.title: Reading the lesson card
docs.text:
The card shows the current objective and the actions that are valid now. Some actions are mouse buttons in the card, some are keyboard controls, and some are buttons that open another perspective.

The lesson uses semantic input hints such as forward, brake, and left. The displayed key is resolved from your current input bindings, so re-binding an action changes both the actual control and the lesson text. See Controls.

A tour and an exercise look similar but behave differently. A tour advances when you choose Next; an exercise waits for the world. If an exercise card does not advance, the current objective has not been observed yet. Read the objective and the hint before assuming the application is stuck.

docs.title: Driving the rover
docs.text:
Selection is not control. Clicking the rover selects it; it does not send your input to it. Use Take control in the lesson card, or click the input endpoint, before driving.

The default bindings are:

Action Default Forward W Reverse S Steer left A Steer right D Brake Space Release control G Pause P

The lesson displays the bindings that are actually configured, not a hardcoded key name. If a binding reads unbound, the action has no key and the lesson cannot be completed with the keyboard until you assign one in Settings → Keybindings.

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
Under the lesson there is a normal Twin:

  • A USD scene owns the rover, the ground, the flag, the camera, and the sensors.
  • A Modelica model owns the rover's continuous drive behavior.
  • A Rhai scenario owns the lesson steps, hints, objectives, and completion checks.
  • The runtime projects the scene into physics, steps the model, and delivers events back to the scenario.

That division is the main idea behind LunCoSim. The lesson is not a special mode with a separate physics implementation; it is an authored scene and an authored scenario running through the production runtime.

docs.title: If the lesson does not advance
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause What to do The rover ignores input You have not taken control Click Take control or the input endpoint The rover moves but the marker does not trigger You stopped outside the marker radius Drive fully inside the glowing area and stop The card shows a key that does nothing The binding is unbound or remapped Open Settings → Keybindings and check the action The viewport is empty The lesson scene did not load Reopen the lesson; check the status bar for an asset hold The rover rolled over The slope or speed exceeded the authored limit Use Right rover, then approach more slowly A graph is empty The simulation is paused or the channel is not selected Resume, then select a live channel in Telemetry

docs.title: After the lesson
docs.text: Continue with Create a Twin to turn a working scene into your own project, or read How it fits together to understand the layer boundaries in more detail. If you want to inspect the values behind the lesson, open Inspect telemetry.

docs.title: Script a mission
docs.text:
A scenario is an ordinary .rhai file attached to an entity. This tutorial builds a small mission that drives a rover to a marker, reports arrival, and shows an objective on the HUD. It then turns the same scenario into an authored test with a verdict.

The tutorial assumes a scene with a rover that has an authored drive law and a marker at a known position. The First Drive sandbox is a suitable starting point; use Save as Twin… to make an editable copy.

docs.title: Create the file
docs.text:
Add a scenario inside your Twin:

my-rover-twin/
└── scenarios/
    └── drive.rhai

docs.title: Write the policy
docs.text:
fn marker() {
    [12.0, 0.0, 8.0]
}

fn task(me, ctx) {
    let goal = marker();
    seq([
        once(|m| notify("Driving to the marker")),
        step(|m| nav_to(m, goal, 1.2, 2.0),
             |m| arrived(m, goal, 2.0)),
        once(|m| {
            brake(m);
            emit("MARKER_REACHED", goal);
        }),
    ])
}

fn mission(me, ctx) {
    let goal = marker();
    [
        objective("reach_marker", #{
            text: "Drive to the marker",
            done: |m| arrived(m, goal, 2.0),
        }),
    ]
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "MARKER_REACHED" {
        notify_kind("Marker reached", "success");
    }
}

What each part does:

Part Role task(me, ctx) Returns a task tree that the native behavior kernel advances seq([...]) Runs steps in order once(...) Runs one action and advances step(act, done) Repeats act until done is true, then advances wait(secs) Suspends for simulation seconds wait_until(pred) Suspends until the predicate becomes true wait_for("NAME") Suspends until a named event arrives mission(me, ctx) Declares objectives checked against live state on_event(...) Reacts to an event outside the task tree

nav_to is a prelude helper that publishes a waypoint to the authored drive law. It does not integrate motion itself. arrived reads the authoritative pose and checks the radius.

Do not add on_tick to a production scenario. The task kernel already advances steps, waits, and predicates; a hand-written tick loop duplicates it and makes the scenario less deterministic. on_tick is reserved for test sampling.

docs.title: Attach the scenario
docs.text:
A scenario is not global. Attach it to the entity that owns the behavior, or to a dedicated mission-control entity that never moves:

def Scope "Mission" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
) {
    uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/scenarios/drive.rhai@
}

Place this prim under the entity that should be me. Use @twin://...@ for a file in the open Twin. The scenario must still find its target by name or by an explicit reference; attachment does not automatically pick a rover.

A scenario can also be started explicitly with RunScenario or RunScenarioAsset from the API or another script. A UI-only scenario can pass an empty scene asset.

docs.title: Run and iterate
docs.text:
Open the Twin and load its default scene. The scenario starts when the scene is admitted. To iterate:

  • Edit the .rhai file; the asset watcher hot-reloads a file-backed scenario.
  • The old instance's on_stop runs before the new one starts.
  • Use Restart scene if you changed USD structure rather than script logic.
  • Use Scenarios to load a different declared scene.

Hot reload applies to file-backed assets. A script started from an inline source has no file to watch, so editing a file elsewhere does not replace it.

docs.title: Observe events
docs.text:
Events are the preferred coordination mechanism:

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "MARKER_REACHED" {
        this.reached = true;
    }
    if evt.name == "LOW_FUEL" {
        notify_kind("Fuel is low", "warn");
    }
}

A script emits with emit("NAME", value). Events are delivered on the next fixed step, so ordering does not depend on entity iteration order. Scenarios do not call each other directly; they interact through the event bus and the shared command/query surface.

Events emitted while a pass is delivering its current batch are queued for the following pass. A new or restarted program does not receive events accumulated before its on_start; query current state instead of relying on history.

docs.title: Add a verdict
docs.text:
A scenario can also be a test. Use the prelude assertions and report one typed verdict at the end:

fn on_start(me, ctx) {
    this.start = world_pos3(me);
    this.reported = false;
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name != "MARKER_REACHED" { return; }
    if this.reported { return; }
    this.reported = true;

    let pos = world_pos3(me);
    let distance = if pos == () || this.start == () {
        ()
    } else {
        vlen(vsub(pos, this.start))
    };

    let fails = [];
    fails.push(t_present(pos, "rover position"));
    fails.push(t_moved(distance, 3.0, "rover travel"));
    report_verdict(fails, "DRIVE TEST", "DRIVE_TEST");
}

t_moved uses the measured distance, not a hardcoded pass value. Pairing it with t_present also proves the test read a real position. Run the scenario through the production scene-test binary, not a private harness.

docs.title: Run the authored test
docs.text:
luncosim test --scene path/to/my-rover-twin/tests/drive.usda

The exit code is the verdict:

Exit Meaning 0 PASS 1 FAIL 2 No verdict was produced

A test that exhausts its tick budget without a verdict is exit 2. Keep a negative fixture for the behavior you are guarding; a test that cannot fail is not evidence.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Symptom Cause Nothing moves nav_to has no authored steering capability, so it brakes safely Rover ignores the script The scenario is attached to the wrong entity, or a session holds manual control Objective never completes done reads a stale or missing owner value Event handler never runs The event name differs, or the scenario was replaced before delivery Hot reload does nothing The script was started from an inline source, not a file-backed asset Test exits 2 The scenario never published a verdict

docs.title: Validate and share
docs.text:
A Twin is ready to share when another person can open it, resolve its assets, run its authored behavior, and understand what the evidence does and does not prove. This tutorial walks through that gate in the order the application exposes it.

Validation is layered. Each layer answers a different question, and a clean result at one layer does not imply a clean result at the next.

docs.title: Decide what you are proving
docs.text:
Question Evidence What it does not prove Do the authored files parse and compose? luncosim --validate, ValidateAsset That the scene runs or behaves correctly Does the Twin resolve its names and assets? ValidateTwin That a runtime owner does not collide Is the loaded scene structurally sound? RunLint That the behavior matches a requirement Does the authored scenario meet its verdict? luncosim test --scene That the model is physically accurate Does a SysML requirement pass? --verification with a Twin registry entry That every requirement is covered Is the live runtime healthy? /api/ready, CosimStatus, GetBrokenConnections That the authored design is correct Does it look right? Screenshot or recording That the numbers are right Is it accurate for my mission? Comparison with reference data and documented assumptions That it is accurate outside that evidence

LunCoSim provides a test and evidence harness. It does not issue a generic accuracy certificate.

docs.title: Preflight the files
docs.text:
luncosim --validate \
  path/to/twin/scene.usda \
  path/to/twin/models/Drive.mo \
  path/to/twin/scenarios/drive.rhai

Supported inputs are .mo, .usda, .sysml/.kerml, .wesl, and .rhai. The command runs without a window, GPU, or application instance. It exits 0 when every report is valid and 1 when any report fails.

--validate is parse- and loader-oriented. It catches syntax errors, broken references, invalid Modelica declarations, missing authored wheel attributes, and unparsable Rhai. It does not execute the scenario, run the solver, or prove that a value is physically correct.

From a running session, the same file-level checks are available as the ValidateAsset query. It admits one operation and returns an operation ID; poll that ID until the report is ready. Use ValidateTwin when the question spans a whole Twin folder and its resolver closure. ValidateTwin reports namespace collisions; use policy: "error" when a collision should fail the check.

docs.title: Lint the loaded scene
docs.text:
A file check cannot see entities spawned at runtime or edits made after load. After loading and editing a scene, run the explicit live lint:

{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "RunLint", "params": {}}

Then poll GetDiagnostics until the report is complete before treating it as clean. Loaded-stage lint can see runtime-owned ports that file validation cannot. It remains an explicit check; nothing lints automatically on load or on a physics tick.

Use RunLint when you need to know whether the scene as composed will behave correctly, not merely whether its files parse.

docs.title: Run the authored behavior test
docs.text:
luncosim test --scene path/to/twin/tests/drive.usda

The scene test runs the authored Rhai observer with manual, fixed-step time advancement. The exit code is the verdict:

Exit Meaning 0 PASS 1 FAIL 2 No verdict was produced

A passing test must come from a real verdict, not from the absence of a failure. A test that exhausts its tick budget without a verdict is exit 2. Keep a negative fixture for the behavior you are guarding; a test that cannot fail is not evidence.

Useful selectors:

Option Use --list Discover test scenes and their execution kind --verdict-channel NAME Accept the verdict only from a named channel --verification QUALIFIED_NAME Bind the run to a Twin SysML verification case --max-ticks N Bound cumulative simulated steps; default 20000 --tick-hz HZ Select the manual update rate; default 60 --readiness-timeout SECS Bound scene preparation time; default 420 --determinism-reference PATH Load a typed state reference for comparison

A component suite can use:

luncosim test-component --twin path/to/twin --component rover.wheels

The component manifest owns the scene and observer, so the test and its fixture stay together. Run scene tests through the production luncosim binary; do not substitute a private harness or --validate.

docs.title: Verify requirements with SysML
docs.text:
A Twin can keep its requirements in .sysml/.kerml source and map a verification case to a scene and Rhai observer:

[verification]
[[verification.cases]]
name = "Project::VerifyDrive"
scene = "tests/drive.usda"
script = "scenarios/tests/drive.rhai"
verdict_channel = "DRIVE_REQUIREMENTS"

Run the mapped case:

luncosim test --scene path/to/twin/tests/drive.usda \
  --verification Project::VerifyDrive

ValidateSysml checks source validity and structural policy. AnalyzeSysml returns typed facts for Rhai policy. --verification checks that the qualified name, scene, observer, and verdict channel match the Twin registry before the run starts.

This is a bounded subset: scalar constraints and authored observations are supported; full KerML execution and automatic requirement-to-USD projection are not. Keep the requirement text and limits in SysML, and keep provider selection and runtime observations in the Twin's Rhai observer.

docs.title: Read runtime evidence
docs.text:
Before treating a live value as final, check readiness:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/ready"

Require ready: true, world_hold: false, and pending_count: 0. A missing port is not a zero; it can mean the owner is still preparing.

For the coupled chain, read:

  • CosimStatus for per-entity model timing, status, and propagated values.
  • GetBrokenConnections for rejected wires and dropped writes.
  • CausalTrace for an admitted input edge and its producer identity.
  • ListTelemetryChannels then QueryTelemetryHistory for retained samples.
  • ExportTelemetryRecording for a columnar times/series export.

A single sample proves a moment; a history query proves a trend. Use one ReadPortsBatch response when comparing values from the same simulation tick. The telemetry t value is simulation seconds; epoch_jd gives the absolute mission frame when one is authored.

docs.title: Make an accuracy claim
docs.text:
Separate three questions before saying a model is accurate:

  1. Model form. What equations, assumptions, and neglected effects define the model?
  2. Numerical verification. Which solver, step size, tolerances, units, and initial conditions were used? Did refinement change the answer?
  3. Validation. What reference data was used, over what range, with what tolerance, and on which build?

Record the answer with the run. Compare the exported telemetry against a reference run or an external tool. A reference FMU can be run through native FMI import when you need an independent implementation, but that is a comparison setup, not an automatic equivalence proof.

A useful evidence record contains:

  • the Twin revision and luncosim build;
  • the exact scene and scenario paths;
  • the passed requirements and verdict channels;
  • the reference data source and tolerance;
  • the readiness and cosim diagnostics;
  • a screenshot when the claim includes presentation.

Do not use a render screenshot as numerical evidence, and do not use a green scene test as an accuracy certificate.

docs.title: Prepare the handoff
docs.text:
Before zipping or committing the Twin:

  1. Remove .lunco/ session state and any local build output.
  2. Confirm that every external asset is declared in Assets.toml.
  3. Confirm that default_scene opens on a clean machine.
  4. Run --validate, ValidateTwin, RunLint, and the scene test.
  5. Include the evidence record with the build and paths.
  6. State the limitations that apply to the result.

A Twin is an ordinary folder, so the handoff can be a Git repository, an archive, or a shared drive. Do not include downloaded cache bytes or private tokens.

docs.title: A practical gate
docs.text: Stage Run While authoring luncosim --validate on every changed asset Before opening a Twin ValidateTwin and RunLint Before sharing a behavior luncosim test --scene … Before claiming a requirement is met luncosim test --verification … Before publishing a result Reference comparison, versioned evidence, and a saved recording or screenshot

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text: Trap Better check Treating --validate as a runtime test Run the authored scene test Treating a missing port as 0.0 Check readiness and ListPorts Accepting a test with no verdict Require exit 0, not merely no failure Comparing samples from different ticks Use one batch read Calling a screenshot "validation" Pair it with numeric evidence Claiming FMI conformance from one imported FMU State the exact FMI profile and tested limits

docs.title: UI & Settings
docs.text:
The LunCoSim window is a workbench around a live 3D viewport. The workbench owns the shell: menus, docks, panels, the status bar, and the task layouts. The viewport owns the world. Twin-facing HUDs and cards are a separate, runtime-authored layer that can be changed without recompiling Rust.

This chapter describes the interface as a system: where a control lives, which owner decides whether it is visible, and which file or command changes it. It does not repeat every keyboard shortcut; the complete binding reference is in Controls.

docs.title: The shell
docs.text:
The standard layout has six regions:

Region Contents Owner Menu and title bar File, Edit, View, domain menus, Settings, Help, Time, transport, perspective tabs, window controls Workbench shell Left dock Twin browser; Entities, Telemetry, and task-specific panels Workbench dock Center Live 3D viewport, document editor, or analysis surface Perspective Right dock Inspector, Environment, Requirements, Change History Workbench dock Bottom dock Console, Graphs, Timeline, task tools Workbench dock Status bar Simulation time, speed, selection, body, FPS, latest status event Status bus and HUD owners

The 3D scene is rendered full-window by the scene camera. The egui host camera paints the chrome into the same shared texture, with the scene pass clearing and drawing first. That is why a panel can be translucent over the live scene without the viewport being tiled or resized.

A perspective changes which panels are docked and what the center is for. It does not reload the Twin, stop the simulation, or duplicate the project. The five pinned tasks are View, Analyze, Build, Editor, and Lunica; specialist tasks such as Terrain and Keybindings are available under View → Perspectives. See Perspectives for the task-by-task description.

docs.title: Presentation layers
docs.text:
LunCoSim does not have one undifferentiated UI layer. From front to back:

  1. Menus and popups.
  2. Floating windows, dialogs, guided cards, and notices.
  3. The general HUD: clocks, toasts, and global notices.
  4. The specific HUD: scene- and vehicle-owned readouts.
  5. Docked workbench panels.
  6. Runtime-authored HUI surfaces, which paint before the egui pass and therefore stay below every egui tier.

The ordering matters for both appearance and input. A menu always wins over a HUD. A visible modal runtime surface can claim the scene-pick gate; an ordinary full-window HUD does not, and scene clicks pass through everywhere except its authored buttons.

docs.title: What is configurable
docs.text: You want to change Surface Where it is owned Panel layout for a task Perspective Workbench layout, remembered per Twin User preferences Settings menu settings.json Project-wide behavior Project settings <project>/.lunco/settings.json Behavior that travels with a Twin Twin settings twin.toml [settings] HUD visibility Settings → HUD, or a Twin setting The HUD's owning resource HUD content and placement Runtime surface manifest, template, stylesheet Twin or application assets/ui/ Colours and typography Theme Theme resource and settings.json Key bindings Keybindings perspective input_bindings settings section Telemetry readout Analyze perspective or HTTP API Live port registry

docs.title: Reading this chapter
docs.text:
Section Question it answers Settings Which settings exist, where are they stored, and which scope wins? HUD Which heads-up surfaces ship, who controls their visibility, and how do they take input? Theming How do Dark and Light mode, semantic tokens, fonts, and diagram colours work? Runtime UI How does an authored HTML/CSS surface become a retained UI tree? Telemetry How do I read live values and record evidence?

For the authoring walkthrough, start with Compose a HUD. For the USD metadata that attaches a surface to a subject, see USD → Programs and USD → Authoring.

docs.title: HUD
docs.text:
A HUD is presentation drawn over the live scene. It is not a dock panel and it is not a document. HUDs answer questions about the running world: which body is in view, how fast the vessel is moving, whether a download is holding the simulation, or which lesson step comes next.

LunCoSim has three HUD families:

Family Visibility owner Examples User-controlled A persisted setting or a Twin setting Time HUD, surface-view switcher, performance HUD, input HUD, camera/status HUD Automatic Scene, possession, or lifecycle state Rover HUD, lander control cards, terrain and download progress, guided and notification cards Twin-authored A runtime surface manifest plus its exposure Mission-status cards, vehicle controls, program browsers, custom Twin HUDs

Settings → HUD is the discoverable view over the user-controlled family. It does not become a second visibility registry: each row writes the same resource, Twin setting, or typed command that the owning feature already reads.

docs.title: User-controlled HUDs
docs.text:
Surface Position Default Owner and switch Time HUD Top-left Off OverlaySettings.sky_clock; also in the Time menu Surface view switcher Top-centre Off OverlaySettings.view_switcher; also in the Camera menu Performance HUD Status bar Off PerfHudSettings.enabled; TogglePerfHud Input HUD Bottom-centre Off InputOverlaySettings.enabled; ToggleInputOverlay Camera/status HUD Top-right On Twin setting ui.camera_status, authored default true Graphs HUDs Measured view area Per instance GraphHuds; + Add in Settings → HUD Camera views Measured view area Per instance CameraFeeds; + Add camera view, limit eight

The Time HUD shows the shared celestial epoch. The surface-view switcher is both a control and a readout: it selects Surface, Moon, or Earth and shows which body the camera is focused on. Both are opt-in; a fresh install shows the terrain and nothing on top of it.

The performance HUD occupies the status bar and reports rendering FPS, frame time, physics step time, and Modelica worker time per physics step. Its samples come from the shared engine-health publication, so the graph remains live before a Twin is active. When space is tight the metric text shortens and scales rather than wrapping.

The input HUD visualizes live keyboard and mouse input. It is intended for recording, teaching, and input debugging, not for normal operation.

The camera/status surface shows the active camera identity. It is a runtime surface with a Twin-scoped boolean gate, so a Twin can hide it with "ui.camera_status" = false without changing the user's global settings.

Graphs HUDs are independent native windows, each with its own grid, parameter selection, visibility, and measured geometry. A card can plot up to four measured channels; each quantity keeps its own unit and Y scale while the time axes stay linked. The title-bar × removes the instance; the Settings row only toggles visibility, so a hidden card keeps its selection. The picker closes on Done or an outside click. Scene teardown releases every HUD-owned grid and plot, including while hidden.

Camera views are independent render feeds. + Add camera view creates the first view without needing an existing camera window; the view's own toolbar then selects a live camera. The limit is eight views.

docs.title: Automatic HUDs
docs.text:
These surfaces are listed in Settings → HUD under Automatic HUDs with their owner, but they are not user-toggled. Their visibility is a consequence of state:

Surface Owner Rover HUD Driven-vessel possession and capability state Lander control cards Authored USD control-HUD metadata on the active scene Terrain and scenario-download progress Transient terrain and network lifecycle state Guided, notification, and blackout HUDs Authored guidance and runtime session state

The rover HUD appears only while a vessel is possessed, because it answers a question the user just asked by taking control. The lander cards are authored on the scene, not generated from a model class. Download and terrain progress are transient: dismissing the preparation window keeps the required-data hold, and the window reopens when a new runtime requirement appears.

Tutorial presentation is a separate guided layer. Its lesson HUD is a specific-HUD readout; its ring, coach card, and completion prompt use the guided overlay order. Menus and window controls remain in front of both.

docs.title: Runtime surfaces
docs.text:
The shipped application manifest registers these Twin-facing surfaces:

Surface Placement Gate vessel-hud Full viewport View perspective vehicle-control-left Bottom-left window ui.vehicle_controls, default on vehicle-control-right Bottom-right window ui.vehicle_controls, default on camera-status Top-right window View perspective; ui.camera_status, default on celestial-view Top-centre window View perspective; view_switcher gate program-browser Top-left window Always registered; content decides visibility lunica-schema Top-centre window Modelica schema presentation terrain-progress Top-centre window Terrain lifecycle scenario-download Top-centre window Download lifecycle asset-consent Full viewport Required-data consent; non-modal

A Twin can replace any of these by stable ID or add its own surfaces. Closing the Twin restores the application surfaces. The full manifest contract is in Runtime UI.

The celestial-view surface also carries the lunar map and the mission-site card. The map is gated by the Twin setting ui.lunar_map; omission means hidden. The map marker is projected from the canonical surface pose, not from a render transform. The mission-site card appears only while the Moon orbital pin is active and the scene has a valid lunar site anchor.

docs.title: Stacking and input
docs.text:
HUD layers are ordered. From front to back: menus and popups, floating windows and dialogs, the general HUD, the specific HUD, docked panels, then authored runtime HUI. A HUD area belongs inside the viewport rectangle. Docked panels are not above a HUD that overlaps them.

Pointer ownership follows the same explicitness:

  • A full-window runtime surface is transparent to scene clicks. Only visible controls that declare an HUI on_press callback enter the scene-pick gate.
  • A window surface can be dragged only by a descendant tagged tag:ui_drag_handle="true". Dragging a button never moves the panel.
  • A modal surface must be interactive and use viewport placement. While visible, its root claims the full-window scene-pick gate. Escape emits its declared dismiss_action; Rhai owns what dismissal means.
  • A non-modal data window such as asset consent consumes clicks only inside its own panel. The rest of the viewport stays interactive while its work continues.

Hiding a surface destroys its retained tree. When the exposure returns, the runtime creates a fresh root from the manifest, so template-owned build state cannot survive a hidden transition.

docs.title: Guided HUD cards
docs.text:
Rhai scripts can publish hint, objective, and action cards through lunco-workbench-guided-ui. This is separate from the runtime surface manifest: the cards are script-owned presentation, not HTML templates.

hud_perspectives(ids) sets a card-specific allowlist. The default is View (sandbox_view); an empty list allows every perspective. Unknown perspective ids reject before state changes. Hiding a card preserves its state; visible cards stack by stable owner identity and measured height.

An implicit card belongs to the executing script's stable identity. Unscripted API or REPL calls use a distinct command-context card. An explicit hud name creates a scene-owned card that several producers can share:

hint("mission", "Align with the landing site.");
objectives_hud("mission", [
    #{ id: "align", text: "Align with the site", done: false },
]);
guided_hud_actions("mission", "rover", "on_guided_action", [
    #{ id: "take_control", label: "Take control" },
]);

Action sets carry a ToolHookBinding lease. Replacing or clearing the actions despawns the previous lease, so a queued click cannot bind to a new same-name card or a different Twin.

docs.title: Layout persistence
docs.text:
A draggable window surface stores only a validated logical top-left override in the active Twin's workspace state. The manifest remains the default geometry and visibility authority. Overrides are pruned when the manifest no longer authors their surface ID, clamped after a resize or DPI change, and cleared when the Twin closes. A primary-button double click on the drag handle restores the authored anchor.

Settings → HUD → Surface view switcher position → Reset position removes only the celestial-view override. It does not reset other draggable surfaces or the shared layout store.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text:
To reduce clutter while presenting:

  1. Open Settings → HUD.
  2. Turn off the performance HUD, input HUD, and any graph or camera view you do not need.
  3. Leave automatic HUDs alone; they disappear with their scene state.
  4. If a Twin hides the camera/status surface, check ui.camera_status in the Twin settings rather than looking for a global toggle.

To diagnose a missing HUD:

Symptom Check Surface absent Namespace, visible, perspective filter, gate, and placement rectangle Surface visible but empty Declared template properties and binding source names Button ignores clicks Callback spelling in the template and manifest, then the Rhai action handler Surface moved and will not return Double-click its drag handle, or reset its position in Settings → HUD Text renders as boxes The stylesheet must import lunco://ui/runtime_fonts.css Surface remains after its state ended Check the exposure's visible value and the surface lifecycle; hidden surfaces are destroyed

For the full authoring contract, see Runtime UI. For the walkthrough, see Compose a HUD.

docs.title: Runtime UI
docs.text:
LunCoSim has a small runtime-authored presentation layer for HUDs, telemetry cards, progress overlays, and other Twin-facing surfaces. It looks like HTML and CSS, but it is not a browser. Templates become retained Bevy UI entities, and styles become Bevy Node and visual components through bevy_hui and bevy_flair.

The design goal is a fast, reloadable interface boundary that native and web-facing presentation can share without moving simulation authority into markup. A surface may read a named engine capability and emit a semantic action. It cannot inspect ECS state or directly mutate the simulation.

The committed dependency baseline is bevy_hui 0.8.0, bevy_flair 0.9.0, and Bevy 0.20.0. Keep Cargo.lock as the version evidence and re-check upstream release notes before changing the contract.

docs.title: The boundary
docs.text:
authoritative engine state
        │  change detection + bounded presentation cadence
        ▼
EngineExposures ────────────────► ReadExposures / telemetry / remote clients
        │
        │ named snapshot, revision-gated
        ▼
HUI template properties + Flair CSS custom properties
        │
        ▼
retained Bevy UI tree ───────────► WorkbenchEguiHost / window

HTML button ─► HUI callback ─► RuntimeUiAction(action, HookValue map)
          ─► Rhai policy ─► typed command/event

Each layer owns one concern:

Layer Owns Does not own Engine/domain producer Authoritative values, sampling, visibility, capability names HTML ids, CSS, layout, widget-specific code EngineExposures Typed named snapshots and change revision Renderer or presentation policy runtime_surfaces.json Surface registration, bindings, gates, actions, modal/input policy, placement Simulation state, subject selection, visibility policy Active Twin LunCoPolicy / Rhai Subject visibility, scalar presentation, recording selection Retained tree, simulation authority, renderer details .html template Retained tree shape, declared properties, callback names ECS queries, domain commands, CSS layout .css stylesheet Appearance, internal layout, transitions, custom-property mapping Engine state and command dispatch Workbench / egui Shell, editors, complex panels, docking tree Runtime surface content

The generic exposure namespace is the contract. Do not add a special domain_to_view path or a Rust producer for one particular template. Ports, telemetry, physics, scripts, and derived capabilities all publish through the same registry.

docs.title: Manifest and lifecycle
docs.text:
A scope admits one typed lunco.runtime-ui-manifest.v1 document. The application manifest supplies shared surfaces; the active Twin's manifest replaces matching surface IDs and adds new ones. Duplicate IDs or namespaces within a composed manifest, duplicate manifests in one scope, and invalid contracts produce a structured runtime fault.

Template, stylesheet, and collection-template paths are relative to that scope's asset root. The owner qualifies them with the exact lunco:// or twin:// authority before publishing the retained tree. Explicit logical URIs are also accepted, so a Twin stylesheet can import shared fonts:

@import "lunco://ui/runtime_fonts.css";

The manifest cache belongs to open source scopes. Scene teardown retires the resolved presentation and republishes it even while paused. Exact TwinClosed identity removes that Twin's source; late snapshots from a retired Twin are rejected. Replacing the active Twin rebuilds the retained surface roots from the current composition and restores application surfaces where no override exists. Rhai still owns exposure contents, visibility, and action meaning. Rust owns source admission, validated composition, and retained-tree lifecycle.

The headless and server compositions do not link the runtime UI or its file watcher.

docs.title: Register a surface
docs.text:
Every surface needs a stable id, template, stylesheet, namespace, and placement:

{
  "id": "mission-status",
  "template": "ui/status.html",
  "stylesheet": "ui/status.css",
  "namespace": "mission-status",
  "bindings": {
    "title": { "source": "title" },
    "state": { "source": "state" }
  },
  "actions": [
    { "callback": "runtime_status_focus_moon", "action": "view.body.moon" }
  ],
  "visible_in_perspective": "sandbox_view",
  "interactive": true,
  "placement": {
    "mode": "window",
    "anchor": "top_right",
    "offset": [-16.0, 16.0],
    "width": 260.0,
    "height": 84.0
  }
}
Field Meaning id Stable manifest identity; unique within the manifest template, stylesheet Asset paths under the normal Bevy asset root namespace Exact key in EngineExposures; use a capability name, not a widget name bindings Optional map from template property to exposure property. A map translates exact rendered values. css: true projects a binding into a CSS custom property collections Optional keyed row collections; see below actions Maps a unique HUI callback to a built-in semantic action or a Twin-authored action identifier visible_in_perspective Optional workbench perspective id or array of 1–32 distinct nonempty ids; omission means unrestricted gate Optional named host gate. Unknown gates are closed setting Optional namespaced boolean in the active Twin's [settings] table; false hides the surface setting_default Value used when setting is absent, including when no Twin is active interactive Enables input ownership for authored controls carrying HUI on_press modal Requires an interactive viewport surface and makes its visible root claim the full-window scene-pick gate dismiss_action Optional authored semantic action emitted by Escape while the surface is visible draggable Allows a window surface root to move with primary-button dragging placement The outer rectangle and its relationship to the workbench

The loader rejects unknown fields, duplicate surface IDs or namespaces, duplicate callbacks, unsafe relative paths, empty contract names, and non-finite or non-positive window geometry before any surface is mounted. A modal surface must be interactive and use viewport placement.

The manifest remains the default geometry and visibility authority. Dragging a window surface stores only a validated logical top-left override in the active Twin's workspace state. Overrides are pruned when a manifest no longer authors their stable surface ID, clamped after a resize or DPI change, and cleared when the Twin closes. A double click on the drag handle restores the authored anchor.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
The stable runtime contract uses a deliberately small HUI vocabulary:

<template>
  <property name="title">Status</property>
  <property name="state">offline</property>

  <node id="status-root">
    <text id="status-title">{title}</text>
    <text id="status-state">{state}</text>
    <button id="status-pause" on_press="runtime_status_pause">
      <text>Pause</text>
    </button>
  </node>
</template>

Rules that matter:

  • Use <template>, <property>, <node>, <text>, <button>, and standard <input type="text|number">.
  • Every template, including a keyed collection row, must have exactly one <node> root.
  • Put buttons and text elements beneath that root. A leaf element at the root can panic when HUI reapplies its type during reload.
  • A button's visible caption must be a nested <text> node. Raw text directly under <button> can render as an empty control.
  • Use stable id values and #id selectors.
  • HUI 0.8 does not turn an HTML class attribute into a ClassList; it parses the attribute as an unknown style property and rejects the template. Use ids.
  • A property declaration needs a nonempty initial text value to register. The producer may later project an empty string; an empty declaration is omitted by the parser and cannot receive a binding.

on_press is the stable callback. on_enter, on_exit, on_spawn, and on_change remain available for a tested surface-specific need, but they are not part of the shared convention.

For dynamic controls, use the project convention:

<button id="status-action"
        on_press="runtime_ui_authored_action"
        tag:action="{action}">
  <text>{label}</text>
</button>

The action tag is a dynamic scalar property supplied by the exposure or Rhai policy. The typed event resolves it from the pressed node. Other tag:* values form a typed HookValue map on the event. The runtime transports the map without concatenating it into the action name; Rhai owns its interpretation.

There is no DOM query, JavaScript execution, direct resource mutation, or widget-specific Rust callback in an authored template.

docs.title: Text and number inputs
docs.text:
Standard authored <input type="text"> and <input type="number"> map to Bevy's editable text widget. Inputs support pointer focus, caret and selection editing, character limits, numeric character filtering, and authored tab order.

Put tag:ui_form and tag:ui_field on the element. Values are strings until the Twin's Rhai policy validates them. This is a deliberately small native form contract: browser placeholder behavior, sliders, selects, automatic validation messages, and form submission are not provided. Simple authored viewport modals use the generic modal and dismiss_action fields; rich source editing and dialogs remain owned by the egui workbench.

docs.title: Keyed collections
docs.text:
Declare a collection with its exposure source, HTML container id, row-template asset, and stable record key:

"collections": [
  {
    "source": "programs",
    "container": "program-list",
    "template": "ui/program_browser_row.html",
    "key": "key"
  }
]

The row template is ordinary authored HUI markup with a single <node> root. Its scalar properties can populate text, ids, and tag:* action or input attributes. The runtime keeps one retained row per stable key, updates changed template properties in place, removes retired keys, and orders children to match the published array.

Engine-owned lists use their normal EngineExposures producer. Twin Rhai policies can publish UI-owned rows with SetRuntimeUiCollectionData, which accepts an ordered array of string maps. The command requires an active Twin, checks the namespace and source against the active authored manifest or the mounted surface, rejects missing or duplicate keys, and bounds row, field, and payload sizes. Validation uses the manifest declaration before HUI mounts the surface, so startup scripts can publish initial rows without racing presentation creation.

Publications are removed when the owner Twin closes or another Twin takes ownership. Application code, Rhai policy, and HTML templates therefore share one generic collection path without giving scripts direct resource access.

A collection may list scalar row fields in css, for example "css": ["details_display"]. Those fields keep their ordinary template values and also publish inherited --ui-details-display custom properties on that row. An optional scrollbar names the retained scrollbar container. Undeclared row text never enters CSS.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Flair is CSS-like and maps properties to Bevy UI components. The practical subset includes:

  • display, flex layout, supported grid layout, absolute positioning, dimensions, margin, padding, and gaps;
  • borders, radii, backgrounds, colours, opacity, z-order, and transforms;
  • text size, weight, colour, alignment, and inherited font properties;
  • #id, type, class, descendant and child selectors, state selectors such as :hover and :active, @import, custom properties, var(...), transitions, and keyframe animations.

Keep the outer rectangle in the manifest and use CSS for the contents of that rectangle. For a value that changes at runtime, expose a property and consume its explicitly selected --ui-<property-name> custom property:

"bindings": {
  "state": { "source": "state", "css": true }
}

#status-state {
  color: var(--ui-state-color);
}

The bridge projects bound values to HUI template properties. A binding with css: true additionally writes a CSS variable named --ui-<property-name> (underscores become hyphens). Text-only bindings and implicit same-name bindings never enter the CSS token stream. Mapping values can themselves be CSS values, for example var(--accent-color).

The runtime retains HUI's compiler style context outside its active style system. Flair remains the only rendered style owner. Do not write Bevy Node, BackgroundColor, TextColor, or HUI style components from Rust under a runtime surface; HUI and Flair will overwrite them.

The manifest owns the outer rectangle. HUI replaces a template root's Node while building, so placement is applied after HUI and Flair finish their authoritative style work. The runtime pins the root's minimum and maximum size to the resolved rectangle and clips child overflow at that boundary. Authored profiles must fit their contents within the registered size. The correction is change-detected for the initial build, an actual resize, or a style rebuild, not a per-frame placement loop. During startup, a zero-sized target is ignored until the primary window has valid dimensions.

Use the bundled theme and font stylesheets described in Theming. A hardcoded dark palette will not follow Light mode.

docs.title: Actions and Rhai
docs.text:
A surface callback receives only the pressed entity. The manifest turns it into a RuntimeUiAction. Built-in actions remain in the host; any other identifier becomes a typed runtime.ui.action event for Rhai policy.

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name != "runtime.ui.action" { return; }
    if evt.value.action == "mission.pause" {
        pause();
    }
}

Authored semantic actions are intentionally open-ended. Their meaning belongs to the active Twin's Rhai program, not to the runtime UI crate. A dismiss_action follows the same path when the user presses Escape over a visible modal or non-modal surface.

The camera-status surface is the reference composition for a typed option list. Rust publishes the full current camera fact and a compact identity projection through the generic camera-status exposure. Rhai adds a typed option array and authored dimensions to that snapshot. The manifest declares only the option field names and the trigger action. The shared egui renderer reads the generic records and forwards the selected authored action as a typed runtime.ui.action event. The runtime UI crate knows no camera names, camera commands, or camera-selection rules.

Action sets from guided HUD cards carry a ToolHookBinding entity lease. The shared tool queue checks that lease, the immutable endpoint, the registered tool scope, the active Twin, and the scene generation before admitting and executing work.

docs.title: Exposures and readiness
docs.text:
An engine producer resolves authoritative state and writes generic values:

let mut ui = exposures.writer("mission-status");
ui.visible(has_mission);
ui.property("title", mission_title);
ui.property("state", state_label);
ui.property("state_color", "var(--ok-color)");

The producer should be scheduled with the engine and protected by Bevy change detection or a producer-owned fingerprint. Continuous inputs are coalesced to the bounded exposure cadence (EXPOSURE_UPDATE_HZ, currently 20 Hz). Discrete lifecycle facts should use an event observer. Equal snapshots retain their published view; advancing a caller's time sample or sequence alone does not rerun a projection. Clocked animation belongs to the presentation owner.

EngineExposures.revision advances only when a complete surface changes, including its preparation state, or is retired. It is not a frame counter.

A surface's state is pending, ready, or failed:

State Meaning pending New or replaced identity; hidden with no properties ready Validated visibility and properties are published failed Invalid policy result; terminal until the source or identity changes

Existing ready samples remain available during continuous refresh. A failed policy publishes an error and no partial view; inspect it instead of repeatedly waiting. Hidden surfaces have no retained tree.

Subject-scoped surfaces are discovered from composed USD. A prim opts in with lunco:ui:surfaceId; lunco:ui:visibilityMode supplies possessed or always for the built-in Rhai policy. Keep these fields on a prim with LunCoUiSchemaAPI. The surface ID is the exposure namespace; Rust does not construct names from model classes, slots, or vehicle counts. Live edits invalidate authored-surface discovery at the USD stage-revision boundary without recreating the prim subtree or resetting simulation state below the same scene scope.

The single runtime.ui.surface hook returns #{ visible: bool, properties: map } for one captured fact snapshot. Both fields are validated before the surface is published. There is one backend fact conversion and one hook call per admitted surface snapshot.

Runtime surface facts expose a subject's retained SimulationObjectPaused as pause: #{condition, detail}, or unit when the subject is running. This is a typed snapshot of the co-simulation owner state, invalidated when the marker changes. Rhai chooses the wording; it must not infer a paused state from a transient model output.

Preparation holds also publish typed facts. The vessel status can show WAITING FOR TERRAIN while required ground is held, including while a download awaits user action. The built-in Rhai visibility policy can temporarily show an authored surface during scene, terrain, script, or Modelica preparation. Once preparation clears, the authored possessed or always mode controls visibility again; neither Rust nor the template adds a second visibility rule.

Inspect a running surface over the API:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"ExecuteCommand","command":"ReadExposures",
       "params":{"surface":"mission-status"}}'

The response contains revision and each surface's state, error, visible, and typed properties. Wait for ready before reading prepared properties, and retain your view while the revision is unchanged.

docs.title: Visibility and placement
docs.text:
A surface is mounted only when all applicable gates agree:

  1. The exposure's visible value is true.
  2. If visible_in_perspective is authored, the active perspective is in the list.
  3. If gate is authored, the named host gate is open. Unknown gates are closed.
  4. If setting is authored, the active Twin's boolean is true. An absent key uses setting_default.

The perspective filter gates interactive rendering and capture readiness, not just paint. Omission means unrestricted.

The three placement modes are:

Mode Use viewport Full-window overlay, useful for HUDs that frame the 3D scene dock_panel Surface aligned to a workbench panel, using its authoritative PanelRects rectangle and an optional logical-point inset window Fixed logical-point rectangle anchored at a window corner or center, with an offset and explicit width and height

Set interactive: true only when the surface contains controls that should own pointer input. A control becomes an input owner by declaring HUI on_press="callback". The runtime uses that explicit marker plus Bevy's computed layout rectangle and registers it with the same scene/chrome press latch as egui dock cards. The surface root is never registered, so a full-window HUD remains transparent to scene clicks and camera drags everywhere except on its authored buttons.

The retained UI picker uses Bevy's marker filter because its camera renders after the scene camera and would otherwise block the scene with every visible node, including decorative or transparent layout nodes. Only visible on_press controls on interactive surfaces and visible HUI nodes in draggable window surfaces are marked Pickable.

A window surface may opt into movement with "draggable": true. Only a descendant tagged tag:ui_drag_handle="true" can move or reset it. viewport and dock_panel roots cannot opt in. The manifest remains the default and visibility authority; the workbench stores only the validated logical top-left override.

A modal surface must be interactive and use viewport placement. While visible, its root claims the full-window scene-pick gate. Escape emits its declared dismiss_action. This is a simple modal primitive, not a rich dialog queue. Focus, queued rich-dialog outcomes, and typed CloseModal dispatch remain with the shared egui modal host.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
Offline recording is Twin-owned. While capture is active, the runtime.ui.recording policy receives typed lists of stable manifest IDs and currently visible IDs, and returns the IDs required in the shot. Candidate visibility uses the same exposure, perspective, gate, and Twin-setting predicate as mounting and rendering. A perspective or gate change refreshes the contract even when exposure values stay unchanged.

The runtime validates that selection and acknowledges actual retained and rendered surfaces through the status bus. Unknown, hidden, duplicate, or malformed selections produce an explicit readiness error. Capture selection is not stored in the reusable manifest.

Initial recording readiness requires a mounted tree that has consumed a real exposure snapshot, camera targeting, and nonzero layout and render extraction. Later global exposure revisions do not invalidate that initial projection, because live producers may publish after the UI update phase. Property updates keep using the revision fast path independently of the presentation lifecycle.

docs.title: Reloading
docs.text:
On a native desktop session, the Bevy asset watcher reloads runtime UI assets:

Edit What reloads Relaunch? assets/ui/*.html HUI rebuilds the affected retained surface tree No assets/ui/*.css or an imported stylesheet Flair reparses and reapplies the affected stylesheet No assets/ui/runtime_surfaces.json The manifest bridge replaces registered surface roots and re-registers actions No assets/ui/runtime_fonts.css The stylesheet is reapplied; verify the font asset is available No, normally Rust exposure producer or action observer Requires a rebuilt binary and a controlled session replacement Yes ReloadShader Reloads active WESL assets only; unrelated to HUD assets No RunScenario Hot-reloads Rhai policy only; not an HTML/CSS reload No

Keep one production luncosim process while editing assets. For a rebuilt binary, send the API Exit, verify the old process and port are gone, then launch the new binary with an explicit --api PORT.

HUI has an upstream limitation when templates are nested: reloading a component template can temporarily break a higher-level template. Reload the top-level surface template again if that occurs. Avoid recursive imports, keep one root per template component, and do not manually write Bevy styling components from Rust under a runtime surface.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
The runtime layer is cheap by design, but CSS does not make a large UI free:

  1. Keep templates small and retained. Prefer a few surfaces with stable ids to thousands of per-value nodes.
  2. Publish only values a surface can read. Use change detection, revisions, and dirty flags before resolving a view model.
  3. Let the exposure cadence coalesce continuous telemetry. Do not publish a string every render frame unless the presentation needs it.
  4. Let identical values remain identical. The revision gate is the retained UI's invalidation boundary; do not add JSON hashing or a per-frame rebuild.
  5. Mount optional surfaces lazily through visibility and gates. A hidden surface has no presentation tree; when exposure returns, the runtime creates a fresh root from the manifest.
  6. Prefer CSS custom properties and text replacement over rebuilding the hierarchy. Use transitions sparingly and measure large animations.
  7. Profile the complete frame. Runtime UI, egui, physics, terrain, and the renderer share one budget.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
This is a minimum native UI language, not full CSS:

  • no browser DOM, JavaScript, networking, or browser layout engine;
  • no full CSS standards guarantee; unsupported properties are reported or have no effect rather than being polyfilled;
  • one stylesheet per styled subtree; use @import for shared rules;
  • no global stylesheet, and !important is detected but ignored;
  • custom-property fallback values are not supported;
  • calc() is limited by Bevy's Val types; calc(100% - 20px) is not a safe assumption, while calculations using compatible variables are useful;
  • limited font support: one explicit @font-face, with no browser-like local or fallback font chain;
  • unsupported web units and features such as em and text-decoration are not available;
  • no automatic form controls, focus model, accessibility tree, or DOM event propagation contract beyond the authored HUI callbacks;
  • no native select or accessibility tree for option lists; the shared egui popup is the low-level dropdown primitive;
  • rich dialog queues and accessibility semantics are not provided by the authored layer.

Use the workbench for editors, docking, rich text, large inspectors, and controls that need semantics outside this contract. Use runtime HTML/CSS for Twin-facing presentation that should change without recompiling Rust.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Symptom Check Surface absent Namespace, visible, perspective filter, gate, setting, and a valid placement rectangle Blank value The target <property> is declared and the binding source name matches exactly Button does nothing Callback spelling in HTML and manifest, then the host observer or Rhai action handler Text renders as boxes Import runtime_fonts.css and confirm the bundled font path Surface jumps on startup or resize Keep placement in the manifest; do not add per-frame compensation Style keeps reverting Remove Rust writes to Node, BackgroundColor, TextColor, or HUI style components beneath the surface Collection row missing Source, container id, row template, stable key, and publication state Need the engine side Query ReadExposures and compare its revision before reading rendering code

For the guided walkthrough, see Compose a HUD. For shipped surfaces and their gates, see HUD. For colours and fonts, see Theming.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
