LunCoSim settings have three scopes. A user preference belongs to the person at the machine; a project preference belongs to one checkout; a Twin preference travels with the Twin. Keeping those scopes separate is what lets a project enforce behavior without overwriting a user's editor preferences.

Scope Stored in Typical content User-global <OS config dir>/lunco/settings.json Theme, window geometry, HUD visibility, key bindings, editor behavior Project <project>/.lunco/settings.json Local overrides for the open project; excluded from Twin distribution Twin twin.toml under [settings] Shared project policy that must travel with the Twin

LUNCOSIM_CONFIG replaces the user configuration directory. With LUNCOSIM_CONFIG=/tmp/lunco-config, the settings file is /tmp/lunco-config/settings.json. On Linux the default is normally ~/.config/lunco/settings.json.

For a key that exists in all three scopes, the effective value is the Twin value, then the project value, then the user-global value. An omitted value inherits from the next scope. An explicit false is a value, not an omission. A command-line flag, where one exists, overrides every persisted scope for that run.

docs.title: Open the Settings menu
docs.text:
Settings is a top-level menu. Its first row is the current theme; selecting it switches between Dark and Light. The submenus follow, contributed by the feature that owns each preference.

Submenu What it controls General Load the default scene on Twin open; contain bodies outside finite physics worlds Project The active project's local override for those scene and physics choices; reports a Twin or CLI override when one wins Keybindings Opens the application-owned Keybindings perspective Appearance Translucent tab content; Modelica diagram controls, authored colours, hover values, and semantic zoom; egui debug overlays in debug builds Graphics Renderer backend, samples per video frame, rendering-quality preset, and shadow-map budget where the adapter exposes one HUD Visibility of user-controlled heads-up surfaces; read-only inventory of automatic HUDs Data & libraries Download concurrency and retry policy; the registry-backed asset and library catalog Entity list Display preference for system-managed rows Debug Windows console behavior for the next launch Debug visualization Temporary joint, wheel-force, mass, force, and frame diagnostics Sim Core Test-content preference contributed by the application's Rhai policy Updates Build identity, update channel, and update actions Avatar Avatar collision policy for the active Twin, when the avatar feature is present Performance The status-bar performance HUD Modelica Code editor, component palette, diagram projection, and source-library preferences Collaboration Presence cursors and teach mode, when the networking UI is built

Some submenus are context-dependent. Avatar appears when the avatar feature is installed; Performance comes from the performance UI package; Modelica comes from the Modelica editor; Collaboration requires the networking UI feature. Sim Core is contributed by the application's Rhai policy through the same replaceable Settings-submenu contract; no Rust crate registers it.

Settings submenus are content-sized in both axes, capped at 640 logical pixels wide and 24 interaction rows high. A longer submenu scrolls; it does not reserve empty popup space.

docs.title: User-global settings
docs.text:
settings.json is one JSON document with namespaced keys. Each feature owns a typed section; it does not get its own file. The shape is deliberately close to VS Code's settings model:

{
  "theme": { "mode": "Dark" },
  "perf_hud": { "enabled": true },
  "input_overlay": { "enabled": false },
  "overlays": { "schema_version": 1, "sky_clock": false, "view_switcher": false },
  "input_bindings": { "bindings": {}, "command_bindings": {} }
}

Each key is flat and names the feature that owns the section. The Settings UI groups rows by submenu rather than by JSON nesting.

Key Owner Purpose theme lunco-workbench Active theme mode workbench_appearance lunco-workbench Translucent tab content; debug overlays window lunco-workbench-window Restored window geometry overlays lunco-luncosim-ui Sky clock and surface-view switcher perf_hud lunco-workbench-perf-ui Status-bar performance HUD input_overlay lunco-input-ui Input visualizer input_bindings lunco-input-core Resolved keyboard and pointer bindings entity_list lunco-luncosim-edit-ui System-managed entity rows diagram_presentation lunco-theme Diagram controls, authored colors, hover values, semantic zoom modelica_code_editor lunco-modelica-ui Word wrap, auto indent, text scale modelica_journal_panel lunco-modelica-ui Journal panel display welcome_progress lunco-modelica-ui Welcome learning-path progress library lunco-modelica-library Modelica source-library settings experiments lunco-experiments Experiment defaults download lunco-settings Download concurrency, retry budget, backoff renderer lunco-render Raster or path-traced backend rendering_quality lunco-render Rendering budget and per-feature limits telemetry lunco-telemetry Telemetry defaults telemetry_display lunco-viz Telemetry browser display preferences scene lunco-workspace Default-scene loading physics lunco-workspace Finite-world escape guard updates lunco-updater Update channel and actions

A missing file, a missing section, or an unreadable section falls back to that section's default. A file that is not valid JSON is preserved as settings.json.bad and the app starts from defaults rather than silently overwriting the user's preferences. Writes are atomic.

Settings are saved when their resource changes. There is no separate "apply" step for user-global preferences.

docs.title: Project settings
docs.text:
Settings → Project edits the active project's local override. The file is <project>/.lunco/settings.json, uses the same section format as the global file, and is excluded from Twin distribution. It is the right place for a preference that depends on this checkout, not on the project's shared behavior.

The Project submenu reports when a shared Twin value or a command-line flag takes precedence. A plain folder has neither project nor Twin settings. Changes to scene-loading and physics-containment choices apply when the Twin is next opened.

For example, a local project can choose not to load the default scene:

{ "scene": { "load_default": false } }

A malformed project file or a non-boolean Twin override rejects the candidate open and preserves the current workspace instead of guessing.

docs.title: Twin settings
docs.text:
The generic [settings] table in twin.toml is the per-Twin extension seam. Keys are dotted, namespaced scalars: booleans, integers, numbers, or strings. Adding a project preference does not require a Rust field, a new settings section, or a new command.

[settings]
"ui.camera_status" = true
"ui.vehicle_controls" = false

A surface that consumes a Twin setting declares its key and its omitted value:

"setting": "ui.camera_status",
"setting_default": true

An omitted key uses the authored default. Rhai reads the same map with get_twin_setting(key) and writes it with set_twin_setting(key, value). Both the runtime surface gate and the script API converge on the workspace's generic SetTwinSetting command.

The Twin settings panel walks the active Twin's map as a change-driven view. It groups keys by their namespace and renders the stored scalar type directly. Edits dispatch SetTwinSetting; Reset dispatches ResetTwinSetting, which removes the key so the consuming surface's declared default applies. The panel is intentionally limited to the generic scalar map. Structured sections such as [usd] and [journal] remain with their domain owners, and user-global preferences remain in settings.json.

The panel excludes scene.load_default and physics.finite_world_escape_guard because those have dedicated rows under General and Project. It clears immediately when its Twin closes.

docs.title: Keybindings
docs.text:
Settings → Keybindings opens the application-owned input_settings perspective. The binding document is the typed input_bindings section in settings.json; there is no separate keybinds.toml.

Authored defaults are discovered as a runtime asset with kind lunco.input-bindings.v1, not compiled into the input contract. The same resolved resource feeds the live input map, help surfaces, input injection, and Rhai lesson labels. A persisted override that omits the look button inherits the authored value when that asset loads.

command_bindings maps an identity to a physical chord, a reflected command, typed scalar arguments, and an explicit text-focus permission. Menu hints and Rhai input_hint(...) read the effective map. SetCommandKeyBinding validates the command name and arguments before persisting; SetInputIntentBinding edits semantic alternatives through the same owner.

Twin composition removes conflicting lower-priority physical bindings from the transient effective map. Global preferences stay stored and return when the Twin closes. Conflicts publish warning telemetry and appear in Recent Events; identical snapshots do not repeat the warning.

docs.title: Appearance and Graphics
docs.text:
Appearance owns workbench presentation rather than simulation behavior:

  • Translucent tab content keeps the live scene visible behind tab bodies. Turning it off uses the same opaque background in every tab.
  • Diagram editing and navigation controls hides Modelica toolbars, zoom buttons, and connection-view controls for presentation while leaving model geometry, wires, diagnostics, and live values visible.
  • Preserve authored diagram colors stops the dark-theme icon remapping.
  • Diagram hover values and Modelica semantic zoom control diagram interaction.
  • Egui debug overlays is a debug-build diagnostic for widget alignment and changing widget IDs.

Graphics owns renderer and GPU budgets. It selects the raster or path-traced backend, the samples per video frame, and the rendering-quality preset. A Twin can override the renderer preference; when it does, the submenu says so. A renderer error is reported in the submenu instead of being hidden.

Rendering quality is a budget, not a shader. It changes shadow resolution, effect availability, and similar renderer-wide costs; it does not replace the USD-authored sky, terrain, or material shaders. See Shaders → Quality.

docs.title: HUD and debug settings
docs.text:
Settings → HUD is the discoverable view over the HUD visibility owners. It does not maintain a second visibility registry. The page HUD lists every shipped surface and its owner.

Settings → Debug visualization toggles temporary physics diagnostics: joints, wheel forces, selected-body mass, selected-body forces, and selected-body frames. These rows are not persisted; the lease store is cleared at scene teardown. They are diagnostic overlays, not authored scene content.

Settings → Debug appears on Windows and controls whether the next launch allocates a debug console. The preference is read before the app process starts, so it cannot be changed by Rhai or by the running UI.

docs.title: Commands and automation
docs.text:
Settings changes are commands, not direct UI-only mutations. The important generic commands are:

Command Effect SetTwinSetting Writes one key in the active Twin's [settings] map ResetTwinSetting Removes one key so its authored default applies SetTheme Sets "dark" or "light"; omit mode to toggle SetCommandKeyBinding Validates and persists a command chord SetInputIntentBinding Edits a semantic input alternative TogglePerfHud Shows or hides the status-bar performance HUD ToggleInputOverlay Shows or hides the input visualizer

SetTheme accepts persist: false to apply a theme for the current session without rewriting the user's preference. That is the seam for a scene-authored appearance override. See Theming.

A script or external client should use the command API rather than editing settings.json while the app is running. The settings owner keeps an in-memory mirror and flushes atomically; an external write can be overwritten by the next flush.

docs.title: Adding a setting
docs.text:
A feature adds a setting by owning a typed section:

#[derive(Resource, Serialize, Deserialize, Default, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct PerfHudSettings {
    enabled: bool,
}

impl SettingsSection for PerfHudSettings {
    const KEY: &'static str = "perf_hud";
}

app.register_settings_section::<PerfHudSettings>();

After registration the section is a normal Bevy resource. Mutating it marks the section changed, and the central flush writes settings.json. A new setting needs one struct and one registration call; there is no central allowlist.

Use a dotted key when several sections share a domain prefix. Keep one owner per key. Do not create a per-feature JSON file for a new preference: the documented exceptions are recents.json (high-churn list state), workspace-state/<hash>.json (per-project, path-keyed workspace state), and the layout store, which is structural rather than a preference.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Check A setting reverts after restart The write did not reach settings.json, or another scope wins Inspect the file, then check project and Twin scopes A Twin setting has no effect Key spelling differs, or the consumer declares a different default Compare twin.toml, the manifest setting, and the producer A shortcut does nothing The chord is displaced by a Twin binding or focus permission denies it Open Keybindings and inspect the effective map Settings file is ignored Invalid JSON Look for settings.json.bad beside the original HUD row is missing Its feature or Twin context is absent Check the feature build and the active Twin

Continue with HUD for the surfaces those settings control, or Runtime UI for the authored presentation layer.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Telemetry is a first-class runtime surface. Read it from the Analyze perspective or from the HTTP API. Do not tail a log or poll a screenshot for a number that the port registry already publishes.

Telemetry answers three different questions, and they should not be confused:

Question Read What is exposed at the wiring boundary? ReadPorts or the Telemetry panel What does the Modelica solver currently hold? SnapshotVariables Is the end-to-end Modelica → physics chain healthy? CosimStatus

docs.title: In the window
docs.text:
1. Switch to Analyze.
  2. Open Telemetry. It lists the live port-bearing entities and their channels.
  3. Select an entity to see its current values. An absent port is not a zero; the entity may still be preparing.
  4. Open Graphs and add a channel to see it over time. This is the right tool for settling, oscillation, and arrival checks.
  5. Use Ports to inspect the resolved direction and kind of each port before wiring a target.

The graph records real simulation samples. It is not a render-frame animation. When the world is paused, the last sample stays visible. Pausing does not rewind, interpolate, or replay rendered frames.

The Analyze perspective brings Telemetry, Ports, and Graphs together. Select a channel in Telemetry to plot its samples in Graphs.

A port's direction is part of its contract. Write inputs; read outputs. A value that appears in the inspector is not necessarily a value that another model may write. If a wiring target rejects a connection, inspect the resolved direction and kind first.

docs.title: From the HTTP API
docs.text:
Start LunCoSim with an explicit port:

luncosim --api 4101

Find an entity:

PORT=4101

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ListEntities"}'

The response contains each entity's api_id. Use that identity for reads:

# Discover the port names first; ReadPorts requires explicit names.
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "ListPorts",
       "params": {"api_id": 42}}'

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "ReadPorts",
       "params": {"api_id": 42,
                  "port_names": ["throttle", "steer", "speed"]}}'

ReadPorts returns the selected rows for one entity. It does not dump every port; name what you need. Use ReadPortsBatch when you need one shared sim_tick across several entities.

The request envelope, discovery endpoint, and error shape are documented in HTTP API.

docs.title: Modelica state
docs.text:
A rendered port is not necessarily the whole solver state. To inspect the Modelica side:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "SnapshotVariables",
       "params": {"api_id": 42}}'

SnapshotVariables answers "what does the model currently hold?" Use ReadPorts for "what is exposed at the wiring boundary?" and CosimStatus for the end-to-end Modelica → physics chain.

docs.title: Readiness matters
docs.text:
Before treating a value as final, check readiness:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/ready"

Require:

  • ready: true
  • world_hold: false
  • pending_count: 0

A port may be momentarily absent while its model is compiling or its scene is still being admitted. That is different from a valid zero. A required-data hold keeps the world held even when the window is responsive; dismissing the preparation window does not release that hold.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Numbers answer "what value?" A screenshot answers "does the scene look right?" Capture the visible production window, not a headless substitute:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "CaptureScreenshot",
       "params": {"save_to_file": true, "path": "target/telemetry-check.png"}}'

The path is relative to the process working directory. Read the resulting PNG before reporting a visual result.

docs.title: Recording evidence
docs.text:
A useful telemetry check has three parts:

  1. Readiness. Record ready, world_hold, and pending_count at the time of the read.
  2. Identity. Record the entity api_id, the exact port names, and the sim_tick or batch tick that produced the values.
  3. Trend. Use a graph or a series of reads for settling, oscillation, or arrival. A single sample is not a trend.

For an operator lifecycle, see Mission control. For turning a live value into a repeatable check, see Validation.

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text:
Trap Better read Polling stdout for a value ReadPorts or the Telemetry panel Treating a missing port as 0.0 Check readiness and ListPorts Using a single sample for a trend Record a graph or a time series Reading a render FPS as simulation cadence Inspect the clock and timing profile Comparing values from different ticks Use one ReadPorts or ReadPortsBatch response Looking only at ports for solver state Also call SnapshotVariables Treating a dismissed preparation window as released hold Check world_hold and the required-data state Using a headless screenshot as visual evidence Capture the visible production window

Continue with HTTP API for the request envelope, or Analyze for the perspective that arranges Telemetry, Ports, and Graphs.

docs.title: Theming
docs.text:
LunCoSim ships two themes: Dark and Light. Dark is the default. The themes are built from the Catppuccin Mocha and Latte palettes, then projected through semantic design tokens so a panel, a plot, a Modelica diagram, and an authored HUD do not each invent their own colours.

There is no High Contrast mode in the current build. A feature that needs a higher-contrast presentation should use the existing semantic tokens rather than adding a second theme enum.

docs.title: The theme model
docs.text:
lunco-theme owns one Theme resource:

Part What it provides ColorPalette The raw Catppuccin palette DesignTokens Semantic colours: accent, success, warning, error, text, subdued text, raised and sunken surfaces, borders, scrim, overlay backdrop TypographyScale Named roles from display and title down to dense data and code SpacingScale Shared spacing increments RoundingScale Shared corner radii SchematicTokens Wire and class-kind colours for block diagrams JournalTokens Edit-history row colours by category PlotTokens Signal-series colours for plots ModelicaIconPalette Anchor and inversion rules for authored Modelica icons overrides Code-registered per-domain token overrides

Consumers read tokens; they do not read raw palette entries for functional UI. That is what lets the same panel render correctly in both modes. A new UI surface should choose a role such as tokens.overlay_backdrop, not a literal #181825.

The typography roles are display, title, section, body, button, label, tree, caption, dense_data, dense_code, and code. The workbench applies them in ThemeApplySet; render systems that paint their own egui must run after that boundary.

docs.title: Selecting a theme
docs.text:
The first row of the Settings menu shows the current mode. Selecting it switches between Dark and Light. The choice is persisted in the theme section of settings.json:

{ "theme": { "mode": "Dark" } }

The same change is available as a command:

{ "type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "SetTheme", "params": { "mode": "light" } }

SetTheme accepts "dark" and "light" case-insensitively. Omitting mode toggles. The command normally persists the new mode. Passing "persist": false applies the theme for the current session only and leaves the user's saved preference untouched.

That non-persisted path is the seam for scene-authored appearance. A film take that records dark must not rewrite the operator's editor preference. While the live theme equals the non-persisted override, the preference sync stands down; the moment another action changes the theme, the override clears and normal persistence resumes.

docs.title: What the theme reaches
docs.text:
Surface How it follows the theme Workbench chrome and panels Palette-derived egui Visuals, semantic tokens, typography roles Docked panel bodies overlay_backdrop by default; optional opaque mantle surface Status bar and HUD tiers Shared theme tokens Plots and graphs PlotTokens signal colours Modelica diagrams SchematicTokens for wires and class kinds; ModelicaIconPalette for authored icons Change History JournalTokens row colours Runtime-authored HUDs Semantic CSS custom properties written by the runtime bridge Authored Modelica icon colours Remapped in dark mode unless Preserve authored diagram colors is on

The Modelica icon palette is not a simple invert. Canonical source-library colours (black outlines, white fills, primary blue and red) are mapped through an anchor table, and other colours have their lightness inverted within a clamped range. Light mode uses the identity palette because the source library was designed for a paper-white canvas. Settings → Appearance → Preserve authored diagram colors disables the remapping when the authored diagram is itself the presentation.

docs.title: Workbench appearance
docs.text:
Settings → Appearance exposes two workbench-level choices:

  • Translucent tab content keeps the live scene visible behind every tab body and its standard panel surface. Turning it off uses the same opaque background in every tab.
  • Egui debug overlays is available in debug builds and draws widget alignment and changing-widget-ID diagnostics. It is off by default and should stay off during ordinary interaction.

The same submenu owns Modelica diagram presentation: editing and navigation controls, authored colours, hover values, and semantic zoom. These are presentation settings, not model edits. Hiding controls does not reload or change the model.

docs.title: Runtime UI colours and fonts
docs.text:
An authored stylesheet should import both shared runtime stylesheets:

@import "runtime_fonts.css";
@import "runtime_theme.css";

runtime_fonts.css declares the bundled LunCo UI font. Bevy's minimal default font is ASCII-only; relying on it turns telemetry and status glyphs into boxes on some platforms. The runtime contract supports one explicit @font-face, with no browser-like local or fallback chain. A surface that needs another glyph set must bundle and author that font asset.

runtime_theme.css declares the semantic custom properties. The runtime bridge rewrites the same properties from the active Theme whenever the theme changes:

Property Semantic source --panel-background Overlay backdrop --panel-border Overlay border --panel-inner Sunken surface --button-background Raised surface --button-border Raised-surface border --text-color Primary text --muted-color Subdued text --accent-color Accent --active-text-color Sunken surface --ok-color Success --caution-color Warning --warm-color Warning --danger-color Error

The values in runtime_theme.css are dark defaults. They cover the stylesheet before its retained root mounts; once the surface is live, the bridge supplies the active theme's values. A light-mode surface therefore does not need a second stylesheet.

Use semantic variables in authored CSS:

#status-root {
  background-color: var(--panel-background);
  border: 1px solid var(--panel-border);
  color: var(--text-color);
}

#status-state {
  color: var(--ok-color);
}

A manifest binding with "css": true adds a per-property custom variable named --ui-<property-name>, with underscores converted to hyphens. That is the supported way to project a changing value into CSS. A text-only binding never enters the CSS token stream.

Do not hardcode a dark palette into a Twin stylesheet if the surface should work in both themes. If a surface is deliberately theme-independent, say so in its own comments and keep the authored colours accessible against the scene.

docs.title: Theme extension
docs.text:
Domain code can register a token override:

theme.register_override("terrain", "contour", color);

The override is keyed by domain and token and bumps the theme revision. This is a code-level extension point for a domain that needs a shared semantic colour; it is not a user-facing theme editor. A per-surface colour that changes at runtime belongs in the surface's exposure and a css: true binding.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check HUD stays dark in Light mode The stylesheet must import runtime_theme.css; literal colours do not follow the theme Text is unreadable over the scene Use --panel-background and --text-color, not a transparent background with a fixed text colour Glyphs render as boxes Import runtime_fonts.css and confirm the bundled font asset is available Diagram colours look inverted Turn on Preserve authored diagram colors or use theme-aware authored colours Theme reverts on restart The change was applied with persist: false, or another scope owns the preference Theme changes but a custom panel does not The panel is painting before ThemeApplySet or caching derived colours without the theme revision

For the runtime surface contract, continue with Runtime UI. For the settings that expose these choices, see Settings.

docs.title: USD
docs.text:
OpenUSD is LunCoSim's scene and composition format. It describes what the world is made of: hierarchy, transforms, geometry, materials, physics schemas, and the typed connections between parts. Integration, continuous equations, and mission policy live in the runtime, Modelica, and Rhai.

The distinction matters because USD is often asked to do too much. A USD stage can carry a reference to a Modelica model, but it does not contain the model's equations. It can carry a rigid body and a joint, but it does not integrate them. It can carry a connection between two ports, but it does not decide what value should flow. Those jobs belong to the runtime, to Modelica, and to Rhai respectively.

docs.title: What USD owns
docs.text: Fact Authored as Consumed by Prim hierarchy and identity def prims under a defaultPrim Projection, selection, authoring tools Placement xformOp:translate, xformOp:orient, xformOp:scale Rendering, physics, mounts Geometry Mesh, Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane, NurbsPatch Rendering and collision cooking Appearance UsdShade material networks and WESL sources Render binder Physics UsdPhysics bodies, colliders, masses, joints, drives Avian projection Typed ports inputs:<name>, outputs:<name>, connectors:<name> Co-simulation and telemetry Connections .connect on a consuming property Co-simulation wiring Programs LunCoProgramAPI prims Modelica, Rhai, Python runtimes Composition Sublayers, references, payloads, variants, inherits Stage resolver Scene policy LunCoPolicy, LunCoEnvironment, LunCoUiSchemaAPI Authored runtime policy

docs.title: Units and orientation
docs.text:
A LunCoSim scene uses metres and a Y-up, right-handed world. A normal root stage declares that explicitly:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "MyTwin"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
)

def Xform "MyTwin" (kind = "assembly")
{
}

The defaultPrim matters: it gives the stage a stable root for references and for the runtime projection. A stage without one is still readable, but a reference to it cannot omit the target prim path.

The engine converts a supported non-canonical stage once, at the importer. A Z-up or centimetre stage is valid interchange content; it is not a valid runtime frame. metersPerUnit, upAxis, and kilogramsPerUnit are read at the stage boundary, and unsupported values reject projection instead of being silently approximated. Authoring a non-SI document is allowed; admitting it as a live world is not.

docs.title: The three document layers
docs.text:
A running scene is not one editable file. The document system keeps three authored layers over one composed stage:

Layer Lifetime Saved to Purpose base Durable The source .usda file The authored scene runtime Durable .lunco/runtime/<scene> when enabled Edits that must survive but stay out of the source file view Disposable Never Derived presentation such as route ribbons

The composed CanonicalStage resolves references, sublayers, variants, and the three layers in strength order. It is the projection engine: an authored operation replayed onto it fires the change sink, and the runtime reconciles the ECS world from that notice. The stage is thread-affine and lives on the main thread; the serializable layers are what save, journal, and network sync touch.

This is why editing a large scene does not re-flatten it on every change. The typed operation is applied to the document, journaled with its inverse, and replayed onto the live stage. A full reload is a separate contract and does not invent an authored edit.

docs.title: Compose, do not duplicate
docs.text:
USD composition is how large scenes stay maintainable. A scene can reference a reusable rover, place two instances with different transforms, and select a variant without copying its geometry:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "PracticeYard"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
)

def Xform "PracticeYard"
{
    def Xform "RoverA" (
        prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 0, 0)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }

    def Xform "RoverB" (
        prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (8, 0, 4)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }
}

lunco:// addresses the installed asset library. twin:// addresses a file in the open Twin. Use the narrowest authority that owns the file; do not escape an asset root with ...

docs.title: Physics is authored as SPD schemas
docs.text:
LunCoSim uses standard USD physics schemas rather than custom body objects. A movable part generally has:

  • a rigid body (UsdPhysics.RigidBodyAPI)
  • one or more colliders (UsdPhysics.CollisionAPI and a shape)
  • mass properties (UsdPhysics.MassAPI)
  • a joint when it is attached to another body

A movable mounted part needs both a rigid body and a joint. Being a child in the hierarchy is not an attachment. The scene linter reports a nested body without a joint.

docs.title: Programs are prims
docs.text:
A Modelica model or Rhai scenario is attached through the LunCoProgramAPI schema. The schema applies to the physical prim itself when the behavior is intrinsic, or to a child Scope when the behavior is separable. The example uses a child Scope, so deleting it removes the behavior without deleting the rover:

def Xform "Rover" (kind = "assembly")
{
    def Scope "Controller" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
    )
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover/models/Drive.mo@
        uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true
    }
}

A shipped model uses @lunco://models/...@; a Twin-owned model uses @twin://...@. The source path is an asset address, not a relative path from the current working directory.

docs.title: Connections are USD facts
docs.text:
A connection is authored on the prim that consumes the value:

def Xform "DescentLander" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["PhysicsRigidBodyAPI", "LunCoProgramAPI"]
)
{
    uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @lunco://models/Lander.mo@
    uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true

    float inputs:external_throttle = 0.0
    float outputs:throttle

    def Scope "MainPropulsion"
    {
        float inputs:valve_opening.connect = </DescentLander.outputs:throttle>
    }
}

The composed stage resolves references, payloads, variants, and the connection graph. The runtime then derives a SimConnection from the authored wire. A model output becomes externally connectable only when the component prim declares the matching outputs:<name> property; a connection target alone does not create a public port.

docs.title: Reading this chapter
docs.text:
Section Question it answers Composition How do layers, references, payloads, and variants form one stage? Physics How do bodies, colliders, joints, and gravity become a live simulation? Ports and connections How does a value travel from one component to another? Programs How is a Modelica model or Rhai scenario attached to a prim? Materials How does a prim get a shader, and how are parameters authored? Addresses and assets What do lunco:// and twin:// mean, and where do bytes come from? Authoring How do the Editor and Build perspectives change a stage safely?

The composed stage is inert. It becomes a live world only when the runtime projects it and the admitted programs start.

docs.title: Addresses and assets
docs.text:
Every reference in an authored file is an address. LunCoSim recognizes exactly two scene schemes, and one rule decides which to use: the root that owns the file.

Scheme Root Use lunco://<path> The installed engine asset library Shipped assets, engine libraries, bundled models and shaders twin://<authority>/<path> A registered Twin or folder root Anything the user opened or authored in the project

A bare relative path is an input to an open command only. It does not survive past the command boundary as a scene address. An absolute filesystem path is what a file picker produces; it is converted to a rooted address before the scene lifecycle starts.

This is not ceremony. A bare relative path means "resolve against the default source", but once a Twin is open the same string resolves against the Twin instead. A miss then becomes a silent no-load: an empty scene with no error. Two spellings of the same intent with different, context-dependent meanings is a correctness hazard.

docs.title: The Twin authority
docs.text:
A Twin is mounted under a percent-encoded authority derived from its display name. The authority is not necessarily the manifest name spelled literally: spaces, Unicode, percent signs, and URI delimiters are encoded injectively. Reopening the same folder assigns a fresh authority while keeping the authored logical source identity.

Scripts should read the current authority with twin_name() rather than reconstructing it from the manifest:

let authority = twin_name();
let path = `twin://${authority}/models/Drive.mo`;

A retired origin fails before binding. A transport request without an origin retains its exact authority and cannot revive a closed source.

docs.title: Relative references inside a layer
docs.text:
USD references are relative by design:

def Xform "Rover" (
    prepend references = @./assets/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
)
{
}

A relative reference resolves against the layer that authored it, not against the process working directory. That is why a scene cannot be loaded in isolation: it always resolves through a root.

The same rule applies to sublayers, payloads, and asset-typed shader inputs. A layer that hardcodes ~/.cache/lunco/... is not portable and bypasses the asset registry.

docs.title: Do not escape the root
docs.text:
.. traversal that leaves an asset root is rejected. A reference that needs a sibling root should use the correct scheme, not a longer relative path.

This is a safety boundary, not a style preference. The loader validates every authored composition arc before OpenUSD's identifier callback, and a rejected identity is recorded as a diagnostic before the stage is published.

docs.title: Where the bytes come from
docs.text:
A twin:// address names a logical file. The bytes may be:

  • a file the author saved in the Twin;
  • a file produced by a processing step;
  • a file downloaded into the Twin-local cache;
  • a shared artifact in the global cache.

Assets.toml declares the external ones. It is a manifest, not a cache and not a scene file:

[modelica_standard_library]
name = "Modelica Standard Library"
version = "4.1.0"
url = "https://github.com/modelica/ModelicaStandardLibrary/archive/refs/tags/v4.1.0.tar.gz"
dest = "library"
sha256 = "<sha256 of the archive>"

dest is a portable relative path. Absolute paths, parent traversal, and platform-specific syntax are rejected.

The runtime does not download in the background on launch. A missing declared dataset is shown to the user, and the download starts only after an explicit request. The same declarations are visible in Settings → Data & libraries.

A required dataset holds simulation until it is available. A recommended or optional dataset remains available in the catalog and does not block an unrelated scene. Dismissing the preparation window keeps the hold; a new scene or runtime dependency reopens the window.

docs.title: The cache is not an address
docs.text:
Platform Default cache Linux ~/.cache/lunco/ macOS ~/Library/Caches/lunco/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\lunco\

Set LUNCOSIM_CACHE to override the cache root. Twin-scoped declarations write beside the Twin by default unless the entry is marked shared = true.

Authored files never address these physical paths. They address the logical URI; the asset registry resolves it to installed bytes. A physical path in a scene breaks portability and bypasses hash validation, processing, and cache lifecycle.

docs.title: Asset-typed inputs
docs.text:
Shader inputs, program sources, and texture roles are asset-typed:

# On a prim applying LunCoProgramAPI:
uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://rover/models/Drive.mo@

# On a shader prim:
asset inputs:albedo_map = @twin://terrain/site/albedo.png@

The asset owner resolves the path, checks the source scope, and publishes the loaded asset. A missing source is an explicit error at that owner, not a fallback to a similarly named file.

For a script that needs to resolve a document-relative path without reading the filesystem, use the shared URI helper:

let uri = asset_source_relative_uri(document, "textures/hull.png");

It preserves the document's registered source authority and performs URI algebra only. It does not read the file or create an asset handle.

docs.title: glTF payloads
docs.text:
A .gltf or .glb file is an external mesh or scene asset, not a USD layer. USD composition does not parse it. A prim points at the file with a standard payload or reference arc, and the render adapter reads that arc from the composed prim and imports the asset through the glTF loader:

def Xform "Lander" (
    prepend payload = @twin://rover/models/lander.glb@
)
{
    string lunco:assetMode = "scene"
}

The default lunco:assetMode is "scene": the whole glTF scene is attached as a child and keeps its hierarchy, materials, and lights. Set lunco:assetMode = "mesh" to attach one mesh primitive as Mesh3d, which is the form a mesh collider can consume. lunco:assetLabel selects the sub-asset label, for example "Mesh0/Primitive0"; an empty label uses the loader's default.

The arc may live in a referenced USD wrapper. The adapter reads it from the composed prim stack and anchors the URI to the layer that authored it, so scene → wrapper.usda → model.glb renders on the composed prim. A def Cube placeholder with lunco:placeholder = true gives external tools a stand-in that hides once the glTF visual loads.

External USD tools need a glTF SdfFileFormat plugin to compose the same arc. LunCoSim reads the authored arc itself and does not synthesize a USD layer.

docs.title: Composition and missing arcs
docs.text:
A missing sublayer, reference, or payload does not discard the siblings that did resolve. The loader publishes the available stage and records a scene-scoped warning naming both the referring layer and the dependency.

The usd.scene_composition policy decides whether to keep the partial stage or reject it. The shipped policy allows partial composition. A Twin can require a complete closure with reject_scene.

Other failures remain terminal at their owner: unsafe traversal, permission errors, malformed required input, and exceeded closure limits are not treated as missing files. The loader never rewrites a stale URI to a different asset. Fixing an old reference is an authored migration, not a Windows-path fallback.

docs.title: Browser and native
docs.text:
Native readers use the filesystem and registered asset sources. Browser readers use HTTP or mounted OPFS through the same logical paths. Filename components are encoded once; / separators stay separators, and a literal %20 is not the same file as a space.

A browser build has no native file URI support. A file: URI is rejected explicitly rather than being interpreted as a relative path.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Use lunco:// for shipped assets and twin:// for project files.
  • Read the Twin authority with twin_name(); do not build it from a name.
  • Keep relative references inside their root.
  • Point at glTF with a payload or reference; USD composition does not parse the binary.
  • Declare external bytes in Assets.toml; do not commit a cache path.
  • Treat a missing arc as a visible fact, not as an empty scene.
  • Fix a stale address by editing the authored file, not by adding a resolver fallback.

Continue with Authoring, which covers the tools that write these files.

docs.title: Authoring
docs.text: LunCoSim has two USD authoring surfaces and one document model behind both. Build composes the live world from assemblies and entities. Editor opens one explicit USD document and edits its internals. Neither surface writes text behind the document's back.

docs.title: Build and Editor
docs.text:
Perspective Scope Use it for Build The composed live scene Placing assemblies, moving objects, environment settings, spawn catalog Editor One explicit USD document Reusable assembly internals, prim hierarchy, materials, authored properties

Build edits the live scene, so the simulation keeps running while you work. It is the right place to compose a world from existing assets and to adjust placement. Editor opens a file as an editing preview; it does not replace the running scene.

The split matters because a composed scene and a reusable asset are different authoring problems. A change to the practice yard's rover placement belongs to the yard. A change to the rover's wheel mount belongs to the rover asset, where every instance sees it.

docs.title: The document model
docs.text:
Every edit is a typed operation on a UsdDocument:

UsdOp ─apply→ UsdDocument (base ⊕ runtime, generation++)
        │
        ├─ journal records op + inverse (undo / sync)
        └─ replay op → CanonicalStage.author_*
                │ fires the change sink
                └─ reconcile the affected ECS entities

The operation is the single description of the delta. Views do not re-derive it by reading state back. This is the author-once coherence invariant: the text editor, the scene tree, the property inspector, and the 3D viewport all observe the same document generation.

The current operation set includes:

Operation Effect ReplaceSource Replace a whole layer's text AddPrim Add a prim, optionally with a reference RemovePrim / RestorePrim Remove or restore a subtree MovePrim Rename or reparent SetTranslate / SetRotate Set a transform SetAttribute / RemoveAttribute Author or remove a property MoveProperty / CopyProperty Rename or copy a property spec SetRelationship Set a relationship target list SetConnection Author a dataflow edge SetTimeSample / RemoveTimeSample Author animation

Programmatic and UI edits go through ApplyUsdOp or ApplyUsdOps. Both return a generation acknowledgement. Direct source mutation is out.

Multi-op intents use one change set. AttachProgram is the typed source-backed program authoring intent; it lowers its complete source, port, and wire contract to the same USD operation path.

docs.title: Layers and save semantics
docs.text:
The document has three layers:

  • base — saved to the source file;
  • runtime — durable edits kept out of the source file;
  • view — disposable derived presentation.

Saving the document publishes the exported base bytes to the document's existing asset identity before acknowledging success. Later reference composition therefore sees the same bytes that are on disk.

The runtime layer is persisted only when the Twin opts in with usd.runtime_persistence = true. The view layer is never saved, journaled, or included in the sidecar. Route ribbons and visited-marker colors disappear when the document closes.

Undo and redo are journal operations. Removing a prim captures only its authored SDF subtree and the owning parent's sibling order, so undo does not serialize the entire layer. Sibling order merges against the current parent list, retaining unrelated later children.

docs.title: The Editor workflow
docs.text:
1. Choose a USD file in Twin, or use File → Open. The file opens as an editing preview.
  2. Select a prim in Prims or click it in the preview. Inspector shows its properties.
  3. Edit in the Inspector, or switch between Visual and Text.
  4. Use the viewport transform gizmo for placement. Left-drag pans, right-drag orbits, the wheel zooms.
  5. Review the journal in Change History. Save and Undo apply to the active document, not to the live scene.

To find a prim's file in the Twin browser, right-click the prim and choose Reveal in Twin.

The text panel borrows a generation-matched authored or composed snapshot. It does not create a preview-state transition, and painting it must not wake render-layer reconciliation. Text-layer and mode changes use typed intents.

docs.title: Assembly authoring
docs.text:
The reusable assembly_edit tool owns explicit-document USD editing. Its operations include:

  • add_prim, transform, attribute, schema, variant, relationship, connection, and batch;
  • attach_component and detach_component;
  • attach_program;
  • rigid_body_plan, revolute_joint_plan, program_input_*, and program_output constructors.

The higher-level assembly_builder tool provides semantic frame and shape construction, placement, geometry, retrofit-body, reference-target, and alignment plans. Both are policy wrappers over the journaled command surface. USD remains the scene and topology authority; Modelica remains the equation and graph authority.

The normal sequence is:

let context = model_authoring::model_context(doc, root, "@root@");
let ready = model_authoring::readiness_report(doc, root, "@root@", policy);
let recipe = model_authoring::scene_recipe(doc, "@root@", scene, context.generation);
let graph = model_authoring::port_graph(doc, root, "@root@");
let wires = model_authoring::wiring_plan(
    doc, "@root@", root, connections, context.generation);

model_context is one composed, path-addressed read: children, references, variants, component and frame facts, bodies, joints, colliders, ports, generation, and available actions. readiness_report returns stable checks for topology, physicality, mounts, connections, controls, and runtime evidence. An omitted check is not_requested; it is not an implicit pass.

After review, apply the operations through assembly_edit::batch or the normal proposal/review/commit flow, then re-read the new generation. Do not write USDA text directly.

docs.title: References and variants
docs.text:
Use references for reusable assets. A reference composes the asset's prim tree under the instance; an override changes only the opinions that differ.

def Xform "RoverA" (
    prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
)
{
    double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 0, 0)
    uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
}

Use variants for authored alternatives, not for runtime state. A variant selection is an authored opinion and enters the journal.

docs.title: Programs and ports
docs.text:
AttachProgram authors a LunCoProgramAPI child, declared scalar ports, defaults, and connections as one change set. The program is a child prim, so deleting the owner deletes the behavior.

A model output becomes externally connectable only when the component prim declares the matching outputs:<name> property. Declare every value another component consumes, then verify that the generated network exposes it and the composed source connection resolves to it.

See Programs and Ports and connections.

docs.title: Validation while authoring
docs.text:
The lightest useful checks are:

Question Tool Does the document parse and compose? ValidateAsset, luncosim --validate Is the loaded scene structurally sound? RunLint { scope: "scene" } Does the Twin resolve its names and assets? ValidateTwin Does the behavior meet its verdict? luncosim test --scene

A clean parse does not prove a clean run. Keep the evidence with the project. See Validation.

docs.title: External tools
docs.text:
USD is an interchange format. Blender, Omniverse, USDView, and other tools can open the same files. LunCoSim-specific facts live in standard schemas where possible and in lunco: properties where the engine needs them.

A round trip through an external tool must preserve the standard schemas and relationships. If a tool drops a lunco: property, the scene may still render but lose a behavior. Keep a validation step after any external edit.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Use Build for placement, Editor for asset internals.
  • Author one typed operation at a time; let the journal record it.
  • Save through the document, not by rewriting text.
  • Keep durable edits in the runtime layer only when they should not touch the source file.
  • Treat the view layer as disposable.
  • Re-read the document generation after a batch of edits.
  • Validate before sharing a Twin.

The reference chapter documents the exact command-line and file-format contracts: Reference.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
A USD stage is the resolved result of one root layer plus every layer it pulls in. Composition is the mechanism that lets a small, readable scene describe a large, reusable world: a rover is authored once, referenced many times, and varied per placement without copying its prim tree.

LunCoSim does not add a second composition system. It uses OpenUSD's resolver and then projects the composed stage into the runtime. The rules in this section are therefore USD rules first and LunCoSim rules second.

docs.title: The root layer and the stage
docs.text:
The organizing unit in USD is a single root layer (.usd, .usda, or .usdc). Opening one file and resolving its composition arcs produces the stage. Core USD has no project-level entry point: it cannot decide which file in a folder is "the scene."

LunCoSim fills that gap with twin.toml:

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

default_scene is a Twin-relative path. It is the only way a Twin selects its starting scene. The manifest points at a USD root; the root owns composition. Do not grow the manifest into a scene description.

Open entry point What becomes the active stage Open Twin with default_scene That exact stage Open Twin without default_scene None; the viewport explains that no scene was selected Open Folder without a manifest None; clicking a USD file opens an isolated preview Open Scene (loose USD file) That file, after its owning folder is opened as a folder Twin

Other .usda files in a Twin remain a referenceable library. They are indexed and shown in the browser but are not mounted automatically.

docs.title: Composition arcs
docs.text:
Arc Authored as Effect Sublayer subLayers = [@lighting.usda@] Adds another layer at a defined strength in the same prim hierarchy Reference prepend references = @rover.usda@ Composes another layer's prim tree under this prim Payload prepend payload = @terrain.usda@ A loadable reference; may be unloaded until needed Variant variants = { string look = "dusty" } Selects one of several authored opinions Inherit inherits = </_BaseRover> Applies a class prim's opinions to this prim Specialize specializes = </_BaseRover> Applies fallback opinions weaker than the local stack

The composed stage resolves all of these before the runtime sees a prim. A query such as QueryUsdPrim reads the composed result, not the root layer's text. That is why a property authored in a referenced asset is visible on the instance, and why an override on the instance wins.

docs.title: Reference or payload?
docs.text:
Use a reference when the asset is part of the scene's identity and should load with it. Use a payload when the asset is large or optional and the scene can be meaningful before it arrives. Terrain and high-resolution props are typical payload candidates.

LunCoSim's loader treats a missing reference or payload as a missing composition arc. It publishes the available stage, leaves the arc unresolved as OpenUSD requires, and records a scene-scoped warning naming both the referring layer and the dependency.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
Variants are the correct way to offer alternate geometry, materials, or configuration without duplicating the prim tree:

def Xform "Rover" (
    prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    variants = {
        string wheel_set = "physical"
    }
    prepend variantSets = "wheel_set"
)
{
    variantSet "wheel_set" = {
        "raycast" {
            over "Chassis" { uniform token lunco:wheelType = "raycast" }
        }
        "physical" {
            over "Chassis" { uniform token lunco:wheelType = "physical" }
        }
    }
}

A variant selection is an authored opinion like any other. Changing it is a USD edit and enters the journal; it is not a hidden runtime toggle.

docs.title: The live document layers
docs.text:
The authored stage a user edits is a UsdDocument with three layers. They compose in this order:

view   (weakest authored layer, disposable)
runtime (durable document edits, kept out of the source file)
base   (the source file)

The diagram below places USD in the larger layer model:

USD owns the composed scene; the manifest, Modelica, Rhai, and the runtime own the surrounding layers.

The base layer is saved to the source file. The runtime layer holds durable edits that should survive a reload without rewriting the authored source; a Twin can persist it under .lunco/runtime/<scene-path> by setting usd.runtime_persistence = true. The view layer holds derived presentation such as route ribbons and visited-marker colors. It is never saved, journaled, or included in the runtime sidecar.

Composition happens once, on the CanonicalStage. Edits do not re-flatten the scene; the typed operation is replayed onto the live stage, which fires the change sink and reconciles the affected ECS entities. A full reload rebuilds the stage from the composed source.

docs.title: Scene resolution in practice
docs.text:
The runtime never guesses a scene from a folder of files. The resolution rule is:

  1. The Twin manifest is parsed and twin:// is mounted.
  2. The authored twin.lifecycle policy selects the declared default_scene or clears the viewport.
  3. The typed OpenTwinScene command validates the indexed path and loads it through the document-first twin:// path.
  4. The scene loads as a single root under the Grid. Loading another scene re-points that root; it never stacks scenes.

A plain folder has no manifest-backed scene selection. Clicking a USD file opens its document through OpenFile and focuses an isolated preview lease without replacing the running scene. A loose file opened from outside a Twin resolves its owning folder, scans it, and enters the same folder-Twin path.

docs.title: Partial composition
docs.text:
A scene with a missing sublayer, reference, or payload does not discard the siblings that did resolve. After structural projection settles, the loader reports the ordered missing {referring_layer, dependency} pairs to the usd.scene_composition policy.

The shipped policy chooses allow_partial, which preserves the available stage. A Twin can replace that decision with reject_scene. Rejection tears down a partial initial stage and fails the transition; for a dynamic reference it faults and holds simulation while leaving the reference unprojected.

A complete closure does not call the policy. Failures that are not missing files — unsafe traversal, permission errors, malformed required input, or exceeded closure limits — remain visible and terminal at their owner. The loader never rewrites a stale authored URI to a different asset.

docs.title: Composition limits
docs.text:
The canonical asset resolver bounds the closure by layer count, dependency width, depth, retained bytes, and concurrent reads. Independent branches are read in bounded parallel batches, and results are applied in authored dependency order. This keeps I/O completion order from changing the recipe.

On native, composition and prepared-plan extraction run on the async-compute pool. The browser path composes on the main thread until a Web Worker transport is available.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A Twin can keep a reusable rover and a practice yard in separate files:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "PracticeYard"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
    subLayers = [@lighting.usda@]
)

def Xform "PracticeYard"
{
    def Xform "RoverA" (
        prepend references = @assets/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 0, 0)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }

    def Xform "RoverB" (
        prepend references = @assets/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (8, 0, 4)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }
}

Both rovers share one source asset. Moving RoverB authors an override on the instance, not a second copy of the rover. Editing skid_rover.usda affects both on the next composition, which is exactly the intended relationship between a type and its instances.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Give every referenced asset a defaultPrim; give every stage an explicit upAxis and metersPerUnit.
  • Reference reusable assets; override only the opinions that differ.
  • Use variants for authored alternatives, not for runtime state.
  • Keep default_scene a path. Let the USD root own composition.
  • Do not use .. to escape an asset root. Use twin:// or lunco://.
  • Treat a missing arc as a visible composition fact, not as an empty scene.
  • Save authored changes through the document journal; do not rewrite USDA text from a script.

The next section turns the composed hierarchy into a physical world: Physics.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
A material is the authored answer to "what does this surface look like?" In LunCoSim it is also the answer to "how does this surface behave physically?" Both answers use standard USD material binding, with different purposes.

The renderer does not choose a shader by prim name or folder. A UsdShade network selects a WESL source, the source declares its parameters, and the runtime projects that into a ShaderLook. If the network is invalid, the material is rejected visibly; Rust does not substitute StandardMaterial or a guessed shader.

docs.title: The material network
docs.text:
A minimal authored material:

def Material "HullPaint"
{
    token outputs:surface.connect = </Looks/HullPaint/Surface.outputs:surface>

    def Shader "Surface"
    {
        uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
        uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @lunco://shaders/mli_foil.wesl@

        color3f inputs:base_color = (0.72, 0.74, 0.78)
        float inputs:roughness = 0.35
        float inputs:metallic = 0.1
        token outputs:surface
    }
}

Bind it to a prim:

def Mesh "Hull" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["MaterialBindingAPI"]
)
{
    rel material:binding = </Looks/HullPaint>
}

The pieces:

Element Meaning Material The bindable material prim outputs:surface The material's surface terminal Shader A source-backed shader node info:implementationSource Selects a source asset rather than an inline implementation info:wesl:sourceAsset The WESL fragment stage info:wesl:vertexAsset Optional WESL vertex stage inputs:<name> Authored parameter or texture input material:binding The all-purpose visual binding material:binding:physics The physics-purpose binding

docs.title: Source-backed shaders
docs.text:
info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset" is the standard UsdShade selector. info:wesl:sourceAsset follows the standard source-type convention; vertexAsset is a LunCo renderer extension because UsdShade has no second stage selector.

A portable material can keep both entry points in one source asset and use that same asset for both stages. The terrain pair uses separate files:

uniform token info:implementationSource = "sourceAsset"
uniform asset info:wesl:sourceAsset = @lunco://shaders/terrain_layered.wesl@
uniform asset info:wesl:vertexAsset = @lunco://shaders/terrain_geomorph.wesl@

A source used as sourceAsset must declare a callable @fragment entry point. An optional vertexAsset must declare a callable @vertex entry point. One module may declare both and is valid for either role.

The render binder validates the requested stage after the asset loads. An invalid contract rejects the owning material and publishes a structured RuntimeDiagnostics error. An authored Rhai policy may observe that diagnostic and explicitly author a replacement or stop the scenario; recovery is visible and overrideable, not hidden in the renderer.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A shader declares its own parameter block. Rust reflects it into a schema at load time, so adding a parameter means editing a .wesl file, never editing Rust:

//!@ui      dust_density 0 1      "Dust density"
//!@default dust_density 0.35
//!@ui      clump_scale  0 64     "Clump scale (/m)"
//!@default clump_scale  8
//!@ui      tint         color    "Tint"
//!@default tint         0.6,0.6,0.62,1.0

struct Material {
    dust_density: f32,
    clump_scale: f32,
    tint: vec4<f32>,
};
@group(2) @binding(0) var<uniform> material: Material;

A USD-backed parameter edit belongs to the bound Shader prim's inputs:<name> attribute. The editor and SetObjectProperty share the bound-Shader resolver: it follows the composed material:binding network, uses the composed typeName without collapsing USD roles or array shape, validates the USDA literal, and authors a typed UsdOp.

A name that is not in the schema is dropped at pack time with a warning. It is never silently mis-packed into a neighbouring field.

See Shader parameters for the annotation language and the uniform block contract.

docs.title: Texture inputs
docs.text:
Texture inputs are asset-typed inputs: properties:

asset inputs:albedo_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/albedo.png@
asset inputs:normal_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/normals.png@
asset inputs:surface_map = @twin://terrain/apollo15/surface.png@

The projection maps the authored role to the named TextureLayer the shader declares. A shader that does not declare a binding is unaffected by that layer being set. The same slot set serves every shader.

Rasters used as material data must be produced by the correct asset pipeline. A grayscale orthophoto is not intrinsic albedo; the albedo processor removes the low-frequency illumination field before encoding the material colour. A generic map output is analysis/display data and must not be bound directly as inputs:albedo_map.

See Texture layers for the role list and the channel-packing rules.

docs.title: Physics materials
docs.text:
Friction and restitution are not bare properties on a body. They are UsdPhysicsMaterialAPI opinions on a Material prim, bound through the physics-purpose relationship:

def Scope "PhysicsMaterials"
{
    def Material "Regolith" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["PhysicsMaterialAPI"]
    )
    {
        float physics:dynamicFriction = 1.0
        float physics:staticFriction = 1.0
    }
}

def Cube "Ground" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["PhysicsCollisionAPI"]
)
{
    rel material:binding:physics = </World/PhysicsMaterials/Regolith>
}

Friction comes off the bound material, never off a bare physics:friction on the body prim. That name is not defined by UsdPhysics, so no other physics-aware consumer reads it.

Binding resolution — namespace inheritance and the purpose-to-all-purpose fallback — is shared with the renderer. One material can drive both look and friction when it carries both sets of opinions.

docs.title: Binding strength and purpose
docs.text:
material:binding is the all-purpose visual binding. material:binding:physics is the physics-purpose binding. A purpose-specific binding wins over the all-purpose binding for that purpose; the fallback lets a single material serve both.

Bindings compose through references like any other relationship. An instance can override the material without editing the referenced asset:

def Xform "RoverB" (
    prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
)
{
    over "Chassis" {
        rel material:binding = </Looks/DustyPaint>
    }
}

The binding cache is shared across prim and purpose resolution in an immutable snapshot. A resolved binding that targets a missing or non-material prim rejects admission visibly.

docs.title: Display color
docs.text:
primvars:displayColor is a standard UsdGeom primvar, not a shader parameter namespace. It is appropriate for simple unlit markers, debug geometry, and assets that must render without a material network. It is not a generic place to put shader inputs.

Route markers are a good example: their unvisited color is authored in primvars:displayColor and primvars:displayOpacity, and the generic route_follow policy changes the visited state through the transient view layer.

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text:
Failure Result Shader source missing Material rejected, RuntimeDiagnostics error No fragment entry point Material rejected, stage contract error Parameter name not in schema Dropped with a warning at pack time Binding targets a non-material prim Admission rejected Malformed authored literal Typed edit rejected before authoring Unsupported texture format Asset load fails

The renderer never repairs a malformed material by guessing. An authored Rhai policy can observe the diagnostic and choose a replacement; that choice is visible policy, not a renderer fallback.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Use one Material per appearance, not one per prim.
  • Prefer sourceAsset over inline shader text.
  • Declare every parameter in the WESL Material block; do not rely on undeclared uniforms.
  • Bind physics friction through material:binding:physics.
  • Keep display color for markers, not for material parameters.
  • Treat a rejected material as an authoring error, not as a reason to add a fallback.

Continue with Addresses and assets, which explains where the referenced files live.

docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
LunCoSim projects standard UsdPhysics schemas onto the Avian physics engine. There is no LunCoSim-only body object and no parallel physics scene. A prim either carries the standard schemas the adapter understands, or it remains visual geometry.

The projection is intentionally narrow. Avian is a rigid-body engine; it does not implement reduced-coordinate articulations, general USD collections, or skinned deformation. The adapter advertises the schemas it can realize and rejects the ones it cannot. Authoring a schema that does nothing is treated as a defect, not as harmless metadata.

docs.title: Bodies, colliders, and mass
docs.text:
A movable part generally has four pieces:

Purpose Schema Notes Make the prim a dynamic body PhysicsRigidBodyAPI Mass and inertia come from PhysicsMassAPI or from colliders Give it a collision surface PhysicsCollisionAPI plus a UsdGeom shape The shape is cooked into an Avian collider Set mass properties PhysicsMassAPI Explicit mass, center of mass, diagonal inertia, and principal axes Attach it to another body A Physics*Joint prim Being a child in the hierarchy is not an attachment

A minimal dynamic cube:

def Cube "Crate" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["PhysicsRigidBodyAPI", "PhysicsCollisionAPI", "PhysicsMassAPI"]
)
{
    double size = 0.5
    double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 1.2, 0)
    uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]

    float physics:mass = 12.0
    point3f physics:centerOfMass = (0, 0, 0)
    float3 physics:diagonalInertia = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)
    quatf physics:principalAxes = (1, 0, 0, 0)
}

If physics:mass is omitted, the adapter uses the collider's density and volume. If the mass is authored, it must be positive and finite; the native reciprocal and the rotated inverse inertia tensor must also be valid. A failure raises a typed diagnostic and holds physics rather than admitting a body with a degenerate tensor.

docs.title: Collider geometry
docs.text:
Primitive colliders keep their authored dimensions and axis. A finite UsdGeomPlane has no invented thickness: its width and length map onto the schema-defined perpendicular axes before the surface is rotated onto the authored normal. Mesh colliders support none, convexHull, and convexDecomposition; unsupported approximation modes reject instead of substituting a different shape.

UsdGeomNurbsPatch is not directly a mesh collider. The generic PlanNurbsCollisionProxy query and nurbs.rhai authoring tool derive an invisible, source-linked UsdGeomMesh through the same geometry cook used by Avian. Projection re-cooks deterministically and rejects stale proxy data.

docs.title: Joints
docs.text:
All USD-authored joints are translated by lunco-usd-avian from standard UsdPhysics joint prims. Endpoints are physics:body0 and physics:body1 relationships; anchors are physics:localPos0 and physics:localPos1.

USD prim Avian joint Notes PhysicsRevoluteJoint RevoluteJoint 1-DOF hinge; angle (rad), angular_velocity (rad/s), reaction torque (N m) PhysicsPrismaticJoint PrismaticJoint 1-DOF slider; displacement (m), velocity (m/s), reaction force (N) PhysicsFixedJoint FixedJoint Rigid weld; no co-simulation port PhysicsSphericalJoint SphericalJoint Ball joint; cone limits map to swing, lower and upper limits to twist PhysicsDistanceJoint DistanceJoint Tether within [minDistance, maxDistance]; no co-simulation port PhysicsD6Joint / PhysicsJoint Reduced per-DOF joint Per-DOF PhysicsLimitAPI; genuinely multi-DOF warns

Only revolute and prismatic joints expose co-simulation ports. angle and displacement are bidirectional: the input side commands the native motor target, and the output side measures the solved coordinate. The rate and reaction ports are outputs only.

A revolute or prismatic joint can carry a UsdPhysicsDriveAPI:

def PhysicsRevoluteJoint "Shoulder"
{
    rel physics:body0 = </Rover/Chassis>
    rel physics:body1 = </Rover/Arm>
    point3f physics:localPos0 = (0.3, 0.2, 0)
    point3f physics:localPos1 = (0, 0, 0)
    uniform token physics:axis = "Y"

    float drive:angular:physics:targetPosition = 30.0
    float drive:angular:physics:targetVelocity = 0.0
    float drive:angular:physics:maxForce = 40.0
}

physics:targetPosition enables the motor at load, so an Omniverse-authored mechanism seeks its setpoint with no wire. A co-simulation wire on the joint's angle or displacement port overrides the target per tick.

D6 joints are reduced to the matching primitive when only one DOF remains free. A genuinely multi-DOF joint warns rather than pretending to be exact.

docs.title: Seating and readiness
docs.text:
Joints are seated after the initial body poses are validated and are installed disabled. PhysicsJointPrepared keeps their measurements available while body readiness prevents solver-island admission. Activation waits for real Avian body nodes and removes only the owner's temporary disable.

Seating preserves world, static, and kinematic endpoint authority. A declared Mobility::Dynamic endpoint is treated as movable even while initial admission holds its native body kinematic. The owner moves endpoint 1 when eligible, otherwise endpoint 0 with reversed frames and signed slider bounds.

The complete seated pose and velocity are validated before publication. Incompatible prescribed endpoints, incompatible hinge axes, and coincident distance anchors that require positive separation report physics-joint-seating-invalid, appear in Recent Events, and hold physics without constructing a constraint. Compatible all-static definitions remain native-disabled because they have no solver island.

docs.title: Gravity
docs.text:
lunco-usd-avian owns standard PhysicsScene gravity admission and live refresh. Magnitude converts from stage units per second squared to metres per second squared; direction converts from stage axes to canonical axes.

Omitted or finite negative magnitude selects standard Earth gravity. An omitted or zero direction selects stage down. Malformed, non-finite, or out-of-range values, and conflicting scenes in one physical world, report usd-physics-gravity-invalid with the offending prim, property, and value. The previous valid environment remains intact.

A celestial body takeover retains its Gravity::Surface model while the refreshed PhysicsScene facts remain available for diagnostics.

docs.title: Collision filtering
docs.text:
Two mechanisms exist, and only one is automatic.

Jointed pairs are filtered by Avian: every joint built by the loader carries JointCollisionDisabled, so a body never collides with the body it is jointed to. That covers parent and child and stops there.

Everything else is authored, through PhysicsFilteredPairsAPI:

def Cube "Pad" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["PhysicsCollisionAPI", "PhysicsFilteredPairsAPI"]
)
{
    rel physics:filteredPairs = </Lander/Hull>
}

Filtering is symmetric: one opinion is the whole pair. A body endpoint filters every attached collider; a collider endpoint filters only that authored surface. Resolution runs in PhysicsSystems::Prepare, ahead of the narrow phase, because Avian's broad phase skips any pair already in the contact graph. A filter applied later does not remove an existing contact.

Group-versus-group filtering uses PhysicsCollisionGroup:

def PhysicsCollisionGroup "Wheels"
{
    prepend rel collection:colliders:includes = </Rover/Wheels>
    prepend rel physics:filteredGroups = </Scene/Groups/Chassis>
}

Membership is a UsdCollectionAPI with the standard expandPrims rule. physics:mergeGroup lets groups in different layers share one bit. physics:invertFilteredGroups makes the listed groups the only ones the group collides with, read literally. Ungrouped bodies keep colliding: groups take bits from 1 up, never bit 0 and never the trigger layer.

Nothing is inferred beyond joint adjacency. There is no "a vehicle does not collide with itself" rule, because vehicle is not a fact the physics knows. A rover on a lander deck is one or two bodies depending on the minute, and an arm should collide with its own base.

docs.title: Wheels
docs.text:
Wheel kind is selected by standard USD authoring, not by a LunCo-specific token. Every wheel prim applies PhysxVehicleWheelAPI. If any PhysicsRevoluteJoint in the stage names the wheel through physics:body1, the wheel is realized as a physical wheel: an Avian RigidBody, a Collider, the authored joint, and the generic Modelica/engine shaft boundary. Otherwise it is realized as a raycast wheel: WheelRaycast, RayCaster, and entity splitting.

Raycast wheels need identity rotation so the ray casts straight down. The system splits the USD wheel into a physics entity with identity rotation and no mesh, and a visual child with the correct orientation and mesh. Traction is decomposed in the actual contact plane, so a leaning single-track vehicle gets correct lateral grip.

Physical wheel geometry is independent of its shaft axis. Analytic axial primitives use the USD axis basis because their native meshes and colliders use local +Y; an authored mesh already contains its local orientation.

The heading axis is lunco:wheel:headingAxis (wheel-local double3, required). A raked motorcycle fork can author (0, 0.91, 0.42). The final heading is an authored output, not a vehicle-type rule in Rust.

docs.title: Sensors and observations
docs.text:
The engine exposes Avian's native rigid-body facts directly: position, linear velocity, quaternion, angular velocity, mass and inertia, and collider contact. Those ports are not semantic flight sensors. They exist because the physical component exists.

A mounted single ray applies LunCoRaycastAPI. Rust performs the Avian spatial query and publishes raw distance, validity, hit position, hit normal, and sample time. It also publishes the effective ray origin and direction in the rigid body's local frame, composed from the sensor's authored transform hierarchy. A miss remains invalid; it is never converted to ideal altitude or another fallback.

IMU, altimeter, attitude estimator, and touchdown logic are ordinary Modelica programs. USD authors their connections to the raw Avian ports and environment probe outputs. Adding a new conversion changes a Modelica asset and its USD topology, not a Rust sensor registry.

docs.title: Supported schema boundaries
docs.text:
Schema Status Reason PhysicsArticulationRootAPI Authored, deliberately inert Avian has no reduced-coordinate articulation UsdGeomPointInstancer Composed reader and visual projection Animated arrays and arbitrary prototype subtrees fail visibly instanceable = true Not read Every spawned copy is a full prim tree UsdCollectionAPI Read only where PhysicsCollisionGroup applies it Membership resolution is group-specific UsdGeomSubset Not read No per-face material or collider use case in the fleet proxyPrim Not read purpose covers the proxy-sibling case extentsHint Not read extent itself is read UsdSkel Not read No skinned geometry in the fleet

The rule for adding a row is simple: if an asset authors it and the engine ignores it, it belongs in this table or the authoring should be deleted. Silence is the failure mode in both directions.
